RESUMO
A Transformação Digital Healthcare (HCDT) refere -se à integração de tecnologias digitais
aplicadas tanto para os cuidados clínicos quanto aos processos administrativos nas operações
de saúde. Essa transformação busca a personalização em tempo real dos serviços para pacientes
e profissionais, facilitando a transição para um ambiente centrado no paciente. A literatura sobre
HCDT tem demonstrado quais tecnologias digitais são adotadas e onde podem ser aplicadas.
Além disso, estudos empíricos têm identificado associações positivas entre a adoção dessas
tecnologias e a melhoria tanto nas melhorias dos pacientes quanto da eficiência operacional dos
sistemas de saúde. No entanto, a HCDT tem sido majoritariamente abordada sob uma
perspectiva tecnocêntrica, onde o foco recai predominantemente sobre a identificação das
tecnologias em si e suas aplicações, enquanto a estruturação organizacional que antecede a
implementação da HCDT tem sido negligenciada. Por outro lado, o sucesso da transformação
digital nas organizações depende de uma estrutura organizacional sólida, que leve em
consideração diferentes elementos organizacionais p ara apoiar o processo de implementação.
Diante disso, esta tese tem como objetivo geral propor uma estrutura organizacional que integre
estratégias digitais, recursos digitais, tecnologias digitais e os microfundamentos d e rotinas
operacionais – compreendidos como as interações entre indivíduos, estruturas hierárquicas e
processos – para a implementação da HCDT . O estudo adotou uma abordagem mista,
combinando métodos qualitativos e quantitativos, organizada em três artigos. Na vertente
qualitativa, correspondente ao Artigo 1, foram analisados três estudos de caso em hospitais com
diferentes tipos de propriedade, utilizando o framework TOE (Technology –Organization–
Environment). Para isso, realizou -se a triangulação de múltiplas fontes de dados, incl uindo
entrevistas semiestruturadas, observação participante e análise documental. Os dados
qualitativos foram analisados utilizando uma abordagem de codificação indutiva, partindo de
conceitos de primeira ordem centrados no informante para temas teóricos de segunda ordem e
dimensões agregadas . Os resultados revelam três configurações possíveis para estruturar
organizacionalmente a HCDT, considerando as estratégias e diferentes modelos de gestão dos
recursos digitais , cuja escolha depende do modelo de negócio da organização . Na vertente
quantitativa, correspondente ao Artigo 2, a tese apresenta um estudo survey conduzido com 303
hospitais no Brasil. Os dados foram analisados por meio de técnicas de Análise Fatorial
Exploratória e Confirmatória, regressõ es hierárquicas por Mínimos Quadrados Ordinários
(OLS) e análises de mediação e moderação para o teste das hipóteses . Os resultados indicam
que há uma associação positiva entre o alinhamento da estratégia digital e os recursos digitais

(seja gerenciados interna ou externa mente) na implementação de tecnologias que apoiam os
profissionais nos serviços de saúde , analisad as sob uma perspectiva social da visão
sociotécnica. No entanto, não foram encontradas evidências significativas dessa associação no
caso da a doção de tecnologias voltadas para a automação de processos , analisadas sob uma
perspectiva técnica. Além disso, os resultados indicaram que a inserção em uma rede de atores
da área da saúde, geograficamente próxima, modera positivamente a relação entre a estratégia
digital e os recursos digitais externos, mas não os recursos internos. Adicionalmente, também
vertente qualitativa, um estudo de caso qualitativo , correspondente ao Artigo 3, foi realizado
para explorar como a HCDT molda os microfundamentos de rotinas operacionais. Para tanto,
foram mobilizadas múltiplas fontes de evidência, incluindo entrevistas semiestruturadas,
observação participante e análise de documentos institucionais . Os resultados indicam que a
HCDT pode emergir a partir das interações entre os microfundamentos organizacionais, nas
quais o conhecimento, as experiências e os processos de tentativa e erro vivenciados pelos
profissionais de saúde orientam o alinhamento entre estratégias, recursos e tecnologias digitais.
Além disso, os achados evidenciam que a gestão da HCDT não precisa ocorrer exclusivamente
de forma top -down, como tradicionalmente observado, podendo também ser impulsionada a
partir do nível operacional. Finalmente, uma estrutura organizacional é apresentada como
principal p roduto resultante dos achados dos três artigos. Esta tese demonstra que a
implementação da HCDT requer, de fato, uma estrutura organizacional que considere as
estratégias digitais, a gestão dos recursos digitais e dos microfundamentos antecipadamente a
implementação de tecnologias digitais . Sua principal contribuição é fornecer evidências
empíricas que auxiliem sistemas de saúde a estabelecerem uma estruturação organizacional
sólida para a implementação do HCDT, considerando não apenas aspectos técnicos, mas
também ambientais, sociais e organizacionais.

Palavras Chaves: Transformação Digital, Healthcare, Estruturação Organizacional.

ABSTRACT
Healthcare Digital Transformation (HCDT) refers to the integration of digital technologies
applied to both clinical care and administrative processes in healthcare operations. This
transformation aims to enable real -time personalization of services for pat ients and
professionals, facilitating the transition to a patient -centered environment. The literature on
HCDT has demonstrated which digital technologies are adopted and where they can be applied.
Moreover, empirical studies have identified positive associations between the adoption of these
technologies and improvements in both patient outcomes and the operational efficiency of
healthcare systems. However, HCDT has predominantly been approached from a technocentric
perspective, focusing mainly on identifying the technology itself and its applications, while the
organizational structuring that precedes HCDT implementation has been neglected. On the
other hand, the success of digital transformation in organizations depends on a solid
organizational structure that considers different organizational elements to support the
implementation process. Considering this, the general objective of this thesis is to propose an
organizational structure that integrates digital strategies, digital resource, digital technologies,
and the microfoundations of operating routines —understood as the interactions among
individuals, hierarchical structures, and processes —for the implementation of HCDT . The
study adopted a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative and quantitative methods, and
was structured into three articles. The qualitative stream, corresponding to Article 1, analyzed
three case studies of hospitals with different ownership types using the Technology –
Organization–Environment (TOE) framework. Multiple data sourc es were triangulated,
including semi -structured interviews, participant observation, and document analysis. The
qualitative data were analyzed using an inductive coding approach, moving from first -order
informant-centric concepts to second-order theoretical themes and aggregate dimensions . The
findings reveal three possible configurations for the organizational structuring of HCDT,
considering digital strategies and different models of digital resource management, with the
choice of configuration depending on the organization’s business mo del. The quantitative
stream, corresponding to Article 2, presents a survey study conducted with 303 hospitals in
Brazil. The data were analyzed using Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis,
hierarchical Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regressions, and mediation and moderation analyses
to test the proposed hypotheses. The results indicate a positive association between the
alignment of digital strategy and digital resources (whether managed internally or externally)
and the implementation of technologies that support healthcare workers, as analyzed from the

social perspective of the sociotechnical view. However, no significant evidence of this
association was found for the adoption of technologies aimed at process automation, analyzed
from a technical per spective. Additionally, the findings indicate that embeddedness in a
geographically proximate healthcare network positively moderates the relationship between
digital strategy and external digital resources, but not internal ones. Additionally, within the
qualitative stream, a qualitative case study corresponding to Article 3 was conducted to explore
how HCDT influences the microfoundations of operating routines. Multiple sources of
evidence were mobilized, including semi-structured interviews, participant observation, and the
analysis of institutional documents. The results indicate that HCDT can emerge from
interactions among organizational microfoundations, in which healthcare professionals’
knowledge, experiences, and trial -and-error learning processes g uide the alignment between
strategies, digital resources, and digital technologies. Moreover, the findings demonstrate that
HCDT management does not need to occur exclusively in a top-down manner, as traditionally
observed, but can also be driven from the operational level. Finally, an organizational structure
is presented as the main product resulting from the findings of the three articles. Overall, this
thesis demonstrates that the implementation of HCDT requires an organizational structure that
anticipates the definition of digital strategies, the management of digital resources, and the
configuration of microfoundations prior to the implementation of digital technologies. Its main
contribution lies in providing empirical evidence to support healthcare s ystems in establishing
robust organizational structuring for HCDT implementation, considering not only technical
aspects but also environmental, social and organizational aspects.

Keywords: Digital Transformation, Healthcare, Organizational Structuring.

1. INTRODUCTION
The demands for improvements in healthcare systems have grown significantly in recent
decades, requiring new perspectives for delivering healthcare ( Deloitte, 2020). This issue has
become more relevant due to increasing life expectancy and the aging population (WHO, 2019),
reinforcing the need for the development of disruptive approaches (Wang et al., 2018; Kraus et
al., 2021). In this context, digital technologies have played a key role in healthcare systems by
breaking paradigms in management and medical care (Ford et al., 2017; Marbouh et al., 2023).
Since the 1960s, emerging technologies have traditionally been integrated into medical
treatments and administr ative processes in healthcare settings ( Baytechit, 2018). However, it
was only after the 1990s, with the advancements of the Internet, that the importance of digital
technologies was significantly boosted, giving rise to the terms "e -health" and "smart hea lth"
(Aceto et al., 2018).
With the advent of the Industry 4.0 movement, healthcare systems have advanced
toward the modernization of operations and the implementation of smart, connected medical
care ( Tortorella et al., 2020a). This revolution in healthc are is commonly referred to as
Healthcare 4.0 ( Thuemmler & Bai, 2017; Kumari et al., 2018) or Healthcare Digital
Transformation (HCDT) (Kraus et al., 2021). HCDT represents a digital transformation process
in healthcare environments, adapting the principles and applications of Industry 4.0 to the sector
(Thuemmeler & Bai, 2017). This transformation occurs through the incorporation of advanced
technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), cloud computing, big data & analytics,
artificial intel ligence, wearable devices, telemedicine, collaborative robots, augmented and
virtual reality, electronic health records, blockchain, among others, applied to both
administrative processes and patient care (Tortorella et al., 2022a; Saha et al., 2022; Raimo et
al., 2023; Saha & Rathore, 2024 ). This enables the real -time personalization of services for
patients and professionals, facilitating the transition to a patient -centered environment, which
is the focus of Healthcare 4.0 (Alloghani et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Tortorella et al., 2022a).
Studies in the field of HCDT have identified positive associations between the adoption
of digital technologies and improvements in performance, both in terms of patient care ( e.g.,
Wani & Malhotra , 2018; Queenan et al., 2019; Mukherjee & Sinha , 2020 ) and operational
performance (e.g., Devaraj et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020; Tushe
et al., 2025). However, although there is an understanding in the literature about HCDT, when
it comes to its structuring, the role of organizational management that influences digitalization

19


is often overlooked (Kraus et al., 2021). This occurs because most studies h ave emphasized a
technocentric view, focusing on identifying technology and its application (Tortorella et al.,
2020a; Tortorella et al., 2022a; Bardhan et al., 2025). In contrast, the organizational structuring,
which determines how digital transformation should occur, is not addressed with the necessary
depth (Mauro et al., 2024; Bendoly et al., 2025).
In this context, it is essential to understand how to organizationally structure to facilitate
the adoption of digital technologies (Kraus et al., 2021; Verhoef et al., 2021; Oludapo et al.,
2024). Digital transformation should not focus solely on technical aspects (technology), but
also consider other intrinsic organizational factors, such as organizational , social (human
factors) and environmental aspects (Marcon et al., 2022; Marcon et al., 2025). Otherwise, the
adoption of technologies may be unsuccessful (Zimmer et al., 2023), and barriers may arise that
hinder the digitalization journey, especially in complex environm ents such as the healthcare
sector (Tortorella et al., 2021; Iyanna et al., 2022; Mauro et al., 2024).
Organizational structuring for digital transformation refers to the process of planning,
defining, and designing a structure that includes key organizational elements aimed at
facilitating the introduction and integration of digital technologies (Kraus et al., 2021; Verhoef
et al., 2021). Among these organizational elements, digital strategies, digital resources, digital
technologies, and microfoundations of operating routines stand out (Chanias et al., 2019;
Roscoe et al., 2019; Verhoef et al., 2021). This is because HCDT is neither purely technological
nor purely strategic, but rather a complex sociotechnical process that only materializes when
these four elements are aligned and integrated. These four elements are interdependent: digital
strategy guides which technologies should be adopted; digital resources determine whether the
strategy is feasible; digital technologies generate value only when embedded in daily work
practices; and microfoundations, in turn, feed back into the strategy through organizational
learning arising from interactions with these technologies.
More specifically, digital strategy guides the objectives of digital transformation and
establishes organizational priorities; without strategic clarity, the adoption of technologies tends
to be fragmented, reactive, and technocentric (Chanias et al., 2020). Resources—also referred
to as digital resources —represent the organizational means that enable the operationalization
of the strategy and generally constitute prerequisites for digital transformation. These resources
are often scarce or distributed across different actors, which makes their management
particularly relevant (Verhoef et al., 2021). They include, for example, technical resources such

20


as hardware, software, and technological infrastructure that support digital technologies, as well
as financial investments, among others. They also encompass social resources, such as human
resources (e.g., information technology teams), accumulated knowledge, information assets,
and digital culture. Such resource s can be managed through different strategies: they may be
developed internally by the organization itself (in -house), acquired from external partners
(outsourcing), or governed through hybrid models that combine both approaches (Franco et al.,
2024).
Digital technologies, in turn, constitute the most visible facet of digital transformation.
They refer to computing-based tools and systems that use digital data for various purposes, such
as task execution, information processing, and facilitating communi cation across areas and
departments. These technologies materialize the strategy and depend on digital resources for
their implementation; however, they generate value only when effectively integrated into work
processes and practices. A purely technocentr ic perspective tends to overlook the fact that
digital transformation does not automatically reshape organizations but instead requires its
incorporation into the organizational and social context (Bendoly et al., 2025). In this regard, it
becomes essential to consider operating routines, as it is within these routines that healthcare
professionals interact with digital technologies in their daily patient care. Conceptually,
operating routines refer to the execution of known procedures aimed at generating value for the
organization, which can be modified through the adoption of digital technologies ( Roscoe et
al., 2019). These routines are composed of microfoundations, which relate to the effects of
interactions among individuals, structures, and processes, influencing outcomes at the macro -
organizational level. The development, combination, and implementation of operating routines
form the basis of operational capabilities that, over time, become consolidated within the
organization (Roscoe et al., 2019).
Organizational structuring aims to align these four elements (strategy, resources, digital
technologies and operating routines) within an organizational structure so that they function
harmoniously, moving from a macro management perspective to a micro-operational
perspective. Models derived from well-established theories in literature, such as the Resource-
Based View (RBV) (Barney, 1991), Sociotechnical Dynamics (Marcon et al., 2022) , and the
Microfoundations of Operating Routines (Felin et al., 2012) , for example, may serve as
pathways for this structuring. However, each model presents particularities and some
limitations. For example, the RBV does not thoroughly explain how resources can be
orchestrated (Sirmon et al., 2007) ; soc iotechnical dynamics tend not to comprehensively

21


address other aspects, such as organizational and environmental elements (Marcon et al., 2022);
and the microfoundations have been scarcely explored within the healthcare context (Roscoe et
al., 2019) . Therefore, although these models can be considered a relevant theoretical
background, they require critical analysis and potential reformulation when applied to the
context of HCDT, particularly because healthcare is recognized as a complex system composed
of multiple interrelated and interacting elements.
Other studies in literature have proposed organizational structur ing models for digital
transformation. Verhoef et al. (2021) presents three stages of digital transformation:
digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation. The study identifies and delineates
growth strategies for digital firms, as well as the assets, resources, and capabilities required for
a successful digital transformation. The authors postulate that digital transformation requires
specific organizational structures and entails implications for the performance metrics used to
assess outcomes. H owever, the study does not address the different possible governance
arrangements and strategies for these organizational structures, nor does it examine the specific
role of external partners in digital transformation.
Kraus et al. (2021) developed an or ganizational model explaining how different forms
of technology implementation in healthcare can generate operational efficiency gains
associated with HCDT. The model encompasses five interconnected dimensions: operational
efficiency, patient -centered appr oaches, organizational factors and managerial implications,
workforce practices, and socioeconomic aspects. However, it does not specify the
organizational resources required, the strategies for managing these resources, or how the
workforce can systematically contribute to achieving HCDT. Chaudhuri et al. (2023) proposed
a framework of resources and capabilities required for co-creation in implementing 3D printing
services in healthcare. However, although the model addresses technical, organizational, and
environmental aspects with support from external partners, it focuses on a single technology
rather than the broader scope of HCDT. Moreover, it does not consider how resources should
be managed or which strategies may be adopted across different healthcare system settings.
Technological and organizational maturity models have also been proposed in the
literature, such as the Digital Readiness Assessment Maturity (DREAMY) model developed by
De Carolis et al. (2025), which provides a framework for assessing firms’ digital maturity,
identifying strengths and weaknesses, and guiding their transition toward Industry 4.0 and 5.0.
Nevertheless, this model primarily focuses on maturity assessment and does not specify in detail

22


the strategies, resources, or organiz ational changes required for digital transformation,
particularly when applied to sectors beyond manufacturing.
Tortorella et al. (2022a) proposed a model comprising four digital technology packages
focused on healthcare supply chains, diagnosis, treatment, and patient monitoring. Nonetheless,
the model adopts a predominantly technocentric perspective, emphasizing which technologies
can be used and how they can be applied, while overlooking the organizational elements that
support their implementation. Mishra and Sharma (2022) developed the Digital Transformation
Evaluation Model (DTEM), which uses three dimensions —convergence, maturity, and
adoption—to assess telehealth providers. The results of its application suggest that DTEM is an
effective tool for an alyzing these providers and identifying areas for improvement.
Nevertheless, although the model was applied in empirical cases, the study highlights a lack of
standardization in the telehealth field, emphasizing the need for organizations to revisit and
better structure their organizational arrangements to support telemedicine implementation.
However, it can be observed that, among the organizational structur ing or digital
transformation maturity models cited, both present limitations in that they fail to p rovide a
holistic and integrated approach encompassing digital strategies, digital resources,
technologies, and the microfoundations of operating routines. Moreover, they do not explore
how these elements can be aligned and examined from technological, org anizational,
environmental, and social perspectives, which reveals an opportunity to investigate how such
structuring can be carried out to support the broad implementation of technologies.
Studies have emphasized the need to organizationally structure HC DT and to identify
high-impact digital technologies, as well as the factors that hinder, constrain, or influence its
implementation, particularly considering the dimensions technology, organizational and
environmental (Mauro et al., 2024; Duus et al., 2026). In addition, Ahmadi et al. (2018), Mauro
et al. (2024) and Mao et al. (202 4) highlight the importance of considering inter - and intra-
organizational factors for the implementation of digital transformation — or even HCDT —
from a sociotechnical perspective (Kronlid et al., 2024; Green et al., 2026). Kraus et al. (2021)
argue that improvements in the quality of medical care are directly linked to digital
transformation and require organizational structures to support it. Therefore, we decided to
study the organizational structuring of HCDT and propose an organizational structure based on
the four main elements previously mentioned: strategies, resource management, digital

23


technologies, and changes in operating routines, which will be explored throu ghout the three
articles of this thesis.
Based on these considerations, the following research question is proposed: How can
healthcare organizations be organizationally structured to implement Healthcare Digital
Transformation?

1.1 DISSERTATION TOPIC AND OBJECTIVES
The present study focuses on Operations and Technology Management. The general
objective of this dissertation is to propose an organizational structure that integrates strategies,
resources, digital technologies, and the microfoundations of oper ating routines for the
implementation of HCDT.
To achieve this goal, the following specific objectives were proposed:
(i) To propose the main strategies for managing digital resources aimed at the adoption
and development of HCDT.
(ii) To analyze the effects of aligning digital strategy with digital resources, as well as the
moderating effect of network embeddedness, to support the implementation of digital
technology packages.
(iii) To identify how HCDT shapes the interaction effects among the microfoundations of
operating routines and create new healthcare digital operating routines.

Through this proposal, the aim is to develop an organizational understanding that can
assist healthcare managers and decision-makers in implementing HCDT in healthcare systems.
The goal is to make medical operations and care more efficient, improving outcomes for both
patients and professionals, as well as operational performance.

1.2 JUSTIFICATION OF THE RESEARCH PROBLEM
This thesis is justified based on identified theoretical and practical gaps. Regarding
theoretical aspects, it is significant because HCDT represents a new paradigm in the healthcare
field, bringing forth various issues to be researched. Although the topic has garnered interest

24


from researchers worldwide, leading to an increase in academic studies, there are still gaps in
understanding how to manage and develop healthcare systems (Kraus et al., 2021; Tortorella et
al., 2022a; 2022b; Mauro et al., 2024). Specifically, this study addresses the management of the
adoption of digital technologies that support the principle of digital transformation to achieve
the concept of Healthcare 4.0.
HCDT is seen as a strategic approach by organizations seeking a multileve l
transformation that goes beyond basic technological advancements. This includes changes in
the medical model, shifting toward personalized services where the focus is not only on treating
diseases but also on preventive healthcare for patients, as well as transformations in the routines
of healthcare professionals. For this reason, HCDT is widely investigated, with various
solutions proposed to analyze in detail the new technologies that fall within its scope. However,
the concept of HCDT is still conside red complex to implement, primarily due to the intrinsic
nature of healthcare systems, which involve different areas and departments with non -
standardized processes and high uncertainties (Iyanna et al., 2022 ; Bendoly et al., 2025 ).
Additionally, unlike manufacturing, where products can be reworked, in healthcare, the poor
implementation of digital technologies can result in the loss of patients' lives. Most studies in
the literature involving HCDT focus only on the technocentric v iew with a patient -centered
approach (e.g., Tortorella et al., 2022a; Raimo et al., 2023). However, for HCDT to be achieved,
organizational structuring is necessary, ensuring that organizational and social elements are
engaged with digitalization. In this sense, several authors argue that there is a need to structure
HCDT to support decision-making regarding the implementation of technologies as a gateway
and management tool for digitalization (e.g., Kraus et al., 2021; Iyanna et al., 2022; Dal Mas et
al., 2023; Marbouh et al., 2023; Mauro et al., 2024).
From a practical perspective, although numerous studies claim that the implementation
of digital technologies promotes improvements for both operations and patients, this paradigm
still seems distant from the reality of many healthcare organizations ( Tortorella et al., 2020b).
The HCDT journey requires significant organizational effort on the part of healthcare systems
(Dal Mas et al., 2023; Mauro et al., 2024). This may occur because healthcare systems often
lack sufficient knowledge about which elements to consider and which paths to follow to
organizationally structure HCDT ( Kraus et al., 2021). Another possibility is that healthcare
organizations underestimate digital transformation, lacking clarity on pos sible strategies,
considering it a costly process with difficulties in accessing the necessary digital resources to
manage it and understanding how it changes operations ( Iyanna et al., 2022). Therefore,

25


understanding the role of organizationally structuri ng HCDT, as proposed in this thesis, aims
to reduce these conflicts and assist managers in advancing the digitalization of operations and
patient care.

1.3 STUDY DESIGN
This section provides a comprehensive overview of the methodologies and research
approaches used to achieve the general and specific objectives within the thesis theme.
1.3.1. Research method
This thesis adopts a research method based on the development of three sequential
scientific articles, which are articulated to propose an organizational structure for HCDT. These
articles employ qualitative and quantitative methods in a complementary manner to achieve the
research objectives; therefore, the thesis can be classified as a mixed -methods study (Dalfovo
et al., 2008). Figure 1 presents the research methodology.
The research began with a literature review of the main scientific articles on HCDT. For
this purpose, three search criteria were adopted. First, studies published after 2011 correspond
to the emergence of the Industry 4.0 concept; second, articles published in top -tier journals
ranked ABS 3 or 4; and third, journals in the field of technology and operations management,
as this thesis is situated within this research domain. The results of this literature review are
presented in the Appendix of chapter 2 corresponding to Article 1. Subsequently, based on this
review, Article 1 was developed as a qualitative study, employing a multiple case study
approach and the use of semi-structured interviews.
Building on the insights derived from Article 1, Article 2 was developed as a
quantitative study aimed at extending and validating the findings of the first article. In this
second article, statistical analyses of primary data collected through a survey.
Articles 1 and 2 focused on the macro and meso levels of h ealthcare organizations and
revealed a gap in understanding at the micro-organizational level. Article 3 was developed with
the objective of completing the analysis across the different organizational levels. In this third
article, a qualitative approach through a case study was also employed to finalize the analysis.
Finally, drawing on the integrated findings of the three articles, an organizational structure for
the implementation of HCDT is developed and presented, which is discussed in the final chapter
of the dissertation.

26




Figure 1. Research methodology

The research approach for Article 1 can be classified as exploratory, as it aims to analyze
and deepen the understanding of the relationship between the technological, organizational, and
environmental contexts for structuring the management of digital resources for HCDT, based
on a multiple case study (Marconi and Lakatos, 2010). The exploratory approach allows for the
analysis of a research problem whose mechanisms are not yet fully understood and require
further investigation to implement Healthcare 4.0. Additionally, it examines existing
knowledge and empirical reality ( Gil, 2008). Therefore, this article adopts an inductive
approach and uses three different cases to achieve its objective.
On the other hand, for Article 2, a deductive and descriptive approach is employed, as
it starts from a theoretical proposition about empirically studied relationships to provide insights
into how organizational aspects (the alignmen t between digital strategy and digital resources
and the role of network embeddedness ) contribute to the adoption levels of Healthcare 4.0.
Subsequently, hypotheses are formulated and tested using statistical tools. This article relies on
primary quantitative data collected through questionaries to achieve its objective.
Finally, like Article 1, the research approach of Article 3 can also be classified as
exploratory, as it seeks to analyze and deepen the understanding of how HCDT, as a
sociotechnical system, shapes microfoundations — involving the interaction effects between
individuals, s tructures, and processes — in hospitals because of HCDT. This process may
enable the emergence of new digital operating routines (Roscoe et al., 2019), which we aim to
demystify through a case study in the healthcare sector. Therefore, this article also adopts an
inductive approach.

27


However, by employing a mixed-methods approach and a combination of inductive and
deductive reasoning, this thesis aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of
organizational structuring in HCDT, with the goal of contributing to theoretical development
and offering practical insights for healthcare operations management.
1.3.2. Research Design
The research method developed in this thesis follows the theory -building approach
proposed by Van de Ven (2007). According to this theory, the process involves the interaction
between theory and practice to generate conceptual models. Achieving this requires the
following four key stages: problem definition, theory construction, development of an
explanatory model, and proposition of solutions based on the findings (Van de Ven, 2007). The
problem definition was addressed in the introduction section, while the remaining stages are
described in the subsequent chapters.
This thesis aims to bridge the research gap by analyzing its implications and enhancing
the understanding of organizational structuring for HCDT. Therefore, the study is conducted in
three principal phases (Figure 1) , presented in three scientific articles , each with a specific
objective that contributes to achieving the overall goal. Figure 2 illustrates the conceptual
models developed throughout the research phases, while Table 1 provides an overview,
including research questions, objectives, and methods.
Phase 1 aims to explore and understand how hospitals with different ownership
structures organize themselves to manage digital resources for HCDT, using multiple case
studies and in-depth interviews. The studies were conducted in three large hospitals loc ated in
Southern Brazil: Grupo Hospitalar Conceição, Hospital Mãe de Deus, and Hospital de Clínicas
de Porto Alegre (HCPA), representing, respectively, public, private, and teaching and research
management models. To achieve this, a framework is considered (Model 1 in Figure 2), which
evaluates three configurations of digital resource management across three organizational
dimensions for technological innovation: technological, organizational, and environmental.
Building on the insights from Phase 1, Phase 2 aims to understand, through a
quantitative study conducted in Brazilian hospitals with different ownership structures (public,
private, and teaching/research hospitals), the dynamics of aligning digital strategy with digital
resources (whether managed internally or externally) as an organizational approach to
implementing digital technologies as a sociotechnical system. This implementation is analyzed
in two key applications: process automation (smart operations, technical aspect) and support

28


for healthcare workers (smart working, social aspect) (Model 2 in Figure 2). The study is
conducted using primary data collected through a survey carried out by the National
Association of Private Hospitals, Fundação Dom Cabr al, and the Organizational Engineering
Group (NEO-UFRGS).
Finally, based on the findings from Phase 2, it became evident that a detailed micro -
level analysis of the organization was necessary, as this is where digital technologies are
operationalized and integrated into the organizational structuring for HCDT. In this context,
Phase 3 aims to explore, through a qualitative case study, how HCDT as a sociotechnical system
shapes the microfoundations of operati ng routines. To achieve this, a framework is adopted
(Model 3 in Figure 2), which examines how digital strat egy, digital resources and digital
technologies influences the interaction effects of microfoundations —individuals, hierarchical
structures, and processes —potentially leading to the creation of new healthcare digital
operating routines. This case study was conducted at the HCPA, recognized as one of the
leading public hospitals in Latin America. The institution holds several national and
international certifications and is widely acknowledged for its initiatives in digital
transformation. This study was made possible through a collaborative research project carried
out between 2024 and 2025 involving the NEO-UFRGS and HCPA.
In this way, it is possible to develop a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon
of organizational structuring in HCDT.

Article 1 - “Structuring resources in healthcare digital transformation: a comparison across
public, private and research hospitals”.
The objective of this phase was to identify how different hospital ownership structures
handle various digital resource management strategies to adopt and develop HCDT.
Additionally, it aimed to identify the key factors that lead these hospitals to follow specific

31


management models. This phase had a qualitative approach, with eight interviews conducted
with managers involved in healthcare digital t ransformation. The analyzed hospitals are
implementing new digital technologies to digitize operations and medical care. As key findings,
the article presents three different organizational structuring strategy frameworks for resource
management in HCDT. T hese frameworks vary according to the hospital ownership structure
and illustrate the dynamic involvement of the technological, organizational, and environmental
contexts in fostering innovation.
Article 2 – “Aligning digital strategy and resources to create Healthcare 4.0 organizations:
implications for smart operations and smart working”.
The objective of this phase was to validate the previous stage and identify the existence
of an association between the alignment of digital strategy and digital re sources for the
implementation of Healthcare 4.0 as a sociotechnical system , and the role of the network
embeddedness in the alignment. This phase had a quantitative approach, conducted through a
survey involving 303 hospitals engaged in digital transformation. The key findings indicate that
a strong healthcare digital strategy positively influences the adoption of technologies aimed at
process automation (smart operations, technical aspect) and support for workers' activities
(smart working, social aspect). On the other hand, digital resources, whether managed internally
or acquired externally for Healthcare 4.0, positively mediate only the relationship between
digital strategy and smart working. However, no evidence was found to support the same
mediation effect for smart operations . Additionally, healthcare network embeddedness
positively moderates only the relationship between healthcare digital strategy and external
digital resources. In contrast, there was no evidence that network embeddedness enhances the
alignment between strategy and internal digital resources.
Article 3 – “Healthcare digital transformation as a sociotechnical system: shaping the
interactions between individuals, structures, and processes”.
In this final phase, the objective is to deepen the understanding developed in the
previous study by analyzing how HCDT, as a sociotechnical system, shapes the
microfoundations of operating routines. These microfoundations involve interactions among
individuals, hierarchical structures (based on consensus or authority), and processes (rigid or
flexible), which are understood as the social aspect of the organization. This analysis is
particularly relevant because it focuses on the micro -organizational level, where digital
technologies are effectively operationalized and where direct interactions between people and

32


technologies take place. As a result, the consolidation of these interactions over time leads to
the emergence of new operating routines. This phase adopts a qualitative approach, involving
semi-structured interviews, focus groups with healthcare professionals, participant observation
across different areas and departments, as well as the analysis of documents and reports from a
public teaching and research hospital in southern Brazil that is in the process of implementing
digital technologies in its operations. The findings indicate that interactions among individuals,
structures, and processes enable a customized digital transformation aligned with professionals’
needs, as they mobilize their knowledge and experience to define the alignment between
strategies, resources, and digital technologies. Moreover, the results show that HCDT does not
necessarily emerge in a top-down manner, as traditionally observed in healthcare systems, but
can also arise from the micro level of the organization, contributing to the reduction of potential
human–machine conflicts and enabling the emergence of new healthcare digital operating
routines.

1.4 STUDY DEFINITION
For the development of this research, the practical context of Brazil was considered, as
developing countries often face difficulties and barriers in the process of organizational digital
transformation, particularly in the healthcare sector and even more so within public healthcare
systems. Thus, the structured implementation of HCDT in hospitals can contribute to
accelerating national development, fostering digital transformation, and improving population
health outcomes. However, developed countries present di fferent institutional contexts and
levels of technological maturity. Therefore, the territorial scope represents a limitation of this
study. To partially mitigate this limitation, a sandwich PhD research period lasting nine months
was conducted at the Mass achusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), at the Industrial
Performance Center (MIT-IPC), in the United States. This experience enabled technical visits
to leading hospitals and interviews with managers, thereby complementing the understanding
of the organizational structuring of HCDT in a developed-country context.
Moreover, this study does not aim to conduct comparisons between developed and
developing countries, but rather to analyze environmental, organizational, technological, and
social aspects — including elements such as digital strategies, digital resources, digital
technologies, and operating routines — that can be applied in practice to structure HCDT across
different economic contexts. Nevertheless, it is acknowledged that hospitals may require

33


different management models over time, because of institutional, technological, and
organizational changes.

1.5 STRUCTURE OF THE DISSERTATION
This thesis proposal is structured into five chapters. The first chapter provides a detailed
discussion of the research problem, objectives, and corresponding justifications. Additionally,
it outlines the research methodology, study structure, and scope. Building on this foundation,
Chapters 2, 3 and 4 present the core articles developed thus far, each addressing o ne of the
study’s specific objectives, as illustrated in Figure 2. These chapters offer a comprehensive
analysis of the articles, including their methodologies, key findings, and theoretical and
practical contributions, thereby enriching our understanding of the phenomenon.
The fifth and final chapter of this thesis proposal is dedicated to the conclusions and
contributions of this dissertation. It focuses on the overall objective of the research, providing
an integrative overview of the findings identified in the previous chapters. In this way, the fifth
chapter contributes to the cohesion and advancement of the research, bringing to light
opportunities that follow from this thesis.

2. STRUCTURING RESOURCES IN HEALTHCARE DIGITAL
TRANSFORMATION: A COMPARISON ACROSS PUBLIC,
PRIVATE AND RESEARCH HOSPITALS
Lucas Miguel Alencar de Morais Correia, Alejandro Germán Frank

This article has been published in Technovation (JCR: 10,9)
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.technovation.2025.103320

Abstract
Healthcare organizations have witnessed major advances in the use of digital technologies. While prior
research on Healthcare Digital Transformation (HCDT) has focused on the impact of digital
technologies on healthcare operations, understanding how to manage the digital resources necessary for
HCDT implementation remains unclear. We address this gap by examining how hospitals manage digital
resources to foster HCDT. Drawing on the Technological, Organizational, and Environmental (TOE)
framework and supported by the Resource -Based View, Relational View, and hybrid governance
theories, we conduct a qualitative multi-case study of three large hospitals: one public, one private, and
one research-oriented. Data collection includes semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and on-
site visits. Our study reveals that HCDT strategies are shaped by hospital business models and financial
structures, leading to distinct digital resource governance approaches: internal development in public
hospitals, external sourcing in private hospitals, and hybrid governance in research hospitals. We
propose a typology aligned with strategic logics and clarify how each model engages with digital
ecosystems—ranging from internal coordination to external orchestration and collaborative innovation.
Despite their dominant strategies, all hospitals maintain complementary resource bases to ensure
resilience. Additionally, we contribute to theory by conceptualizing hybrid governance in research
hospitals as a funding -driven mechanism, offering a new rationale for its adoption. These insights
advance the understanding of digital resource management in healthcare and provide practical guidance
for designing context-sensitive HCDT strategies.

Keywords: Healthcare; Digital transformation; Digital technologies; Digital resources; Business
models.

2.1 INTRODUCTION
Digital Transformation (DT) has been developed in different sectors, including
healthcare organizations. In this case, it is defined as Healthcare Digital Transformation
(HCDT) (Kraus et al., 2021) or Healthcare 4.0 (H4.0) (Thuemmler & Bai, 2017). HCDT
considers several digital technologies that have been applied and integrated to enhance and
modernize healthcare systems, aiming for efficiency in processes and patient well-being (Raimo
et al., 2023). HCDT has been analyzed from the organizational perspectiv e with the use of

39


digital technologies to support the administration of hospitals (Cerchione et al., 2023) and from
the operational perspective to execute routines like surgeries, emergencies, and related activities
(Beane, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
Several studies have considered the specificities of technologies that can support HCDT
(e.g., Tortorella et al., 2021; Tortorella et al., 2022a). These studies are devoted to discussing
how digital technologies impact healthcare operations. However, a crucial factor for the
implementation and success of HCDT in healthcare environments, and which is usually
dismissed, is the management of organizational resources related to digital technologies,
referred to as digital resources (Piccoli et al., 2024; Verhoef et al., 2021). The view of digital
resources considers what hospitals must have to effectively implement digital technologies and
transform their process from analog to digital (Elia et al., 2021). It acknowledges that digit al
transformation is not just about technology but also about how different resources are combined
to digitalize the processes (Chaudhuri et al., 2024; Franco et al., 2024). In this sense, hospitals
can adopt different strategies to manage the required dig ital resources for developing the
HCDT.
Hospitals may internally develop digital resources to enhance healthcare and
administrative processes through HCDT (Chaudhuri et al., 2023). This strategy aims to create
digital capabilities within the hospital that can be used to improve operational efficiency and
enhance healthcare professionals' skills (Oliveira et al., 2024). On the other hand, hospitals can
focus on outsourcing HCDT to external partners, forming a digital healthcare ecosystem.
Outsourcing can be used to mitigate risks and reduce costs (Ayala et al., 2017). This strategy
enables the formation of external alliances for acquiring knowledge and technology from
partners with expertise in digital solutions (Dalenogare et al., 2023). The disadvantage of this
approach is that it can create a high dependence on a potential strategic area that hospitals can
develop (Dalenogare et al., 2022). Both strategies require different management profiles for
HCDT, as organizational structures have peculiarities refle cting different forms of associated
benefits and risks (Franco et al., 2024). A third way is that hospitals can also manage digital
resources by developing hybrid governance to achieve better operational performance (Mura et
al., 2021). This strategy aims to find a balance in managing and gaining synergies between
exploitation and exploration activities (March, 1991). For example, the complementarity
between internal and external digital resources helps the hospital exploit internal and external
digital resources (Franco et al., 2024). However, in such cases, the cost of maintaining two

40


different forms of digital resources can become higher, and other benefits must be higher to
justify this combination (Parmigiani, 2007).
Although there is a wide understandi ng of resource management to gain a competitive
advantage, how to manage such resources for implementing HCDT remains diffuse (Kraus et
al., 2021). The literature has addressed digital resource management to comprehend the co -
creation process with specific technologies (Chaudhuri et al., 2023). There is also an
understanding regarding developing capabilities from digital resources for HCDT (Oliveira et
al., 2024). Nonetheless, the literature lacks evidence on how these three different resource
strategies are adopted and their modus operandi in HCDT. In this sense, it is still necessary to
understand how internal, external, and hybrid governance digital resource management
strategies are organizationally structured in hospitals to promote HCDT. Therefore, we propose
the following research question: How do hospitals deal with digital resource management
strategies to adopt and develop HCDT?
This study aims to define configurations of digital resource management for HCDT in
hospitals and analyze how they are imp lemented. To this aim, we employ the Technological,
Organizational, and Environmental (TOE) framework to analyze these three forms of digital
resource management in hospitals from a holistic perspective. First, we propose a theoretical
framework for models of digital resource management, considering three governance strategies
(Franco et al., 2024): strategies focused on developing internal digital resources, strategies
focused on developing external digital resources, and strategies oriented towards a combination
of both through hybrid governance. We utilize the TOE framework in a qualitative multi -case
study research approach to evaluate these strategies. The research is based on semi -structured
interviews guided by an open script conducted in three hospit als of different natures: private,
public, and research-oriented. We combine the Resource-Based View (RBV), Relational View
(RV), and hybrid governance to investigate how digital resource management is developed in
hospitals to implement HCDT.
Our research clarifies how digital resource management in hospitals is structured by
describing how hospitals manage and utilize digital resources for HCDT. Our final frameworks
reveal that the management of digital resources for HCDT in hospitals varies according to the
business profile of each institution. Each analyzed hospital presents a distinct business model
that defines how digital resources are accessed to promote technological innovations. We also
demonstrate how the elements of the TOE framework support the structuring of digital resource

41


management for HCDT. In the case of the public hospital, it adopts a complete internal model,
focusing on developing its own resources. This strategy is driven by the hospital's reliance on
bidding processes for acquiring d igital resources, which often require greater financial
investments and significantly extend the timeline for digital transformation with high
transactional costs to deal with technology providers. On the other hand, private hospitals opt
to acquire external resources, outsourcing technologies, and services through direct contracts
while establishing intra -organizational relationships to create an innovative ecosystem in the
healthcare sector based on their power structure that allows them to manage contrac ts with
technology providers based on performance. Meanwhile, the research hospital prioritizes a
hybrid governance model, combining the development of internal resources with an emphasis
on internal R&D with external collaborations. In this case, they aim to create internal platforms
to follow external dissemination and expansion through research collaboration. The TOE
framework clarifies how hospitals organize their digital resources in each model described.
Therefore, we contribute to the theory by clari fying these different digital resource structures,
while our findings also help managers build their digitalization strategies in HCDT.
Our study offers several novel contributions to the understanding of HCDT. First, we
demonstrate that HCDT strategies ar e highly sensitive to the hospital's business model,
challenging the prevailing notion of a uniform digital transformation path in healthcare. Second,
we introduce a typology of digital resource governance —internal, external, and hybrid—each
aligned with s pecific strategic logics (resource -based view, relational view, and hybrid
governance, respectively) and shaped by the institution's financial structure and objectives.
Third, our findings uncover distinct models of ecosystem orchestration: while private hospitals
act as central coordinators of external providers, research hospitals engage in horizontal,
collaborative innovation networks, and public hospitals rely on internal coordination
mechanisms. Fourth, we show that despite the predominance of a specific governance model in
each hospital type, all organizations must maintain complementary resource bases to ensure
resilience and continuity, thereby advancing a more nuanced understanding of the internal –
external resource dynamic. Finally, we contribute to the conceptual development of hybrid
governance by highlighting its use in research hospitals as a funding -driven strategy—distinct
from the balancing rationale commonly found in the literature —thereby revealing a new
explanatory mechanism for its adoption in digital transformation initiatives.
The next sections of this paper are structured as follows. In Section 2, we provide the
theoretical background for managing digital transformation in healthcare organizations, as well

42


as an analytical framework for understanding strategies for managing digital resources for
HCDT. Section 3 presents the research method, discussing our qualitative approach to studying
hospital cases. Section 4 presents the results, followed by Section 5, which presents the
discussion and conclusion.

2.2 THEORETICAL BACKGROUD
2.2.1 Managing DT in healthcare organizations
HCDT is a term used in literature to describe the adoption and implementation of digital
technologies in the healthcare sector (Kraus et al., 2021). It involves technologies such as the
Internet of Things (IoT), cloud computing, Big Data & Analytics (Wang et al., 2018), and
Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Dicuonzo et al., 2023). This enables real -time data collection,
storage, and analysis of healthcare operations, facilitating the transition to a patient -centered
environment (Tortorella et al., 2022). Other digital technologies have been used to support
healthcare operations, including wearable devices and augmented/virtual reality and simulation
(Raimo et al., 2023), telemedicine (Baudier et al., 2023), 3D printing (Chaudhuri et al., 2023),
and collaborative robots (Beane, 2019). Furthermore, ERPs, electronic health records (Raimo
et al., 2023), and blockchain (Massaro, 2023) are also used in the HCDT journey, specifically
in administrative processes and the supply chain.
Managing HCDT involves dealing with various digital resources. First, technological
infrastructure is a key resource to enable the use of digital technologies, including the hardware,
software, and network structure necessary to run digital solutions (Verhoef et al., 2021).
Second, human capital is also an important part of digital resources, which includes having a
team of skilled workers to implement digital technologies, IT workers, and programmers
(Fernandez-Vidal et al., 2022). The models for managing digital resources for HCDT in
hospitals can follow different approaches (Parmigiani, 2007): developing digital resources
internally (in-house), managing the acquisition of external digital resources (outsourcing), and
adopting a hybrid governance that combines both. These three perspectives are grounded on
the competence view of the firms, which considers the choice of whom will be the most
competent part for executing an activity (Ketokivi & Mahoney, 2020).
The internal digital resources’ perspective is rooted in the Resource -Based View
(RBV), which examines the relationship between internal characteristics and performance,
arguing that organizations can define, own, and accumulate specific resources and capabilities

43


that are valuable, rare, and more difficult to imitate or substitute (Barney , 1991). These
resources can be tangible, such as assets, technologies, people, and infrastructure, or intangible,
such as “know-how” and reputation. The main characteristic of this approach is the total control
that the organization has over its internal resources (Parmigiani, 2007). This is because the
organization owns its resources, allowing it to determine how it will enhance operations
(Barney, 1991). Additionally, it contributes to building knowledge and information through the
internal development o f digital resources and enhancing the capabilities and skills of human
resources, qualifying healthcare professionals (Dal Mas et al., 2023; Piccoli et al., 2024).
However, in this governance model, exploring physical resources involves using complex
social resources, such as social relationships, culture, traditions, etc. This social complexity is
a challenge in managing internal digital resources because it involves intangible elements that
the organization often cannot control (Elia et al., 2021). Furthe rmore, it may entail high costs
to maintain the operation of resources (e.g., IT teams to develop digital technologies), which
can be a limiting factor for the hospital.
The external digital resources' perspective is rooted in the Relational View (RV), which
argues that organizations can find digital resources and/or create value through their
relationship with external parties (Dyer & Singh, 1998). The RV suggests that inter -
organizational alliances allow organizations to overcome their limits and access c ritical
routines, resources, and capabilities to become more innovative. Two main characteristics
encompassing this approach are digital resource outsourcing and forming an ecosystem
(Kamalaldin et al., 2020). Resource outsourcing is when an organization h ires services or
acquires goods from suppliers instead of conducting these activities internally (Gambal et al.,
2022). Furthermore, it involves the transfer of specific responsibilities and functions, enabling
the organization to focus on its core strateg ic activities, mitigating risks, and reducing costs
(Kamalaldin et al., 2020). On the other hand, forming a partner ecosystem involves creating an
arena of external alliances in which organizations engage in activities and share a common goal
(Aloini et al ., 2023; Schiavone et al., 2021). The innovation literature defines ecosystems as
“the alignment structure of the multilateral set of partners that need to interact in order for a
focal value proposition to materialize ” (Adner, 2017, p. 40). This implies that, unlike simple
outsourcing, when ecosystems are considered part of external digital resources, the alignment
of external actors comes to the forefront. Such alignment may occur either around a network of
companies with diverse technological capabilities or through technology platforms that
integrate these actors (Gawer and Cusumano, 2014). The digital transformation literature has

44


emphasized the role of digital ecosystems in delivering integrated solutions for compa nies,
recognizing that no single firm can independently manage the full spectrum of technical skills
and competencies required (Benitez et al., 2020). Accordingly, an orchestrated combination of
capabilities offers a more effective approach (Dalenogare et al., 2023). Studies on healthcare
ecosystems have highlighted several benefits of creating an external network of actors,
including the increase of knowledge transfer flow (Secundo et al., 2019) and value co-creation
(Schiavone et al., 2021). However, alth ough this approach offers benefits such as resource
savings and a focus on essential competencies, it also poses challenges, including the
organization's high dependence on external suppliers, hold-up problems, quality control issues,
and potential opportunities in the strategic area of internal development that may go unrealized
(Gambal et al., 2022).
A third option for managing digital resources is combining internal and external
resources into a single management approach (Franco et al., 2024). This approach is called the
'hybrid governance' structure (Blomqvist et al., 2002). Hybrid governance refers to adopting a
strategy that involves both elements of internal and external governance, aiming to optimize
efficiency in specific organizational processes (Blomqvist et al., 2002; Parmigiani, 2007). It has
the advantage of considering the best of both approaches, as it keeps the strategic digital
resources internally but also takes advantage of using strategic partnerships with specialized
partners (Franco et al., 2024). For example, in situations where internal hospital teams are
unable to develop or operationalize a specific digital technology, the hospital may seek to
complement it by acquiring it externally or obtaining knowledge and information from partners
but avoiding total dependence on external suppliers (Parmigiani, 2007; Steinhauser et al., 2020).
Through hybrid governance, hospitals can also adapt to constantly changing conditions, as
evidenced by the COVID-19 pandemic and transaction-specific factors such as uncertainty and
asset specificity (Blomqvist et al., 2002).
However, although this approach may offer various benefits, such as increased
flexibility and exploration of external incentives, it also presents some complexities compared
to the other two approaches (Franco et al., 2024). First, the cost of maintaining two different
forms of digital resources can become higher for the organization because unexpected expenses
and silent risks may arise due to the hospital's ability to deal, for examp le, with contracts and
bidding processes (Parmigiani, 2007). Second, there is the complexity of its organization,
dealing with ambivalences, especially regarding responsibilities when an issue arises
concerning the resources and redundancies of information in the DT process (Blomqvist et al.,

45


2002). Therefore, as demonstrated by Franco et al. (2024), hybrid governance can be a viable
structure, but under specific conditions when the complexity of combining internal and external
resources will pay off with t he value gained through the performance benefits that can be
achieved.

2.2.2 Research opportunities on digital resource management for HCDT – The TOE
framework
Digital transformation literature has previously addressed the role of developing specific
resources devoted to the digitalization process in companies. From an organizational
perspective, acquiring or developing digital resources has been seen as a strate gic imperative
of digital transformation that is deeply connected with the firm's organizational structure and
digital strategy (Verhoef et al., 2021). Moreover, digital transformation has been analyzed from
the strategic alignment perspective between the necessary resources and the environmental
demands (Liu et al., 2011). It has been an important factor in defining the technological aspects
of the readiness for digital transformation (Chwiłkowska-Kubala et al., 2023). Other streams of
the literature have recently addressed the challenging issue of how to manage such digital
resources, including the internal development of organizatio nal digital resources, the external
acquisition through collaboration (Dalenogare et al., 2023), and the development of a hybrid
structure (Franco et al., 2024). Franco et al. (2024) were the first to investigate these three
options for resource developmen t (internal, external, and hybrid) in digital transformation,
considering the supply chain context.
However, when addressing the HCDT literature, little is known about this issue. As
shown in Appendix A, most existing studies on HCDT focus on the implications of technology
implementation in healthcare. In other words, they primarily examine how digital technologies
influence and affect the healthcare domain but not what is required to implement these
technologies. Few studies have considered a resource -based view of HCDT (Chaudhuri et al.,
2023; Dicuonzo et al., 2023; Mauro et al., 2024) or a relational view of HCDT (Malik et al.,
2023). These studies mainly use such theoretical perspectives to explore the adoption or impact
of digital technologies in healt hcare systems. However, none specifically address how these
two types of resources are implemented or the necessary structures for doing so. Furthermore,
the HCDT literature lacks discussion on hybrid governance models, which have been explored
in the supp ly chain management literature (Franco et al., 2024). Such models could offer

46


valuable insights, as digital technologies often operate in complex environments that demand
higher expertise in technology implementation.
We aim to address this gap regarding t he necessary resources for HCDT, first from a
holistic perspective that integrates technological aspects with organizational and environmental
factors. Additionally, we seek to explore the various approaches to resource development,
considering, as Franco et al. (2024) suggest, that resource management may have different
approaches for its development —whether through internal, external, or hybrid digital resource
management models. Following this reasoning, the Technology -Organization-Environment
(TOE) framework (Rocco DePietro et al., 1990) can provide insight into the structure of HCDT
in different organizational dimensions (Kinkel et al., 2022; Tabim et al., 2021). The TOE
framework explains that adopting and implementing technological innovations is influenced by
three elements of the organization's context: technological context, organizational context, and
environmental context (Rocco DePietro et al., 1990). The technological context includes
technologies relevant to an organization's business ecosyste m, including current internal
practices and equipment within the organization, as well as the set of technologies available
externally to the organization. The organizational context refers to various descriptive
characteristics of how the organization works in terms of design, processes, and responsibilities.
Additionally, informal relationships between employees, hierarchy, and the procedures they
operate include decision -making and internal communication. Finally, the environmental
context is where an organization conducts its business – i.e., the industry context, competitors,
and its relationship with other institutions, such as customers, suppliers, and third parties
(Marcon et al., 2025).
Integrating the different factors of the TOE framework allows for understanding the
broader scenario in which the healthcare organization operates and the influence of these factors
on the adoption of new technologies, as well as in supporting the management of digital
resources to deal with HCDT (Rocco DePietro et a l., 1990). We use the TOE dimensions to
define the types of digital resources to be managed according to the analytical framework
presented in Figure 3. The analytical framework is based on three digital resource management
strategies described in Section 2.1, which are related to the three dimensions of the TOE
framework. We aim to understand how these strategies are organized and operate within the
TOE dimensions for HCDT. In this sense, the conceptual framework guides us to discover if
and how the elemen ts of RBV, RV, and hybrid governance are present, supporting managing
digital resources for HCDT.

2.3 RESEARCH METHOD
The literature on HCDT has predominantly focused on the application and impact of
digital technologies, yet limited attention has been given to how digital resources are managed
throughout the transformation process. This study seeks to deepen the understanding of how
hospitals deve lop and structure these resources, offering insights into the “how” of digital
resource configuration. Given this objective, a qualitative research approach is particularly
appropriate, as it allows for in-depth exploration of complex processes and serves as a starting
point for advancing this research agenda. However, such an approach entails limitations in
terms of generalizability, which should be addressed in future studies using complementary
research methods for validation (Voss et al., 2002).
In this context, we adopted a multiple -case study design, guided by the analytical
framework presented in Figure 3. This method is especially effective for investigating
contemporary and emerging phenomena within real -world settings (Barratt et al., 2011).
Following the recommendations of Ketokivi and Choi (2014), we employed a priori
theorization to structure our research framework. While the findings derived from this study
are not statistically generalizable – as would be possible through quantitative methods – the
case study approach offers a valuable foundation for generating novel insights and developing
theoretical contributions (Yin, 2012). Accordingly, our investigation enables a nuanced analysis
of distinct strategies for managing digital resources in HCD T, thereby contributing to the
advancement of theory in this field. The operationalization of our qualitative research followed

48


the methodological guidelines proposed by Voss et al. (2002), as detailed in the subsequent
subsections.

2.3.1 Selection criteria for the cases and the participants
A selection criteria was established to ensure that the cases selected were relevant to the
study's purpose. First, the hospitals had to be from the same region, as we wanted to control the
socio-economic context. Different regions or nationalities can present significant differences in
the management practices adopted between organizations, especially in the healthcare field
(Kaplan et al., 2010). Second, hospitals must have reasonable experience implementing HCDT
(Tortorella et al., 2020) and integrating technological resources into their administrative
processes and patient healthcare. As a third and final criterion, the study included organizations
with different management structures: public, private, and resear ch hospitals. This diversity
allows for identifying the scope of the effects of HCDT on the operational performance and
flexibility of healthcare organizations with different organizational structures and capital
expenditure capacities.
The following criteria were established to select the interviewees representing each case.
First, they should work as hospital managers, assuming a leadership role in the organization.
This would ensure they have a broader view of the hospital and its processes, legitimizing their
perceptions (Tortorella et al., 2022). According to Huy (2001), leaders are crucial in
operationalizing radical changes, such as HCDT. Second, the interviewers should have a
minimum experience time, which we set as at least five years of work experi ence. The
interviewees' experience is crucial, as it provides practical knowledge and a deep understanding
of challenges, patterns, and nuances in the operational environment. Finally, the interviewees
should be involved in the HCDT initiatives.
As a result, we selected three large -sized Brazilian hospitals (i.e., with more than 150
inpatient beds – Brazilian Ministry of Health) that have been operating for over forty years: one
public (Hospital A), one private (Hospital B) and one research (Hospital C), s ummarized in
Table 2. We selected for the interviews a variety of representatives as described in Table 2. We
selected representatives leading the HCDT initiatives, which resulted in variations in the
number of interviewees per hospital. Hospital A had only two leaders for this initiative—the IT
manager and the innovation coordinator —who provided all the necessary information. In
contrast, Hospital C has three leaders overseeing the HCDT initiative: the HCDT coordinator,

49


who works closely with the IT coordi nator and the Data Science coordinator. Additionally,
during on -site visits, two other colleagues —one from quality management and a division
chief—became involved after the formal interviews. Their input helped us better understand
the environment, but they are not cited here as they were not the primary HCDT representatives
interviewed during the formal data collection process. Hospital B, on the other hand, was
represented by two technology sector leaders and one business coordinator. In this case, the
hospital includes an administration representative in its HCDT initiative leadership. These
differences in the number of interviewees reflect the distinct ways in which each institution
structures its HCDT activities. Table 2 also provides further details, s uch as the years of the
institution, the number of beds that represent its operating capacity, and details of the

2.3.2 Data collection procedures
Given the nature of multiple case studies like this research, Galletta (2013) suggests
using semi -structured interview techniques as a more appropriate approach because the
researcher can get closer to the interviewees, allowing for the identification and detailed capture
of their behavioral aspects. Online semi -structured interviews were conducted with the
managers of the hospitals ( Table 2) using a video conference platform. The data were stored
from audio and image recordings and later transcribed, providing greater security in storing
interview information. It is important to note that prior contacts and scheduling were made with
the interviewees to ensure data quality and participant comfort.

50


The interviews were conducted between October and November 2023, and coding,
cross-interview analysis, and report verificat ion were completed during the second half of
November 2023. In this sense, the dimensions to develop HCDT (Figure 3) were presented at
the beginning of each interview to establish a common understanding of the research. In
addition, the anonymity of each i nterviewee was guaranteed to have reliable responses. The
interviews were conducted following a semi-structured interview guideline (Appendix B). The
interviews lasted between 60 and 80 minutes and were conducted by at least two researchers.
According to Dubé & Paré (2003), the presence of more than one researcher increases the ability
to process contextual information with a higher level of confidence. The interviews were
recorded and transcribed for analysis and, besides, interviews' notes were taken by t he
researchers. Finally, at the end of the interviews, a summary of the answers provided by the
interviewees was made to confirm the contributions and eliminate scattered comments that were
out of the topic.
Furthermore, we combined the information obtained from the interviews with other data
sources. Voss et al. (2002) and Yin (2012) recommend data triangulation from multiple sources
of evidence, as it allows different data collection methods to contribute to the understanding of
a specific phenomenon and strengthen construct validity (Carter et al., 2014). In this sense, our
data triangulation approach considered three other different sources as a complement to
individual interviews. First, we mapped hospitals' resources and relationships with their
partners. Second, we analyzed documents and information available on the websites of the
hospitals in this study to identify historical, technological, and organizational aspects, as well
as the evolution of HCDT. Third, on -site technical visits were conducted a t the locations,
allowing for the observation of operations and services. We describe in Table 3 the different
sources of data used for the three cases with additional details of the data collection process.
