3. ALIGNING DIGITAL STRATEGY AND RESOURCES TO CREATE
HEALTHCARE 4.0 ORGANIZATIONS: IMPLICATIONS FOR
SMART OPERATIONS AND SMART WORKING
Lucas Miguel Alencar de Morais Correia, Paulo Renato de Sousa, Alejandro Germán Frank

This article has been published in Technological Forecasting & Social Change (JCR: 13,3)
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2025.124339

Abstract
This study investigates the organizational foundations required to implement Healthcare 4.0 (H4.0) by
examining how digital strategy, internal and external digital resources, and network embeddedness
support the development of smart operations and smart working in healthcare organizations. While prior
research has predominantly focused on technology -driven improvements in healthcare processes, less
attention has been given to the sociotechnical integration of people, processes, and technologies,
particularly from a st rategic and managerial perspective. Drawing on a survey of 303 hospitals, we
assessed the role of digital strategy and digital resources in advancing H4.0, conceptualized through the
dual lenses of smart operations (technology for process automation) and s mart working (technology to
support workers). Using hierarchical regression and bootstrapping techniques, we find that digital
strategy positively influences both smart operations and smart working. However, internal and external
digital resources mediate this relationship only in the context of smart working. This indicates that while
process automation relies primarily on strategic clarity, supporting workers requires stronger resource
structures. Additionally, we find that healthcare network embeddedness positively moderates the
relationship between digital strategy and external digital resources, but not internal resources. This
suggests that external collaborations enhance a hospital’s ability to translate strategic intent into
actionable use of external resources, particularly in support of smart working. Our findings contribute
to a deeper understanding of how strategic alignment and network embeddedness shape sociotechnical
systems in healthcare. They offer guidance for managers seeking to design holistic digital transformation
strategies to build H4.0 organizations.

Keywords: Digital Strategy; Digital Resources; Healthcare 4.0; Sociotechnical Systems.

3.1 INTRODUCTION
The digital transformation of healthcare organizations has been characterized by the
application of advanced digital technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cloud Computing,
Big Data, and Artificial Intelligence in medical devices and healthcare infor mation systems
(Kraus et al., 2021), resulting in what is called as ‘Healthcare 4.0’ (H4.0) (Thuemmler & Bai,
2017). The introduction of these technologies enables real -time personalization of patient and
workers care services, facilitating the transition to a patient-centered environment (Wang et al.,
2018). This transformation involves the interaction of people, processes, and digital
technologies, forming micro-foundations of operational capability (Roscoe et al., 2019). In this

86


sense, the concept of H4. 0 considers the interaction of two main dimensions that form a
sociotechnical healthcare system: from the technical side, the use of digital technologies to
automate operational processes is commonly referred to as healthcare smart operations
(Tortorella et al., 2020), while the social side considers the use of digital technologies to support
healthcare worker activities, usually known as healthcare smart working (Klein & Watson -
Manheim, 2021). When H4.0 is conceived to create a balanced sociotechnical system between
workers, organizational processes, and technologies, both smart working and smart operations
need to be developed as part of the healthcare digital transformation strategy (Grover et al.,
2018).
The literature has focused on understanding which digital technologies are used and
how digital transformation can contribute to achieving better performance outcomes in
healthcare systems (Tortorella et al., 2022a; Tortorella et al., 2022b). Overall, this literature has
been predominantly oriented toward the techno-centric view of smart operations. For example,
Dicuonzo et al. (2023) explore how artificial intelligence can support the process of the
healthcare system; Cannavacciuolo et al. (2023) address the organizational changes through the
implementation of telemedicine in healthcare; and Basile et al. (2024) consider the role of big
data analytics to improve the quality of healthcare services. These studies are concerned with
how digital technologies can boost different operational processes. On the o ther hand, an
emerging stream has highlighted the need for integrating people with processes and
technologies, considering that there is a sociotechnical interplay between them (Grover et al.,
2018). For instance, Klinker et al. (2020) investigate the use of augmented reality technologies
to increase healthcare workers' capabilities and Naslund et al. (2019) consider the use of digital
technologies to scale up healthcare through nonspecialist workers. These are a few of the cases
when digital technologies a re considered for smart working in healthcare, bringing a social
perspective to the technological view. However, the literature has missed the consideration of
what is necessary in the context of strategy and organizational design when smart operations
and smart working are in the spotlight of Healthcare 4.0.
When discussing the adoption and use of digital technologies, the influence of strategic
and managerial aspects is often overlooked (Chanias et al., 2019; Verhoef et al., 2021)
particularly in terms of their roles to balance the organizational system from a sociotechnical
perspective. In this context, achieving organizational clarity is essential to support the effective
adoption of digital technologies (Marcon et al., 2022; Marcon et al., 2025). Otherw ise, the
adoption of these technologies may be unsuccessful or limited to isolated implementations
(Zimmer et al., 2023). This organizational support has often been regarded as a matter of

87


establishing a digital strategy and managing digital resources (e.g., technological infrastructure,
people skills, and financial investments for digitalization) within organizations (Verhoef et al.,
2021; Franco et al., 2024). In this context, the vision of strategic alignment between strategy
and resources is essential (Edelman et al., 2005). This is because H4.0 can be supported through
an appropriate digital strategy, backed by suitable resources, and, as a result, can facilitate the
adoption of healthcare smart operations and healthcare smart working concepts. The alignment
between strategy and resources can be further strengthened when an organization is embedded
within a network of external healthcare actors. Such embeddedness facilitates access to critical
knowledge and resources through ongoing interactions (Granove tter, 1985), including those
that support digitalization efforts (Xing et al., 2023). In this context, network embeddedness
represents a key component of the environmental dimension of sociotechnical systems that
underpin digital transformation processes (Marcon et al., 2024).
However, little is known about the way digital strategy, resources and the connection
with the external environment are associated in the implementation of healthcare sociotechnical
systems in the context of digital transformation. It is well known that organizations need to
define strategies for digital transformation (Chanias et al., 2019) and that managing resources
is necessary for the effective implementation of digital solutions (Dalenogare et al., 2023), but
it is not clear the role these organizational elements play in the development of smart operations
and smart working concepts for H4.0. Since smart operations and smart working focus on
different digitalization objects – the first focuses on the process and the latter on peop le – do
organizational aspects like strategy and resources play the same role for both? And are the
outcomes for both different when healthcare organizations are closer to external healthcare
actors that can help with H4.0 development? The literature has n ot yet considered these
organizational elements connected with the implementation of digital technologies for H4.0
regarding smart operations and smart working. Also, it is critical to understand the role and
need of network embeddedness in H4.0, as hospitals are naturally geographically dispersed and
not always close to external related actors. In such cases, the digital -resources alignment may
need a different approach to deal with. Therefore, we propose the following research questions:
What is the role of digital strategy and digital resources – as organizational strategic alignment
– in the development of Healthcare 4.0 sociotechnical dimensions, namely smart healthcare
operations and smart healthcare working? And what is the effect of healthcare netw ork
embeddedness in this context?
To answer these questions, we conducted a quantitative survey involving 303 hospitals.
We consider the main elements of digital strategies in organizations and the development of

88


internal and external digital resources as antecedents of both smart operations (digital
technologies for healthcare processes) and smart working (digital technologies to support
workers). Furthermore, we analyze the moderating role of healthcare network embeddedness
in the strategy -resources relationship. To investigate these relationships, we use hierarchical
regression and bootstrapping techniques. Our results show that a stronger healthcare digital
strategy positively affects the adoption of digital technologies for healthcare smart operations
and healthcare smart working. On the other hand, the development of internal and external
digital resources for H4.0 positively mediates only between digital strategy and smart working
but there is no evidence for the same mediation in smart operations. We argue that this
differentiates the focus between process automation (smart operations) and people support
(smart working) in healthcare organizations. Smart working demands a stronger resource
structure to embrace workers and reduce tensions related to the use of new technologies, but
smart operations is more technical and less dependent on resource management, needing only
a clear strategic focus for its implementation. Additionally, we found that healthcare network
embeddedness positively moderates only t he relationship between healthcare digital strategy
and external digital resources. This indicates that a hospital’s digital strategy is more effectively
oriented toward leveraging external resources when it is more embedded in a network of
external actors, who help clarify how such resources can be accessed and utilized. In contrast,
we found no evidence that network embeddedness enhances the alignment between strategy
and internal digital resources. These findings suggest that supporting smart working thr ough
external digital resources is particularly complex, as it depends not only on the availability of
these resources but also on the hospital’s contextual embeddedness – that is, having the
necessary external connections to shape and operationalize a foc used digital strategy for
external resource use. Therefore, as main contribution, our study provides the theoretical basis
for structuring the organizational aspects of digital transformation in healthcare by defining the
main elements that consolidate a d igital strategy and digital resources in H4.0. Our findings
also contribute to the understanding of how to align the strategy with resources to support the
implementation of digital technologies in sociotechnical healthcare systems. Healthcare
managers can use these findings to understand how to create a holistic system of digital
transformation aiming to build a Healthcare 4.0 organization.

89


3.2 THEORETICAL BACKGROUND
3.2.1 Healthcare 4.0 and the strategic alignment of sociotechnical systems
With the advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, also known as Industry 4.0, new
information and communication technologies (ICTs) have been incorporated into organizations
to digitally transform environments, enabling greater efficiency and flexibility in processes,
services, and products (Liao et al., 2017). Due to its potential, I4.0 has expanded into other
sectors, including healthcare, denoted as Healthcare 4.0 (H4.0) (Tortorella et al., 2022a). H4.0
adapts the principles and applications of Industry 4.0 to the he althcare sector, allowing real -
time personalization of patient care services, professionals, and caregivers, facilitating the
transition to a patient-centered environment (Thuemmler and Bai, 2017).
H4.0 has been predominantly considered from the technical point of view with the
analysis of digital technologies to increase healthcare performance (Tortorella et al., 2022a;
2022b). However, a growing emphasis has been given to the development of sociotechnical
systems in healthcare organizations (Grover et al., 2018). The sociotechnical view is based on
the premise that for an organization or a workplace to achieve its goals, the social and technical
systems of the organization need to be interconnected and treated t ogether (Clegg, 2000). In
this sense, the literature has highlighted that digital transformation involves the integration of
processes, people, and technologies in an interplay of sociotechnical elements (Roscoe et al.,
2019). In such interplay, digital technologies not only modify processes but also the way human
work is performed and how people interact with them to carry out their tasks (Zimmer et al.
2023). Therefore, when H4.0 is considered from the perspective, it can be represented from two
main dimensions of technology application: smart operations and smart working.
Healthcare smart operations considers the use of digital technologies to automate
operational processes of the healthcare system ( Tortorella et al., 2020a; 2020b). The focus of
technology in this dimension is on task execution. It aims to increase the level of interoperability
and efficiency, with more integrated and flexible processes to provide greater value to
healthcare services and improve patient flow, reduci ng the possibility of errors arising from
manual operations (Wang et al., 2018; Basile et al., 2024). For example, healthcare smart
operations consider the use of cloud computing to store data generated by the organization,
mobile applications for automati c communication, as well as the use of enterprise ICTs, such
as ERP, to integrate different departments and internal and external areas (Raimo et al., 2023;
Tortorella et al., 2022b). Additionally, it includes the use of telemedicine to increase the number

90


of remote clinical consultations (Cannavacciuolo et al., 2023), the use of electronic record
systems, such as electronic medical records for patient management, and digital traceability for
patient and medication tracking through RFID, QR codes, or the us e of process simulation to
predict demands and optimize operational processes (Cerchione et al., 2023).
On the other hand, Healthcare smart working considers the use of digital technologies
to support healthcare worker activities. In this sense, it comprises a sociotechnical evolution of
digital technologies and how they are used by healthcare workers. It is based on the concept of
industrial smart working proposed by Frank et al. (2019) and Cagliano et al. (2019). Healthcare
smart working aims to increase ergonomics and productivity through the interplay between the
worker and technology (Dornelles et al., 2022). The concept goes beyond the operational
efficiency of the organization, as it also seeks to improve the well -being, health, and safety of
workers, enabling the enhancement or creation of new capabilities and skills (Klein & Watson-
Manheim, 2021; Oliveira et al., 2024). From a technology perspective, it considers the use of
wireless or biomedical/digital sensors, wearable devices, big data/analytics , artificial
intelligence, augmented or virtual reality, or collaborative robots to assist workers in their tasks
(Wang et al., 2018; Tortorella et al. 2022b; Raimo et al., 2023). These workers include nurses,
doctors, healthcare technicians, and pharmacis ts, who work in a diversity of areas such as
emergency care, outpatient clinics, hospital wards, pharmacies, or operating rooms, dealing
directly with patient care throughout the entire process of diagnosis, treatment, and follow -up
(Tortorella et al. 2022b).
Strategic alignment plays an important role in the design of sociotechnical systems, as
this alignment is related to the organizational structure that supports sociotechnical dimensions
(Marcon et al., 2022). Such alignment has been considered a matter of establishing strategies,
managing resources, and defining the form of how both are combined (Chanias et al., 2019;
Verhoef et al., 2021). In the context of digital transformation, the strategy considers a
combination of ICT and business model goals (Ch anias et al., 2019). The healthcare digital
strategy can rely on digital resources to drive the digitization of organizations (Constantiou &
Kallinikos, 2015; Vial, 2019). Digital resources include hardware, software, network, and data
analytics resources (e.g., code programming or data science), which deal with the collection,
storage, retrieval, sharing, and use of data, as well as financial resources for investments in
basic infrastructure. Furthermore, they include related managerial domains, such as ne w
capabilities, which typically reside in human, informational, or organizational capital, and new
digital skills, both supported by a digital culture (Fernandez -Vidal et al., 2022). The

91


organizational structure can adopt different models to manage these d igital resources,
implemented according to the organization's capacity and ownership. For example, resources
can be developed internally or outsourced to external partners (Parmigiani, 2007; Chaudhuri et
al., 2023). All these elements when combined will co nsolidate a H4.0 organizational system.
Thus, the strategic alignment between digital strategy and resources, and the development of
healthcare smart operations and smart working will define a form of how digital transformation
can be faced in healthcare o rganizations to create a balanced system in the digital context of
organizations.

3.2.2 Network embeddedness theory
The Network Embeddedness Theory (NET) explains that the economic and
organizational activities and decisions of firms are deeply rooted in the social networks in which
they are embedded (Granovetter, 1985). The term embeddedness refers to the extent to whi ch
actors’ actions are embedded in networks of relationships (Granovetter, 1985). These
networks—or influential intermediaries —facilitate faster and more qualified access to
information, resources, and control mechanisms, which become available through the relational
and structural embedding of organizations (Granovetter, 1985; Dahlke et al., 2024; Chen et al.,
2025). Relational embeddedness involves direct ties between actors, considering the frequency
of interaction and reciprocity, which can enhance loya lty and reduce transaction costs.
Structural embeddedness, in turn, goes beyond relational ties by emphasizing that the transfer
of information and/or resources in social networks does not depend solely on direct contacts,
but also on the overall network structure, including indirect connections with actors close to the
organization (Chen et al., 2025). Furthermore, structural embeddedness refers to an actor’s
position and proximity within the network, and how this influences their behavior, access to
information, resources, and power (Granovetter, 1985). In addition to these elements, NET
considers trust to be an essential operational component. Since institutional arrangements alone
are not sufficient to fully prevent opportunistic behavior or fraud, trust among network actors
often allows formal contracts to be replaced, thereby reducing the risks associated with
partnerships (Granovetter, 1985). Therefore, network embeddedness can be a mechanism
through which organizations seek to adapt to or align with the external environment and acquire
essential resources for specific purposes (Gnyawali & Madhavan, 2001).

92


Recent studies in the field of digital transformation, such as Chen et al. (2024), highlight
the role of network embeddedness in enabling digital ca pabilities through technologies aimed
at production customization. Similarly, Chen et al. (2025) demonstrated the contribution of
network embeddedness in supply chains to strengthening operational resilience through
digitalization. In addition, other studies, such as Lyu et al. (2020), identified the positive effects
of network embeddedness on the relationship between open innovation and innovation
radicalness, while Xing et al. (2023) proposed an approach using the TOE framework,
positioning network embedd edness as an environmental -level factor that supports digital
transformation and enhances innovation performance in manufacturing. Dahlke et al. (2024)
also found evidence that the adoption of artificial intelligence is related to three epidemic effect
mechanisms of network embeddedness. Collectively, these studies demonstrate how network
embeddedness can support both digital transformation and organizational performance and
innovation. Therefore, network embeddedness can be seen as an additional external dimension
of sociotechnical systems applied to DT (Xing et al., 2023). This is because, beyond
emphasizing the importance of organizations being embedded in social networks, this
perspective expands the understanding of DT by incorporating the external envi ronment as a
sociotechnical dimension (Marcon et al., 2022; Xing et al., 2023; Marcon et al., 2025).
However, the literature has not yet explored how the degree of network embeddedness can
support digital transformation in the healthcare context, especiall y when viewed as a socio -
technical system.
In this context, the structuring of H4.0 in health systems requires an appropriate
environment to support its implementation, as highlighted by the sociotechnical literature
(Marcon et al., 2022; Xing et al., 2023 ; Marcon et al., 2024), which also emphasizes the
importance of external context and participation in the digitalization process. As noted in the
previous section, from a technical standpoint, this includes the dimension of healthcare smart
operations; from the social perspective, healthcare smart working; and from the organizational
side, the alignment between digital strategy and digital resources. However, it is evident that
the external environment of healthcare systems still needs to be incorporated to fully realize the
concept of a sociotechnical system —integrating social, technical, organizational, and
environmental aspects (Marcon et al., 2025; 2024). In this regard, network embeddedness can
serve as a reliable approach to acting as the environmental dimension of H4.0, as it can facilitate
the alignment between strategy and digital resources by enabling healthcare systems to access

93


essential digital information and resources—through direct or indirect connections with various
network actors—to support the implementation of the smart dimensions of H4.0.

3.3 HYPOTHESES DEVELOPMENT
3.3.1. Healthcare digital strategies and the development of Healthcare 4.0 dimensions
The implementation of digital technologies demands a strategic definition to set goals
and priorities of which technologies should be applied and how they must support processes
and people (Enrique et al., 2023). From an organizational perspective, a digit al strategy needs
to establish digital goals for the organizational processes that will be changed with the support
of digital technologies (Vial, 2019). When a sociotechnical system is aimed to be supported by
digital technologies, the consolidation of this digital environment with clear rules will become
the organizational driver of the digitalization process (Marcon et al., 2022). Without a clear
digitalization strategy, technologies tend to be implemented to solve local problems, but at the
risk of miss ing the big organizational picture that addresses the systemic problems through
digital solutions (Baiyere et al., 2020).
When it comes to H4.0, the development of a digital strategy should be a priority for the
implementation of both healthcare smart operations and smart working. First, smart operations
consider digital technologies applied to healthcare processes, but which processes are there? Of
course, we can refer to the whole healthcare system and its processes, but these are too many
and too comple x to consider ideally a complete automated system. Healthcare is a
sociotechnical organization especially because it is embedded in human -related activities that
are performed based on intensive use of high-skilled knowledge (Beane et al., 2019). Therefore,
it cannot be simply automated – the digital strategy would be the organizational roadmap to
define priorities and needs regarding the technologies that should be implemented to address
processes that are the aim of digitalization (Baptista et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2020). Another
aspect is the competition for resources: a digital strategy creates financial priorities to invest in
digital technologies of the healthcare organization; otherwise, a corporate strategy without
digitalization as a priority will dilute financial resources in many other demands (Piccoli et al.,
2024). Furthermore, it is important to consider that the digital strategy can also have as an aim
the benefit of healthcare workers, especially in healthcare systems where workers' resilience is
necessary and technologies can play an important role in it (Tortorella et al., 2022c). A clear
digital strategy can set workers as a keystone of the sociotechnical healthcare system and define

94


the development of smart working as a priority, as it also happens in industrial contexts (Marcon
et al., 2022). Therefore, when the healthcare digital strategy is positively associated with both
smart operations and smart working, it can be considered a strategic system of the organization
that has a clear vision of creating a sociotechnical balance. We hypothesize this as follows:
H1: The implementation of an organizational digital strategy is positively associated with
higher levels of adoption of healthcare 4.0 technologies
H1a: The implementation of a digital strategy is positively associated with higher levels
of healthcare smart operations (use of technologies to automate healthcare processes)
H1b: The implementation of a digital strategy is positively associated with higher levels
of healthcare smart working (use of technologies to support healthcare workers)

3.3.2. The alignment of healthcare digital strategy and resources and the role of
network embeddedness
Verhoef et al. (2021) describe strategic imperatives of digital transformation,
considering digital resources as an element to be combined with the strategy and the goal of the
digitalization process. This line of research establishes that for a digital transformation strategy
to be developed, it needs to consider digital resources as a central element o f its digital
technology architecture (Piccoli et al., 2024). It means that digital transformation is not just
about defining what to digitalize (goals) and adopting the technologies (as considered in H1).
Instead, a set of organizational digital resources needs to be established to provide support to
the whole sociotechnical system. These digital resources are necessary to act as support for the
digitalization process which tends to be challenging due to several organizational barriers that
need to be over come during the digitalization (Verhoef et al., 2021). In this sense, a strategic
alignment is necessary between the digital strategy and the resources to manage the
digitalization processes (Fischer et al., 2020). Some authors have considered the digital strategy
as a bundle of goals, organizational structure, and resources (Verhoef et al., 2021; Fischer et
al., 2020), but this may be a consequence of a qualitative analysis of how companies establish
the strategy and organizational requirements. We follow a classic stream of information systems
that differentiates between strategy and resources and consider strategy as the antecedent for
the development of the resources (Kearns and Leder, 2000; Yeow et al., 2018). According to
this view, both are independent but interrelated elements of organizational development (Yeow
et al., 2018). Furthermore, these resources, which can comprise a vast type of elements
including financial, human, and infrastructure factors (Verhoef et al., 2021), can be part of the

95


established internal digital transformation or can be acquired from external partners, as a make-
or-buy condition (Parmigiani, 2007). This is more evident in the digital era, as organizations do
not master the whole set of digital resources necessary to develop the digitalization process
(Dalenogare et al., 2023). This is the case of healthcare systems, which are not essentially born-
digital. Instead, healthcare organizations need to set new strategies for the digital transformation
process (Denicolai and Previtali, 2023). Consequently, healthcare organizations will also need
to build and internalize digital resources that are supported by the strategy and that can help to
implement the digitalization goals (Denicolai and Previtali, 2023). Therefore, we establish the
following hypothesis:
H2: The implementation of an organizational digital strategy is positively associated with
higher levels of development of digital resources
H2a: The implementation of a digital strategy is positively associated with higher levels
of internal digital resources
H2b: The implementation of a digital strategy is positively associated with higher levels
of external digital resources

Network embeddedness suggests that the position an organization occupies within a
network influences its access to information and resources (Lin, 2001). This occurs because
such information and resources are transmitted or reinforced through a chain of interconnected
nodes—where each node represents an external actor —and the proximity and degree of
connection among these actors facilitate the receiving organization’s ability to understand its
strategy and focus on resource development (Granovetter, 1985; Mazzola et al., 2015). Network
embeddedness requires organizations to actively locate, process, and in teract with different
actors in the network that are geographically close and can provide the required information
and resources (Dahlke et al., 2024). Geographic proximity refers to the physical distance
between organizations, which can encourage more fre quent interactions and, consequently,
foster the formation of stronger healthcare environments. Being physically and cognitively
close to these sources can facilitate the understanding of the best pathways for digital
transformation, helping to the formula tion of more effective strategies aligned with the
necessary resources for the digitalization of healthcare (Chen et al., 2025).
On the one hand, geographic proximity to external network actors can help an
organization develop an outward-looking perspective, fostering learning from other actors and,
based on that, formulating a digital strategy aimed at strengthening its internal digital resources.

96


This occurs because, by being embedded in a network, the organization has the opportunity to
observe which dig ital resources are being used by other actors —or which are necessary to
support digitalization —and based on this learning, develop and manage such resources
internally (Miroshnychenko et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025). For example, a
healthcare organization may capture knowledge about the development of technological
solutions from another organization, whether public or private, within the same network and
apply that knowledge internally by training its professionals to create an innovati ve and
customized solution (Miroshnychenko et al., 2021). Alternatively, it may establish partnerships
with universities and research institutions to access information and experiences related to
digital transformation.
On the other hand, proximity to external network actors can assist an organization (e.g.,
a hospital) in identifying the most suitable partners for full access to external resources,
enabling effective strategies to obtain those resources (Granovetter, 1985). This is because
network embedded ness demonstrates that an organization can observe the trust levels and
potential shortcomings among its potential suppliers —allowing for better comparisons —
evaluating competitive advantages and exercising greater flexibility in accessing information
and resources (Granovetter, 1985). For example, by occupying a central position in a network,
an organization may gain access to suppliers offering more innovative solutions within its
geographic context (Chen et al., 2025); it may also engage in collaborative environments that
enable mechanisms for knowledge transfer and digital technologies (Lyu et al., 2020; Chen et
al., 2024); or even establish contact with healthcare operators (such as insurers, health plans,
and provider networks), whose regional commercia l demands can drive the development of
new digital healthcare solutions.
Based on these arguments, network embeddedness plays a crucial role in the digital
strategy-resources alignment, as it provides a source of information and resources which is
important to develop the digital transformation of healthcare activities better. Thus, we propose
the following hypothesis:
H3: The level of network embeddedness hospital can have in a healthcare ecosystem will
positively moderate and strength the alignment between digital strategy and resources
H3a: The level of network embeddedness positively moderates the relationship between
digital strategy and internal digital resources
H3b: The level of network embeddedness positively moderates the relationship between
digital strategy and external digital resources

97


3.3.3. Contribution of digital resources for the development of Healthcare 4.0
dimensions
A good strategy -resource alignment should help to develop the organizational
information system for digital transformation (Yeow et al., 2018). Prior research on digital
transformation has defended the need for structuring also digital resources to enhance
technological implementation in the digital transformation process (Liu et al., 2011; Yeow et
al., 2018). In the H4.0 perspective, this means that digital resources, when aligned to the digital
strategy should support the development of the sociotechnical H4.0 system. It is similar to what
was previously argued by Marcon et al. (2022) in industrial systems, where the combination of
organizational strategies and resources (sociotechnical environment) provided the basis for
Industry 4.0 technologies implementation. In this same vein, digital resources should provide
the basis for the development of smart operations and working technol ogies. For instance,
digital resources include the organizational culture and informational structure necessary to
implement digital technologies in processes and change the form such processes are executed
(Fischer et al., 2020; Marcon et al., 2022; Gillani et al., 2024), as proposed for healthcare smart
operations. Also, digital resources include skills and capabilities necessary to support people,
when they need to learn how to use new digital technologies for their task execution, as
considered in healt hcare smart working (Verhoef et al., 2021; Fernanez -Vidal et al., 2022).
Additionally, digital resources can be managed internally and externally, as these are totally
different sources and can require different strategic management approaches to deal with
(Dalenogare et al., 2023). Consequently, they can have different contributions to smart
operations and smart working. External digital resources can consider the orchestration of
knowledge and new skills through collaboration that can change the way business processes are
executed, affecting smart operations. It also can create new mindsets in workers helping to
shape the way technologies are used in healthcare activities (Fischer et al., 2020). On the other
hand, internal digital resources can help consol idate systems legacy and information systems
teams and knowledge that can provide a basis for automating processes through digital
technologies (Liu et al., 2011) and for expanding workers skills to the use of new digital
technologies (Verhoef et al., 2021 ). Consequently, these different arguments point to a
mediating role of healthcare digital internal and external resources in the strategic alignment
for the development of an H4.0 sociotechnical system. We summarize this in the following
hypotheses H4 (for internal resources) and H5 (for external resources):

98


H4: The development of internal healthcare digital resources is positively associated with
higher levels of adoption of healthcare 4.0 technologies
H4a: The development of internal healthcare digital resources is positively associated
with higher levels of healthcare smart operations (use of technologies to automate
healthcare processes)
H4b: The development of internal healthcare digital resources is positively associated
with higher levels of healthcare smart working (use of technologies to support healthcare
workers)
H5: The development of external healthcare digital resources is positively associated with
higher levels of adoption of healthcare 4.0 technologies
H5a: The development of external healthcare digital resources is positively associated
with higher levels of healthcare smart operations (use of technologies to automate
healthcare processes)
H5b: The development of external healthcare digital resources is positively associated

3.4 RESEARCH METHOD
3.4.1 Sampling
We focused our research unit on hospital management. Therefore, our target
respondents are middle and senior-level healthcare leaders (directors, managers, or supervisors)
who deal with healthcare technologies for hospital management. Also, we focused on internal
elements of the hospitals, like the level of development of digital strategies and resources and
the level of adoption of digital technologies. Therefore, our data source was the single
respondent, as secondary data is not available for this research aim and multiple resp ondents
would not be able to respond to issues related to digital transformation, which are usually under
the coordination of technology/operations managers (Frank et al., 2019). This should be less
biased than selecting experts from specific departments to analyze the system (Ketokivi, 2019).
We defined the population for our sample based on the Annual Report on the Hospital Scenario
in Brazil, developed by the Brazilian Hospital Federation (FBH). To mitigate the
socioeconomic effect, we restricted the sam ple of our study to Brazilian hospitals. Although
this criterion may limit the generalization of our findings, it strengthens the internal validity of
our results. The population consists of 7,242 hospitals registered in the database of the National
Registry of Health Establishments (CNES), DataSUS, and the Ministry of Health (MS).
Considering a 5% error and a 90% confidence interval, it was determined that the minimum
sample size needed to research hospitals and achieve national representativeness is 263. From
this population, the initial sample available with the target contacts consisted of 3,823 hospitals
from all regions of Brazil.
Data collection was carried out through three channels. Firstly, the survey was emailed
to as many hospitals as possible id entified in the sample. Secondly, a search for the sampled
hospitals was conducted on the LinkedIn platform. Thirdly, the survey was manually delivered
in printed forms. Three waves of the questionnaire were sent over three months. As a result,
316 initial responses were obtained; after excluding incomplete and duplicate questionnaires,
we obtained 303 considered valid (response rate of 8%) for this research. The final sample size
can be considered representative of Brazilian hospitals, as it exceeds the minimum requirement
of 263 (90% confidence and 5% error), representing the proportions of the population. Table 5
presents the study sample profile.

3.4.2 Survey instrumentation
Our research instrument was developed based on constructs from the literature and
adapted to the specific objectives of our study. The proposed instrument consists of six blocks
of questions (see appendix A): (i) the level of implementation of healthcare digital strategies
(STRATEGY), adapted from Nasiri et al. (2020) and Verhoef et al. (2021); (ii) the level of
ownership of Internal Digital Healthcare Resources (INTERNAL), adapted from Barney (1986,
1991) and Franco et al. (2024); (iii) the level of outsourcing of External Digital Healthcare
Resources (EXTERNAL), adap ted from Dyer and Singh (1998, 2018), Franco et al. (2024);
(iv) the level of healthcare network embeddedness (EMBEDDEDNESS), adapted from Xing et
al. (2023), Chen et al. (2024), Chen et al. (2025); (v) the level of implementation of H4.0 digital
technologies in healthcare management activities, proposed by Frank et al. (2019), Dornelles et
al. (2022), Tortorella et al. (2022a; 2022b) and Deloitte (2020); (vi) information about the
interviewees and their hospitals was collected to determine the demographic profile of the
sample. Respondent information (e.g., role) was used to verify the legitimacy of their opinions
and ensure a broader understanding of the investigated phenomenon. Meanwhile, hospital
information allowed for controlling some contextual charac teristics (e.g., number of beds,
number of employees, hospital age in operation years, and ownership) that may influence the
healthcare digital transformation process (Raimo et al., 2023).
To ensure the feasibility of survey administration, the instrument items were assessed
and pre-tested by fifteen randomly selected experts (three academics and twelve healthcare
practitioners) to ensure the face and content validity of the scale items (Taherdoost, 2016). The
experts recommended minor terminological chang es to enhance the clarity and
comprehensibility of the survey items. The questions considered in this study were measured

101


on a five -point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) for
evaluating blocks (i), (ii), and (iii), and from 1 (never) to 5 (very frequently) to assess the usage
of digital technologies in sub-block (iv).
3.4.3 Constructs definition and validation
H4.0 digital technologies are typically organized into bundles of applications
representing formative constructs (e.g., Tortorella et al., 2022a). We collected the information
regarding the technologies usage through the questionnaire without using predefined bundles,
as they were determined after through the use of Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). We
conducted the EFA using orthogonal Varimax rotation to minimize potential ambiguities in the
distribution of variables (Hair et al., 2018). We selected those factors with eigenvalues >1 (Hair
et al., 2018), representing 67.953% of the total variance in responses, as shown in Table 6. We
also assessed parameters validating the use of EFA for our selected dataset. These parameters
include the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test (which should be > .500), Bartlett's sphericity test
(which should be < .05), the anti -image matrix for M easures of Sampling Adequacy (MSA)
(which should be > .500), and the percentage of explained variance (which should be > 60%).
All our obtained parameters were in line with the suggested thresholds in the literature (KMO
= 0.930; Bartlett < 0.000; MSA ≥ 0.879; % of variance = 67.953%) (Hair et al., 2018).
Analyzing the results of the factor loadings in each component, we labeled the two
digital application bundles based on the composition of technologies and their predominant
focus, following a procedure similar to previous literature (Tortorella et al., 2022b). As a result:
Healthcare Smart Working (WORK) and Healthcare Smart Operations (OPERATIONS). Table
6 also displays Cronbach's alpha coefficients for these constructs obtained from the EFA,
confirming reliability with values exceeding 0.9. Subsequently, we used the factorial scores of
the two main factors obtained through the Thurstone method. More specifically, standardized
scores were used in the subsequent linear regression analysis.

3.4.4 Response bias and common method variance
To mitigate common method variance (CMV), we conducted a pre -test of the
instrument's questions with a randomized subsample drawn from our target population. For this
purpose, we pretested the questionnaire to ensure the clarity of our research instrument (as
explained in Section 3.2). Additionally, we randomized the order of variables and questionnaire
blocks to enhance their reliability and prevent order bias and primacy bias (Podsakoff et al.,
2003). As pointed out by Ketokivi (2019), in surveys involving questionnaires, it is impossible
to eliminate bias in the research. However, we implemented reasonable countermeasures to
address this concern in our study.

104


3.4.5 Data analysis
To test our hypotheses, we conducted a series of hierarchical ordinary least squares
(OLS) regressions. Before the regression analysis, we standardized the variables using a mean-
centering Z-score. We employed a bootstrap approach based on the ‘Process’ macro proposed
by Hayes (2017) to check for indirect mediation e ffects. To test the moderation effects (H3a
and H3b), we standardized both the independent and moderating variables using mean -
centering Z-scores and multiplied the moderator by the independent variable. This allowed us
to create a multiplicative score to assess the interaction effect.
Before focusing on the interpretation of the results, we conducted a series of post hoc
analyses to verify if all the conditions for OLS regression were met. Firstly, we assessed the
normality condition required for OLS regression, employing three strategies based on the
analysis of residual normality: we examined the density plot (histogram), the standardized
normal probability (P -P) plot, and the quantile plot of the variable against the quantiles of a
normal distribution. All these plots indicated a normal distribution of residuals for our OLS
regression analysis. No model rejected the hypothesis of adherence to the normal distribution
of residuals (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test p-value <0.01). Secondly, we checked linearity through
partial regressions for the independent variables. Thirdly, we also assessed the
homoscedasticity requirements for OLS using visual analysis with standardized residuals
plotted against predicted values. Lastly, we examined the potential issue of multicollinearity in
the OLS model through the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF). The results showed low
multicollinearity, indicating a low VIF (< 3.8 47) for all independent variables, well below the
threshold of 10 (Hair et al., 2018). Additionally, we exami ned the potential correlation of
standardized residuals with independent variables and found no pattern suggesting
multicollinearity.

3.5 RESULTS
The results of the hierarchical regression are presented in Table 9. In the first main stage,
hierarchical regression models were executed in four steps. In the first step, we included only
the control variables. In the second step, we included STRATEGY in both sources of digital
healthcare resources (INTERNAL and EXTERNA L). In the third step, we add
EMBEDDEDNESS, and in the fourth step, we test the moderation effect of
EMBEDDEDNESS×STRATEGY on both sources of digital healthcare resources (INTERNAL

105


and EXTERNAL). In the second main stage, we tested the direct effect of STR ATEGY on
WORK and OPERATIONS (initially including only the control variables and then including
the independent variable STRATEGY). Finally, in the third main stage, hierarchical regression
models were executed, including the independent variable STRATEGY and the mediator’s
variables INTERNAL and EXTERNAL.
As shown in Table 9, the final model (3rd main stage) was statistically significant in
both WORK (F = 15.263; p < 0.01) and OPERATIONS (F = 43.986; p < 0.01), explaining
24.8% and 49.9% of the variance (adjusted R²), respectively. For the first main stage, regarding
STRATEGY, our results showed a statistical association with INTERNAL (B = 0.611; p <
0.000) (H2a is supported) and EXTERNAL (B = 0.375; p < 0.000) (H2b is supported). The
moderation model for EMBEDDEDNESS between STRATEGY and INTERNAL (F = 42.537;
p < 0.01) explains 49.1% of the variance (adjusted R² = 0.491), but we found no statistical
evidence supporting this moderation (H3a is not supported). On the other hand, the moderation
model for EMBEDDEDNESS between STRATEGY and EXTERNAL (F = 12.468; p < 0.01)
explains 21.0% of the variance (adjusted R² = 0.210). We observed a positive moderation effect
between STRATEGY and EMBEDDEDNESS (B = 0.231, p < 0.000) (H3b is supported). To
better understand the effect of this moderation, we plotted the slope in Figure 9, which shows
the positive effect of STRATEGY on EXTERNAL when the level of EMBEDDEDNESS is
high in hospitals. In other words, when a hospital has a high level of network embeddedness
within a healthcare ecosystem, it strengthens the alignment between digital strategy and digital
resources, and this effect is particularly positive in the relationship between digital strategy and
external digital healthcare resources.
For the second main stage, the direct effect of STRATEGY was statistically significant
for WORK (B = 0.258; p < 0.01) (H1a is supported) and OPERATIONS (B = 0.416; p < 0.000)
(H1b is supported). Finally, for the third main stage, the results indicate a complete mediation
effect only in the relationship between STRATEGY and WORK (F = 15.263; p < 0.01). Only
the INTERNAL and EXTERNAL digital healthcare resources become the only statistically
significant variables in the model.

3.5.1 Power analysis
Based on the regression results reported in Table 9, we conducted a power analysis of
the regression models using Cohen’s f2 estimation (Cohen et al., 2003). We also calculated the
population effect size of R2 using Cohen’s f2 estimation (Cohen et al., 2003) from the two final
models in the last stage of o ur OLS hierarchical procedure. For the WORK, we obtained f2 =

109


0.362, representing a statistical power of ≈1.00 at α = 0.01. For the OPERATIONS, we obtained
f2 = 1.045, indicating a statistical power of ≈1.00 at α = 0.01. Therefore, the result of the effect
size for each model is considered an average effect for the explanatory variables (Cohen et al.,
2003).
3.5.2 Robustness checks
We assessed the robustness of our model by applying various strategies to ensure the
stability and consistency of the results. Following the approach of previous studies (e.g.,
Lerman et al. (2022) and Franco et al., 2023), we established an interactive protocol. First, we
removed control variables and checked whether the results remained stable. The removal of
control variables demonstrated that predictor variables were not artifacts of control variables.
Second, we conducted an individual predictor analysis. Lastly, in the third step, we tested a
competitive model, considering the healthcare digital strategy as a moderator betwee n
healthcare digital resources and the implementation of smart healthcare dimensions. However,
we did not find statistical support for this competitive model. Overall, we found stable results,
as there were no significant changes in the coefficients of all models altered in our hierarchical
regression. All these strategies indicated a stable behavior of our proposed model.

3.6 DISCUSSIONS AND CONCLUSIONS
Our results demonstrate that H4.0 encompasses a sociotechnical view through two smart
dimensions, which we refer to as healthcare smart operations and healthcare smart working.
The former focuses on introducing technologies for task execution, aiming to make them more
automated, especially those that are inherently mechanical. The second dimension focuses on
workers, who are the actors responsible for task execution but are supported by the introduction
of digital technologies, enabling an upskilling effect, which means enhancing worker
competence (Dornelles et al., 2023). Both dimensions can be applied acr oss hospital units.
However, despite the digital technologies addressed in this study focusing on the first or second
dimension, some of them can simultaneously encompass both. A potential explanation for this
is the flexibility of application and the impa ct that technologies can have on different areas,
such as telemedicine. Although our research suggests that telemedicine falls within the
healthcare smart operations dimension, in practice, it also plays a significant role in the social
context, as previou sly shown by Cannavacciuolo et al. (2023). Telemedicine is a technology
that supports healthcare workers in providing real-time and virtual care, primarily in emergency

110


situations, allowing for the acceleration of clinical procedures. Furthermore, it benefits patients
by reducing waiting times for care or the need to travel to a closer clinic. Therefore, our results
confirm that smart healthcare dimensions have distinct focuses, one on processes/technical and
the other on people/social, configuring a sociot echnical system. More importantly, our results
add more details, showing that these dimensions should be present and can integrate into an
H4.0 system. These findings elucidate that H4.0 is not only about the introduction of digital
technologies applied to processes, as is typically presented in the literature (e.g., Tortorella et
al., 2022b; Raimo et al., 2023) but also should be evaluated from the perspective of people
(Grover et al., 2018; Roscoe et al., 2019). Otherwise, hospital environments may face
challenges and struggle to succeed with the adoption of digital technologies, as highlighted by
Marcon et al. (2022).
The results indicate that for both dimensions of H4.0 to work within a hospital
organizational environment, the entire organizational struc ture is necessary to support them.
The H4.0 literature has sometimes presented a list of digital technologies that impact operations
(Tortorella et al., 2022a; Tortorella et al., 2022b). However, implementation requires
organizational support for digital t echnologies to succeed, especially for the healthcare smart
working dimension, which is directly related to people (Kleiner, 2008; Baptista et al., 2020;
Klein et al., 2024). Our results show that both healthcare smart operations and healthcare smart
working need alignment with the digital strategic structure for implementation (thus supporting
H1). Hospitals that structure their digital strategy have higher levels of H4.0 development. The
digital strategy role in H4.0 implementation highlights that IT stra tegy and business strategy
for digital transformation are essential to conduct the process of consolidating a sociotechnical
system (Chanias et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020). Furthermore, our findings show that digital
strategy is an antecedent of the d efinition of digital resources, as hypothesized in H2. Prior
research considered digital strategy and resources as a bundle of the strategic initiatives of
digital transformation (Fischer et al., 2020; Verohoef et al., 2021), but our findings point to a
sequential relationship of strategic alignment in which digital strategy is defined and will
support the definition of digital resources. Also, we show that both internal and external digital
resources matter for the development of this strategic alignment. This reinforces the qualitative
prior findings from Fernandez -Vidal et al. (2022) that highlighted the need for governance
structures able to work with internal and external sources that can support the digital
transformation due to its complexity and variety of requirements that need to be attended.

111


We examined whether hospitals’ level of network embeddedness within the healthcare
ecosystem moderates the alignment between digital strategy and digital resources. The results
reveal a significant positive mo derating effect for external digital resources (supporting
Hypothesis H3b), but not for internal resources (contrary to Hypothesis H3a). This distinction
suggests that healthcare digital strategies aimed at leveraging external resources —particularly
to sup port people -oriented digital transformation (smart working) —require strong ties to
external actors. Although the digital transformation literature has emphasized the importance
of external resources for digitalization (Franco et al., 2024), our findings in dicate that, in the
hospital context, this alignment is only effective when network embeddedness is high. That is,
the ability to access and mobilize external resources depends not only on strategic intent but
also on the hospital's level of connectivity w ithin the broader healthcare network —especially
in a sector where digital solutions are highly customized (Bavafa et al., 2021). In contrast, our
results show no moderating effect of network embeddedness on the alignment between strategy
and internal digit al resources. While we initially expected that proximity to external actors
would support internal digitalization through knowledge diffusion and learning, the findings
suggest otherwise. Internal resources appear to be more directly shaped by the hospital’s
internal strategic direction, without strong dependence on external connections. Given the
complexity of healthcare systems (Stevens and Schaik, 2020) and the context-specific nature of
internal capabilities (Mukherjee and Sinha, 2020), these re sources may be inherently less
susceptible to external influence. As a practical implication, hospitals aiming to develop smart
working infrastructures should consider their position within healthcare networks. Those with
high embeddedness can pursue strat egies that leverage external digital resources. However,
hospitals with low embeddedness may benefit more from focusing on internally driven digital
resource development, thereby reducing uncertainties linked to limited external support. It
should be emphasized that, in our analysis, we chose not to examine the moderating effect of
network embeddedness on the relationship between digital strategy and the H4.0 smart
dimensions because we understand that network embeddedness acts as a factor that enhances
the relationship between strategy and digital resources and that, when integrated, can facilitate
the implementation of the H4.0 dimensions. Our focus was to analyze its conditional effect,
considering that this moderating effect does not act solely on digita l strategy in isolation, but
rather relationally, shaping how strategy and digital resources combine to generate digital
capabilities that enable the hospital to develop H4.0.

112


We also tested whether the alignment between healthcare digital strategy and healthcare
digital resources indeed allows for the development of higher levels of healthcare smart
operations and healthcare smart working, as hypothesized in H3. We identified that healthcare
digital resources (internal or external) mediate the relationship between healthcare digital
strategy and the healthcare smart working dimension (thus supporting H3a), but we did not find
statistical evidence for this mediation between digital strategy and smart operations. One
possible explanation for this is grounded in the sociotechnical view (Clegg, 2000). Mostly,
resources are more focused on supporting workers than on processes, regardless of how these
resources are managed, internally or externally. Digital resources should be orchestrated to
provide the best poss ible conditions so that technologies can be well -employed by workers
(Piccoli et al., 2024). These resources create the condition for workers to be capable of dealing
with new technologies, developing new skills, and integrating better their empirical knowledge
of healthcare operations with the technology usage (Fischer et al., 2020; Gillani et al., 2024).
On the other hand, healthcare smart operations involve only the introduction of technologies to
perform tasks, most of the time without the presence of workers, making the need for resources
to support them less critical. Of course, digital resources would be relevant for technology
acquisition and implementation (Liu et al., 2011; Yeow et al., 2018; Verhoef et al., 2021), but
not for its adoption which is dependent on the daily use in healthcare activities. Moreover,
another possible explanation for the absence of evidence regarding this mediation may be that
internal or external resources are less impactful due to regulatory, organizational, or technical
constraints related to DT focused on process automation, which tends to be more flexible. In
this case, certain types of digital resources to support technologies are not necessarily decisive,
since process automation does not always involve human aspects, which might primarily
require compliance with specific regulatory constraints, such as user data protection, or
organizational and technical requirements, such as training and capacity -building for
technology handling. Therefore, our findings suggest that the adoption of technologies aimed
at healthcare smart operations may not necessarily demand a large concentration of institutional
resources and efforts, as regulatory restrictions or internal organizational changes may not be
strong enough to prevent, hinder, or condition the implementation of technological projects.
Our results also highlight a critical aspect, often overlooked but essential in digital
strategies for the implementation of technologies such as IoT, electronic health records, and
artificial intelligence (healthcare smart operations): security risks and cyber threats (Schmitt,
2023; Marcon et al., 2025). In a digital, intelligent, and interconnected environment, the act of

113


automating processes requires the protection of sensitive data in th e face of increasing threats
(Schmitt, 2023). This concern is even more relevant in the healthcare sector, which is
characterized by complex systems and non -standardized processes (Tortorella et al., 2020b;
Stevens & Schaik, 2020; Uysal, 2022). Although our study does not delve deeply into this topic,
the results reinforce the need to integrate cybersecurity structures — enabled by AI, for
example, as proposed by Schmitt (2023) into digital strategies, to mitigate risks associated with
the large volume of sensitive data (Aceto et al., 2020; Uysal, 2022) generated by both healthcare
smart operations and healthcare smart working. Small vulnerabilities can lead to significant
losses and compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of organization al
information, which requires robust strategic cybersecurity measures to protect both the
organization, and the actors involved (Marcon et al., 2025). Therefore, there is a need to explore
and develop cybersecurity resilience in the digital strategy dimen sion, a vital element for the
security of healthcare organizations.
Finally, our findings align with the study by Edelman et al. (2005), which identified a
positive association between the alignment of strategy and resources for performance
improvement in organizations. They also resonate with the studies by Verhoef et al. (2021),
presenting digital resources as a crucial strategic imperative for digital transformation.
Furthermore, they are also related to the findings of a special edition presented by Bap tista et
al. (2020) on the strategic implications across various layers of technologies in the workplace
and organizational structure. Gillani et al. (2024) also highlight the need for organizations to
strategically navigate, including the establishment of an organizational structure as a facilitator
for digital transformation. However, our results add a counterpoint to these studies by
differentiating the role of resources in the strategic alignment, being different when it is
associated with smart working or with smart operations.
3.6.1 Theoretical implications
Our study offers several contributions to existing literature and has various theoretical
implications, as detailed below.
First, our results provide insights into organizational structures that may b e associated
with the implementation of digital transformation. In this regard, we extend previous literature
that suggested considering strategic and management aspects in the adoption of digital
technologies, both for processes and people. We empirically demonstrate these relationships in
the context of healthcare. Additionally, existing literature has primarily focused on the

114


implementation of digital technologies or how digital transformation is associated with
improvements in operational performance. W e broaden this perspective by highlighting the
implementation of healthcare smart working and healthcare smart operations as outcomes of
sociotechnical initiatives. While some researchers have found positive relationships between
organizational factors and performance, we can further expand the sociotechnical view to
achieve higher levels of digital technology implementation by considering social elements.
Second, we offer a theoretical contribution by combining the alignment perspective of
digital strategy with digital resource management. Digital strategy adopts an “integrated view”
approach, where both information technology strategy and business strategy are considered.
Therefore, digital strategies in healthcare settings must be identified, understood, and translated
into social initiatives that can support the implementation of H4.0 dimensions. We contribute
to the theory by demonstrating that digital resources can serve as an operational means between
digital strategy and H4.0 implementation. In sum, an organizational structure that aligns
between digital strategy and digital resources facilitates the implementation of digital
technologies to support he althcare workers, enabling hospitals to adequately consider the
sociotechnical aspects of digital transformation in healthcare. Thus, we expand existing
research by highlighting that alignment between strategy and digital resources leads to higher
levels of technological support for healthcare workers, adding the lens of the sociotechnical
view.
Third, our study clarifies the role of organizational support in the digitization of
healthcare environments. In this case, we demonstrate that this organizational support can
emerge from the management of digital resources, enabling the provision of support for digital
transformation. We show that even though digital resources may be managed in different ways,
they can still be capable of providing this support for adoption and development, especially in
the dimension of smart healthcare workers within H4.0. In other words, internally, hospitals
can develop the necessary digital resources to support this process, just as hospitals can also
outsource these resources s ince both the internal and external dimensions were positively
associated with smart working. This represents possible pathways that reduce the pursuit of
initiatives to support workers as an additional effort for their performance in carrying out
activities. In this regard, an innovative finding is that organizational support through digital
resources aligned with digital strategy can follow different management perspectives,
considering not only the processes but also the people’s perspective for changes in healthcare
professionals’ job roles. In sum, we encourage existing literature to place organizational support

115


in the context of digital transformation, as well as its implications and changes in work in the
digital era.
3.6.2 Managerial implications
Our study has several implications for managerial practice related to sociotechnical,
organizational, and digitization aspects in healthcare, which are presented as follows.
Our findings show hospitals can consider not only the technocentric perspective to
integrate and automate processes but also the sociotechnical view that involves people in
implementing H4.0 in their operations. So far, the focus has been predominantly on processes.
Expanding the potential of the H4.0 concept, sociotechnical initiatives sho uld also be
considered by hospitals to assist healthcare workers, both in the requirements for implementing
technologies and changes in job roles and in maintaining the activities they perform over time,
supported by digital technologies. To achieve this, hospitals must establish a well - defined
digital strategy and have a set of digital resources to support the operationalization of these
technologies by workers. When hospitals seek to increase interoperability and improve tasks
performed by professionals in a high-complexity context, implementing H4.0 dimensions can
help capture real -time information from both processes and patients to support decision -
making, as well as worker support. Similarly, patients and society, among others, can be
included in this context, allowing the integration of all stakeholders.
Secondly, organizational structure can play a significant role in mitigating potential
obstacles to implementing H4.0. From a general perspective, our study recommends that
healthcare managers struct ure the digital strategy to align with digital resources. This
combination acts as an organizational pathway to implement digital technologies to support
healthcare workers. Managers should also consider digital strategies that define operational
targets f or technology implementation, as digital strategy is also strongly related to digital
technologies for healthcare smart operations. By considering these elements, managers can
follow the path toward a sociotechnical organizational development of Healthcare 4.0.
Finally, our findings indicate that hospitals planning to implement smart working
infrastructures should carefully assess their position within healthcare networks. Hospitals with
strong external connections—such as partnerships with other institutions, technology providers,
or public agencies —are better positioned to adopt strategies that rely on external digital
resources. These networks can offer critical support and expertise during digital transformation
efforts. In contrast, hospitals with limited emb eddedness in such networks may benefit more

116


from focusing on internally driven resource development. This approach can reduce uncertainty
and increase control over implementation, ensuring that smart working initiatives are grounded
in the hospital’s own capabilities.
3.6.3 Limitations and future research
This study presents some methodological limitations that point to opportunities for
future research. Regarding the sample data of the study, all interviewees were from hospitals
located in Brazil, a country cl assified as an emerging economy. This may limit the
generalizability of our findings to different socioeconomic contexts. While we have identified
significant and consistent relationships, we suggest that this study could be conducted in other
socioeconomic contexts, involving hospitals from various locations. This would allow for an
international comparative analysis that could contribute to a global understanding, aiding in
identifying international differences and strategies for generating social value. Also, our
constructs of digital resources evaluate the resources used by hospitals to support the
digitization of their operational processes and workers' activities. However, we are limited to
considering only which resources are appropriate for this supp ort. As digital transformation
progresses, other types of resources and/or workers' capabilities may become necessary to
support the implementation and use of different new technologies. For example, the use of
generative AI as a medical support tool is a promising field for future research. Therefore,
identifying which new digital resources and capabilities are needed for this and other
technologies can guide further future investigations.
Lastly, our constructs of digital strategy and digital resources allowed us to analyze the
relationship between them in implementing the H4.0 smarts dimensions. However, other
sociotechnical aspects, such as worker learning analysis, technostress evaluations, and the
development of new digital skills and capabilities, for example, could also be considered. This
enables the development of new research. Additionally, future studies could also investigate
the role of this alignment between digital strategy and digital resources in the performance of
healthcare workers. Moreo ver, another limitation of our study concerns the scope of the
questionnaire, which was restricted to organizational -level questions, without addressing
individual-level aspects within the hospitals. For future research, it would be interesting to
include additional questions specifically directed at healthcare professionals, exploring the
complexity of their tasks, their digital experience, and information about their profiles. We also
suggest grouping participants according to their respective hospital departments to deepen their
understanding of the factors that influence the success of HCDT.
