4. HEALTHCARE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AS A
SOCIOTECHNICAL SYSTEM: SHAPING THE INTERACTIONS
BETWEEN INDIVIDUALS, STRUCTURES, AND PROCESSES
Lucas Miguel Alencar de Morais Correia, Matthias Thürer, Alejandro Germán Frank

This paper will be submitted to International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Abstract
Emerging technologies are widely used to enhance administrative processes and foster a more positive
experience for both patients and professionals in health care systems. Although this Healthcare Digital
Transformation (HCDT) is a profoundly sociotechnical transformation, research on HCDT has primarily
focused on a technocentric perspective. We redress the balance, examining how HCDT as a
sociotechnical system shapes the microfoundations involving individuals, structures, and processes —
viewed here as social aspects. We develop a theoretical model that explains how organizational,
technical, and social aspects are integrated to implement HCDT and how new digital operating routines
emerge. Data was collected through a qualitative case study conducted at a teaching and research
hospital in southern Brazil. We found that changes in the interactions among individuals, structures, and
processes caused by digital transformation enabled the emergence of new digital healthcare operating
routines. This emergence is dependent on the number of professionals involved and the complexity of
each area. This study contributes to sociotechnical theory by empirically demonstrating how technical,
organizational, and social aspects can be integrated to digitalize operations in complex hospital settings.
It also adds to the knowledge -based view, showing how healthcare professionals’ knowledge can be
leveraged to adapt their tasks across different configurations of flexible/rigid processes and
authority/consensus-based structures.

Key Words: Healthcare; Digital transformation; Sociotechnical system; Operating routines.

4.1 INTRODUCTION
Technological innovations have played a beneficial and revolutionary role in operations
(Mithas et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Stark et al., 2023). This includes digital technologies,
which advancement and growing implementation in organizational operations is referred to as
Digital Transformation (DT) (Angelopoulos et al., 2023). DT redefines how interactions occur
between workers, hierarchical structures, and processes (Roscoe et al., 2019; Mukherjee &
Sinha, 2020; Choi et al., 2022; Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Bardhan et al., 2025). This may lead
to conflicts between humans and machines (Kellogg et al., 2020; Abeliansky et al., 2024;
Amaya & Holweg, 2024), making it necessary to establish implementation strategies that
consider the human aspect in technology adoption to mitigate such challenge s (Amaya &
Holweg, 2024; Bendoly et al., 2025). DT in organizations should therefore be seen through the
lens of sociotechnical dynamics (Heim et al., 2021), a perspective that enables an understanding

126


of the interaction and interdependence between social components (e.g., people, practices) and
technical components (e.g., technology, tools) within an organizational system (Malhotra et al.,
2021). The central idea is that social and technical aspects should not be treated as mutually
exclusive but rather as integrated elements, as they are intrinsically interconnected (Bardhan et
al., 2025). This study uses a healthcare setting to explore how routines can be used at the micro-
level to achieve this integration to realize desired macro-level outcomes.
Different sectors adopt digital technologies to increase productivity and efficiency in
their operations, and healthcare is no exception. Significant investments in digital technologies
are made in healthcare system (Wani & Malhotra, 2018; Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020; Dai et al.,
2022) to redefine both administrative and patient care processes (Kc et al., 2020; Bardhan et
al., 2025) to improvements patient care while increasing overall productivity (Devaraj et al.,
2013; Gardner et al., 2015; Bradley et al., 2018; Queenan et al., 2019). This process is referred
to as Healthcare Digital Transformation (HCDT) (Kraus et al., 2021) in the literature.
Healthcare systems are characterized by high levels of technical knowledge —due to the
specialized training of professionals —and intense interactions with patients (Sharma et al.,
2016). Considering sociotechnical dynamics, the implementation of HCDT therefore requires
a harmonious integration of technical and social aspects, as both are essential and inseparable
components of healthcare systems (Tushe et al., 2024; Lowry et al., 2025).
The technical aspect includes defining what is the purpose and application of digital
technologies, whether for clinical care or administrative operations within the organization
(Bradley et al., 2 018; Mukherjee et al., 2020; Stevens & Schaik, 2020). The social aspect
includes understanding how professionals can contribute to the implementation of these
technologies, which they will ultimately use, and how this is shaped by social factors (Sykes &
Aljafari, 2022; Bardhan et al., 2025 ; Bendoly et al., 2025 ). For this, the so -called
microfoundations of operating routines (Roscoe et al., 2019) need to be investigated . The
microfoundations refer to the "interaction" effects that occur between individuals, hierarchical
structures (which may be based on consensus or authority), and processes (which may be rigid
or flexible), leading to macro -level outcomes (Felin et al., 2012). The notion of
microfoundations originates from the Knowledge -Based View (KBV), w hich considers
knowledge as the most valuable resource of a company, with individuals serving as the primary
source of this knowledge (Grant, 1996). In this context, operating routines emerge when
individuals collectively develop sequential interaction pat terns that enable the integration of
their specialized knowledge without the need for explicit communication (Grant, 1996).

127


Healthcare systems are widely recognized as complex systems (Stevens & Schaik,
2020). This complexity arises from the fact that they involve multiple interacting attributes,
such as professionals, operating routines, departments, and areas, as well as non -standardized
processes and high levels of uncertainty that hinder digitalization (Chandrasekaran et al., 2012;
Stevens & Schaik, 2020). HCDT as a sociotechnical system represents a potential pathway to
achieving excellence and success in digitalization in this complex scenario, but could it also
contribute to its failure? This question arises because HCDT shapes the routines of healthc are
professionals by incorporating additional digital tasks into their already demanding daily
activities and may create difficulties related to digital illiteracy. Professionals should actively
participate in the design, implementation, and continuous imp rovement of the use of digital
technologies (Stevens & Schaik, 2020; Malik et al., 2024), which may require time, effort,
knowledge, and availability, potentially leading to adverse effects (Stevens & Schaik, 2020).
How to develop effective strategies to structure and implement HCDT therefore remains
a relevant topic that needs to be further explored. There remains specifically a gap in
understanding — at the micro level of operating routines — as to why some tasks in hospitals
are easier to digitalize tha n others (Sharma et al., 2016; Tushe et al., 2024), why certain
digitalization efforts tend to be more flexible (Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020; Bavafa et al., 2021),
or why there is a higher adoption of digitalization in certain departments compared to others
(Sharma et al., 2016). These questions may help explain variations — or even cases of
excellence — in how HCDT, understood as a socio -technical system, shapes the interactions
among the microfoundations of operating routines, influencing their success or fai lure within
organizations, and how digital changes in these micro-level interactions evolve into new digital
healthcare operating routines.
To answer our research question – How does HCDT, as a sociotechnical system, shape
microfoundations and generate new digital operating routines in healthcare? – we conducted
an in-depth atypical case study at a large Brazilian research hospital. The unit of analysis are
healthcare professionals and the process of implementing an internally developed Hospital
Management System (HMS) that is used by these professionals. We adopted a theoretical
approach based on the sociotechnical perspective to explore how DT shapes the interactions of
the microfoundations of operating routines in the hospital, and we used the KBV to expl ore
how individual knowledge should be considered to create new digital healthcare operating
routines. Data were collected through semi -structured interviews, participant observation, and
documents provided by the hospital under investigation. These data w ere objectively verified

128


using Gioia’s methodology to ensure rigor in qualitative research, following methods aligned
with non-intrusive measures (Webb et al., 1999).
We found that changes in interactions between individuals, structures, and processes
caused by HCDT at the micro level vary according to the complexity of each area and the
number of professionals involved. For example, professionals interact with processes as they
carry out their roles, and under HCDT, they are guided to map these processes to suggest
improvements. When processes are flexible, such as in surgical departments, implementing
HCDT is more challenging due to the complexity of tasks, which demand a more conservative
approach to change, longer learning periods, and more centralized decision-making.
Conversely, in rigid processes (standardized processes), professionals have greater autonomy
and freedom to adapt workflows, converting manual and analog tasks into digital ones using
HMS modules and other associated technologies. Changes in the interaction between
individuals and structures also vary. In departments with smaller teams, a consensus -based
structure enables collaborative work and shared knowledge development to improve digital
technologies. In areas with larger teams, a hiera rchical authority -based structure is more
appropriate. In such cases, the role of a project owner becomes essential to coordinate actions
and represent the teams in decision-making forums. Regardless of the structure, the knowledge
generated and operational feedback from professionals is fed back into the strategic levels of
HCDT, guiding new digital initiatives. This personalized model enabled the emergence of new
digital healthcare operating routines, such as digitizing tasks previously performed on paper, ad
hoc problem-solving, and active participation of professionals in digitalization projects. This
study thus contributes to the sociotechnical theory literature by presenting how the aspects
relate to each other and by offering new pathways for implementing HCDT in complex systems,
such as healthcare. It also advances KBV by demonstrating how the knowledge and experiences
of healthcare professionals can be leveraged to develop personalized HCDT aligned with their
specific needs. Finally, from a practical perspective our findings provide valuable insights for
hospital managers in designing digitalization strategies, as well as for policymakers in
developing guidelines for healthcare digitalization in their respective regions.
The remainder of the article i s organized as follows. We provide the theoretical
background in Section 2, before Section 3 presents research design, data collection, and analysis
methods. Findings are presented in Section 4 and discussed in Section 5. Finally, Section 6
concludes by outlining the study's contribution to theory and managerial practice and proposing
potential areas for future research.

129


4.2 THEORETICAL BACKGROUND
4.2.1 Sociotechnical system
A sociotechnical system integrates social and technical aspects in the design and
management of organizational systems ( Marcon et al. , 2025). It emphasizes the
interdependence between people (social aspect) and technology (technical aspect) in work
environments, arguing that both are equally important and should be managed in a balanced
way to ensure long-term performance (Correia et al., 2025). The sociotechnical theory assumes
that individuals can take on responsibilities and actively participate in the system, promoting
flexibility, autonomy and participation (Malhotra et al., 2021), a s ystemic view of the
environment (Easton & Rosenzweig, 2015), and an improvement in the quality of work life
(Zhang et al., 2025). Following this theory, the interaction between people and technologies
occurs through how work is designed and processes are e xecuted in operating routines (Frank
et al., 2024).
Social and technical aspects are immersed in a dynamic and inseparable organizational
context, in which organizations are understood as organic systems that depend on the interaction
between workers and technologies (Kellogg et al., 2020; Heiberg et al., 2022). In this sense, the
operational performance of an organization is influenced by the harmonious interaction
between various factors that compose these sociotechnical aspects (Kellogg et al., 2020; Zhang
et al., 2025) and impact the functioning of the system (Heiberg et al., 2022). For example, social
factors may include the skills, knowledge, experience, capabilities, and training of individuals,
as well as their well-being, collaboration practices, and participation in group activities, among
others (Rousseau, 1977; Malhotra et al., 2021). Technical factors focus on the typologies of
technologies, purposes, and usability (Choi et al., 2022; Angelopoulos et al., 2023).

4.2.2 Organizational design for the HCDT from a sociotechnical perspective
HCDT introduces digital technologies for providing medical services to patients
(Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020; Li et al., 2021; Delana et al., 2022; Wowak et al., 2023). During
the transition process from analog to dig ital it is important to integrate technologies,
organizational factors and healthcare professionals (e.g., Kc et al., 2020; Sykes & Aljafari,
2022; Tushe et al., 2024; Lowry et al., 2025). But the literature on the implementation of HCDT
has widely neglected the social aspect focusing mainly on the technical aspect (Bardhan et al.,
2025). We therefore propose to consider HCDT as a sociotechnical system based on the

130


principles of sociotechnical theory introduced above. This means that there are three main
aspects that need to be considered.
The organizational aspect of HCDT considers digital strategy and digital resources. The
digital strategy dimension refers to the formulation of paths and investment decisions (Dai et
al., 2022; Bardhan et al., 2025), invol ving, for example, the development of IT master plans
and/or digital transformation plans aimed at improving medical services, optimizing processes,
and enhancing the experience of professionals, patients, and families. The formation of digital
governance committees and IT management committees is also part of this dimension. To
operationalize digital strategy, organizational resources, also known as Digital Resources, need
to be leveraged. Technological infrastructure is the first key resource for enabling the use of
digital technologies. It includes hardware, software, and the network structure necessary to
implement digital solutions and data analytics tools, such as programming and data science
(Gardner et al., 2015; Lowry et al., 2025). Human capital is a second key resource,
encompassing the formation of qualified teams in digitalization, IT professionals, and
programmers (Stevens & Schaik, 2020; Lowry et al., 2025). This is because DT involves
managerial domains related to new capabilities, which often reside in human, informational, or
organizational capital, as well as in the development of new digital skills (Mithas et al., 2022;
Nwafor et al., 2023). In this context, a third intrinsic and essential resource for DT, although
intangible, is the development of a digital culture, which fosters continuous improvement and
adaptation to technological changes. Digital resources can be managed through different
strategies (Correia & Frank, 2025) . For example, the institution may choose internal
development, promoting the complete internalization of its digital resources for the journey
from analog to digital (Correia & Frank, 2025), or it can outsource these resources to external
partners through direct contracts, establishing strategic alliances, and forming a collaborative
ecosystem that provides the necessary digital solutions for the healthcare organization (Correia
& Frank, 2025 ). Hybrid governance (Franco et al., 2024 ; Correia & Frank, 2025 ), which
combines both internal development and external acquisiti on of digital resources, is also
possible allowing for greater flexibility and adaptability to the demands of HCDT.
The technical aspect of HCDT considers which digital technologies should be adopted
and their roles in healthcare operations. For example, the use of the Internet of Things (IoT) for
data capture and real -time monitoring of patients and equipment, big data & analytics for
predicting patient diseases and operational demands (Guha & Kumar, 2018; Nenova & Shang,
2022), artificial intelligence for automating medical tasks (Dai & Tayur, 2022), collaborative

131


robots in surgical procedures (Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020), telemedicine for online consultations
(Bavafa et al., 2021; Delana et al., 2023), 3D printing for prototype development, or immersive
treatments through the use of wearable devices, haptic devices, augmented reality, virtual
reality, and extended reality (Lowry et al., 2025). These technologies aim to provide
personalized medicine and value -based, connected healthcare to promote faster, safer, and
patient-centered care (Kc et al., 2020). Technologies such as blockchain, electronic health
records, and hospital management systems (Wani & Malhotra, 2018; Ransbotham et al., 2021;
Nenova & Shang, 2022) have been adopted to enable vertical integration between different
areas and departments within the hospital, as well as horizontal integration with external
partners (Bradley et al., 2018; Kc et al., 2020; Nwafor et al., 2023).
The social aspect of HCDT considers the interactions between the microfoundations of
operating routines, which encompass individuals, structures, and processes, operating at the
micro level of the organization (Felin et al., 2012). These interactions involve changes in how
professionals and their tasks are shaped by the introduction of digital technologies (Kellogg,
2022; Franke et al., 2024), often contingent on social factors such as the training of healthcare
professionals, adaptation of hospital processes, level of educational background, profession,
work experience, accumulated knowledge (Roscoe et al., 2019; Amaya & Holweg, 2024;
Franke et al., 2024) and the role of professionals – whether individually or in groups – in the
digital transformation process (Kellogg, 2022). A relevant example is the knowledge
accumulated by individuals, which can dictate how technology can be developed and
implemented in operating routines (Nwafor et al., 2023; Amaya & Holweg, 2024). This
knowledge becomes a crucial element in defining the implementation paths of HCDT (Stevens
& Schaik, 2020).
The resulting theoretical model of HCDT as a sociotechnical system is illustrated in
Figure 1 0. In the first part of the model (organizational and technical aspects), HCDT is
structured into three main dimensions: digital strategy, digital resources, and digital
technologies. In the second part (social aspect), these dimensions are incorporated into the
microfoundations of operational routines, which encompass the interaction between
individuals, structures, and processes – it is at this level that HCDT is effectively
operationalized.
The second part of the model presented in Figure 10 is based on the framework proposed
by Roscoe et al. (2019), in which processes function as integration mechanisms, incorporating

132


individuals as sources of knowledge development and sharing. The interaction between
individuals and processes enables the accumulation of experience and knowledge, which, when
applied for a specific purpose, contributes to the continuous improvement of processes.
Additionally, the model includes organizational structures that act as organizing mechanisms,
determining how and how often individuals interact (Roscoe et al., 2019).
Finally, once embedded in the interactions of the microfoundations, new digital
healthcare operating routines can be generated. Digital strategy, digital resources, and digital
technologies precede the microfoundations, as these three dimensions establish the guidelines,
prerequisites, and methodologies for the operationalization of HCDT, positioning them at a
macro-management level. In contrast, the microfoundations represent the operational level of
healthcare activities, being directly shaped by HCDT.

4.2.3 The microfoundations of operating routines
Operating routines emerge when individuals, acting collectively, develop sequential
patterns of interaction that facilitate the integration of their specialized knowledge without the
need for explicit communication of such knowledge (Grant, 1996). When the se routines
stabilize over time, they enable the formation of operational capabilities (Barney & Felin, 2013,
Roscoe et al., 2019). The microfoundations of operating routines refer to the interactions
between individuals, processes, and structures, and the ir effects, that enable these macro-level

133


outcomes (Felin et al., 2012). They provide a detailed understanding how individuals act within
organizations and their specific roles in creating and consolidating operating routines.
In this context, the KBV eme rges as a relevant theory, as one of its fundamental
premises is that knowledge is created by individuals (Grant, 1996; Nonaka, 1994). When
individuals work in an organization, they bring with them knowledge acquired from previous
experiences, e.g., through training, observation of colleagues, or experiential learning (Felin et
al. 2012) in this or other organizations, and apply this knowledge to their new roles (Grant,
1996; Amaya & Holweg, 2024). They develop specialized knowledge in a productive task and
use this knowledge to simplify the future execution of the same task, whether by themselves or
by others (Grant, 1996). A practical example are surgical procedures (Mukherjee & Sinha,
2020; Stevens & Schaik, 2020), where professionals such as doctors and nurses accumulate
knowledge from previous clinical cases, including information about the steps involved,
operational methods, required resources, recovery time, and the likelihood of success or patient
relapse. This specialized knowledge is then applied t o streamline the surgical procedure,
making the process more efficient (Stevens & Schaik, 2020). As a result, both the patient, who
receives faster and more accurate care, and the professional, who improved its productivity,
benefit.
But the microfoundatio ns of operating routines are not limited to individuals in
isolation: they also encompass the level and types of interactions that occur between individuals
within an organization, which, over time, evolve to form a collective. In this context, interaction
is defined as moments when two or more individuals mutually engage through verbal and non-
verbal social mechanisms (Cousins et al., 2006; Felin & Hesterly, 2007). These mechanisms
are understood as instruments or activities, whether natural or established , that facilitate the
occurrence or execution of something (Franke et al., 2024). They can be classified as formal or
informal socialization mechanisms (Cousins et al., 2006). In the case of formal mechanisms,
they refer to structures specifically created to communicate expectations and share useful
knowledge among individuals. Examples include regularly scheduled meetings, conferences,
or team events (Cousins et al., 2006). Informal socialization mechanisms are less structured and
involve spontaneous inter actions, such as impromptu conversations in hallways or social
gatherings after work hours. These activities help build trust among individuals and facilitate
the sharing of ideas in a more organic way (Cousins et al., 2006).

134


Individuals and collectives al so interact with the processes and structures of the
organizational design. A process is defined as a sequence of interdependent events. It can
function as integration mechanism, facilitating the combination of different organizational
elements, such as in dividuals, teams, departments, or multifunctional knowledge resources
(Chandrasekaran et al., 2012). Processes can be classified as rigid or flexible (Felin et al. 2012),
and their design significantly impacts the pattern of interaction among individuals. Rigid
processes refer to highly organized and controlled sequences of events, where individuals have
well-defined roles and responsibilities. For example, in healthcare, this type of process occurs
in surgical procedures, as there are strict protocols with well-defined rules and steps, rigorous
control, and a focus on efficiency (Mukherjee et al., 2020). Another example is inventory
control in hospital pharmacies, where procedures are carefully structured for the receipt,
organization, and distribution of m edications across different hospital departments. Flexible
processes involve sequences of events that can be adapted by individuals to achieve a desired
outcome. An example of this type of process in healthcare occurs in personalized patient care
(Wang et al., 2023), where clinical treatments can follow different paths depending on
individual needs — such as replacing in-person consultations with remote ones (Bavafa et al.,
2021). Another example involves procedures aimed at developing new digital solutions for
hospitals (Lowry et al., 2025). This approach provides individuals with the freedom to
experiment and develop innovative solutions, adjusting the process as needed. The interaction
between individuals and processes creates a self-reinforcing cycle: individuals learn from their
mistakes and, by applying this newly acquired knowledge, continue to refine and improve the
process, generating continuous improvement (Roscoe et al., 2019).
In this context, organizational structures are defined as conditions th at enable or
constrain processes and individual and collective interactions within an organization. A basic
structure for organizing complex social activities involves the use of hierarchies (Grant, 1996)
that can be classified as authority -based or consensus-based (Nickerson & Zenger, 2004). An
authority-based hierarchy relies on centralized decision -making to optimize the transmission
and processing of knowledge, for example, a senior manager that sets guidelines to steer the
search for solutions without necessarily considering the knowledge of other individuals in
detail. A consensus -based hierarchy, in contrast, involves the collective agreement of
individuals on a search path and the creation of a common language that integrates different
specialized knowledge (Roscoe et al., 2019). This promotes the building of a shared identity
within the organization, which reduces communication -related costs and establishes

135


coordination rules that influence the direction of the search for and implementation of solutions.
In consensus-based hierarchies, individuals may receive incentives —such as salary increases,
bonuses, awards, or promotions —to encourage the search for solutions, the transfer of
knowledge to others, and the generation of new knowledge (Grant, 1996; S tevens & Schaik,
2020; Nwafor et al., 2023). Such incentives can also motivate individuals to work
collaboratively, whether in cross -functional teams or projects, to solve problems and propose
improvements that enhance organizational performance (Rousseau, 1977; Kellogg, 2021;
Nwafor et al., 2023).
Since processes necessarily unfold in a structure there is an overlap, and the main
question is a question of fit or alignment. But this alignment alone does not result in the creation
or accumulation of knowledg e without the specific interaction of individuals who share
knowledge. In other words, in processes, the presence of individuals is essential to carry out a
series of productive tasks, while organizational structures lack a real purpose without people to
occupy and perform roles. In this sense, the central argument of the microfoundations of
operating routines is that individuals constitute the essential unit of analysis for understanding
how organizations update or develop new operating routines, and this occurs when individuals
operate at the intersection of processes and structures (Roscoe et al., 2019).
Based on this theoretical background, we developed the model presented in Figure 1 0,
which proposes a new approach to addressing HCDT. In the remainder of this study, we present
a case where we aim to understand whether this approach —focused on explaining how
microfoundations are shaped —contributes to the organization's success with HCDT or,
potentially, to its failures. Figure 10 suggests that HCDT as a s ociotechnical system shapes
microfoundations and can explicitly encourage—or alternatively restrict—the development of
new digital routines in hospital settings. By analyzing the phenomenon at the micro level, the
model enables us to identify the key micro -level elements and to understand why some a reas
or departments are more susceptible to the adoption of digital technologies than others.

4.3 RESEARCH DESIGN
4.3.1. Case description
The Research Hospital studied is a public institution, part of the network of university
hospitals under Brazil's Ministry of Education (MEC) and academically affiliated with a
Federal University in the southern region of Brazil. It aims to provide high co mplexity,

136


humanized, and excellent care within the Unified Health System (SUS). The Hospital offers
approximately 919 inpatient beds and more than 55 medical services. Over the last two years,
it has conducted over 64,300 hospitalizations and 1,035,000 con sultations and employs 6,800
healthcare professionals. Although the hospital primarily serves SUS patients, it also provides
care for private insurance and self -paying individuals. The Hospital's strategic priorities are
patient-centered care, resources an d space optimization, and sustainability. To meet these
strategic priorities, the hospital has established a management culture deeply rooted in
innovation and digital transformation, aiming to enhance administrative and healthcare
processes for patients a nd professionals through the implementation of new digital
technologies. During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, this Hospital innovated by offering
new digital services, such as telemedicine and telehealth, as well as distance health education
for remote communities.
The hospital's organizational structure consists of various directorates, committees,
councils, coordinators, and units. Among the hierarchies related to innovation and DT, the
Digital Governance Committee (DGC) stands out. This committee comprises represe ntatives
from the directorates and several areas of the institution. Its primary objective is to develop,
propose, and monitor Digital Governance policies that address the institution's Information and
Communication Technology (ICT) needs. Another relevant body is the Coordination of
Information and Communication Technology Management (CICTM), whose purpose is to
provide ICT services to the departments of the hospital. Both seek to enhance activities related
to healthcare, management, education, and researc h, in alignment with the Hospital’s master
plan, ICT strategic planning, and digital transformation plan. Additionally, the Innovation and
Technology Transfer Center (ITTC) was established to facilitate and enable initiatives for
innovation and technology transfer. Figure 11 illustrates the bodies of ICT, innovation, and data
established by the Hospital for HCDT, which are divided into strategic management and tactical
and operational management. The former encompasses digital governance and data
governance, determining what needs to be done, while the latter involves the management of
information and communication technologies and data management, translating into how the
actions established in strategic management should be executed. Finally, at the inters ection of
Digital Governance, Data Governance, and Information and Communication Technology
Management lies the Executive Board.

137



Figure 11. Bodies of information and communication technology, innovation, and data

The main driver for HCDT in our study is the HMS of the studied hospital. Operating
since 1971, the studied hospital is well known for its efficient management. Its management
model became a reference for creating a Brazilian hospital services company, whi ch aims to
enhance the structure and processes of all university hospitals within the MEC network. At the
core of this management model is the HMS, a solution internally developed by the institution
itself. The HMS has undergone an evolution spanning more than 40 years, marked by
technological advancements and significant transformations. The journey began when the
progressive growth of administrative demands at the Research Hospital highlighted the need to
automate key processes. Efforts were initiated to internally develop a first system, with the first
functionalities gradually implemented in a mainframe environment. In 1983, the first hospital
applications emerged, such as the outpatient scheduling module, followed by the patient
admission module. In the subsequent years, the focus shifted to patient -centered digitization
efforts, leading to the creation of modules related to exams, medical and nursing prescriptions,
supplies, and more. Starting in 2000, all previously developed systems underwent a migrat ion
from a character -based environment to a graphical environment, adopting a client -server

138


architecture. This transition gave rise to the HMS as it is known today. Among the most notable
advancements were the implementation of the Online Medical Record, S urgical Portal,
Obstetrics Center, Outpatient Module, Care Protocols, Progress Notes, Electronic Prescription
Verification, and Therapeutic Sessions. In 2009, the HMS again underwent a significant
transformation by becoming part of the National Program for the Restructuring of Federal
University Hospitals, coordinated by MEC. This program aimed to restructure and revitalize
federal university hospitals using the HMS from the Research Hospital as a model. By 2014,
the HMS received a comprehensive update to i ts architecture, and its name was rebranded to
reflect its new scope, which expanded beyond the internal confines of the hospital. In 2017, the
HMS Community was established as a collaborative development initiative, making the system
available for use across various healthcare institutions and levels of care.
Two committees were established to manage the HMS: the Strategic Committee, which
is responsible for setting goals and priorities, and the Technical Committee, which is
responsible for implementing updates. Currently, the HMS Community includes the Research
Hospital featured in this study (serving as the coordinating entity), the country’s military forces,
universities, and state health departments. The HMS is structured into more than 16,000
macropoints and consists of 55 modules organized into three major categories: Assistance (24),
administrative (13) and Interoperability (18). The clinical modules address the needs of patient
diagnosis, treatment, and follow -up, while also assisting in the organiz ation of healthcare
professionals’ tasks. The administrative modules focus on the organizational and operational
management of the Research Hospital, ensuring efficiency and support for institutional
activities, while interoperability is related to modules for integration with both internal and
external systems of the institution.

4.3.2. Data collection procedure
To assess how HCDT driven by the HMS aligns with our theoretical model, a
triangulated data collection strategy was employed (Yin, 2014) using three primary sources: (1)
semi-structured interviews; (2) participant observation; and (3) analysis of primary and
secondary hospital documents (Figure 12). Results of the semi-structured interviews where first
corroborated through participant observation, before primary and secondary hospital
documents were collected for further corroborating observations and contextualization.
Combining different data sources enables more precise triangulation of information,

139


contributing to the development of more insightful th eories and enhancing the robustness of
resulting theoretical frameworks (Eisenhardt, 1989; Silva et al., 2025).

Figure 12. Data collection

4.3.2.1 Phase 1: Semi Structured Interviews
25 semi-structured interviews were conducted with 40 interviewees as detailed in the
Table in Appendix A. The main objectives were: to understand the management of the hospital's
digitalization with key leaders, including gaining insight into the digital strategies and resources
utilized, to explore how microfoundations are influenced by the adoption of HCDT as a
sociotechnical system from a professionals' perspective, and to understand the role of these
professionals in developing new digital healthcare operating routines. Our sampling logic was
therefore guided by the collection of data from individuals working in different hospital
departments who are directly involved in the use of HMS and other digital technologies in
clinical and administrative process es. We aimed to cover various areas (outpatient clinic,
surgical unit, pharmacy, emergency department) and roles within the institution, including
directors, department heads, managers, and operational professionals (doctors, nurses,
technicians, pharmacis ts and ICT technicians). The data collection from these multiple
perspectives provided distinct insights into the same phenomenon, offering a detailed

140


understanding of how individuals, processes, and structures interact during HCDT and evolve
into new digital healthcare operational routines. All interviewees have had at least 2 years of
experience with the HMS. Some have used the system since their undergraduate studies over
20 years ago, which allows them to compare the latest HMS updates and the adoption of new
technologies. Gathering the experiences of these key informants is important to ensure the
success of case study-based research (Yin, 2014).
The interviews were conducted online, with durations ranging from 30 minutes to 2
hours and 30 minutes. All sessions were audio-recorded and later fully transcribed. Following
the recommendations of Gioia et al. (2012), interviewees were informed at the beginning of
each session about the anonymity of the information provided, including the confidentiality of
their names and specific roles, to ensure research reliability and participant comfort. A semi -
structured interview script was used in interviews with operational professionals. The script
was divided into a few questions, which are detailed in Appendix B. Additionally, following
the recommendations of Galletta (2013), open -ended and exploratory questions were posed
during the interviews, going beyond the initial script. This approach provided greater flexibility
to the research, enabling the discovery of un expected information and enhancing the depth of
the collected data (Gioia et al., 2012). The interviews were divided into three parts. First, the
interviewees were invited to share information about their roles, length of service, and
experiences with the evolution of the HMS in their positions. Second, the questions were
directed toward the framework in Figure 10, asking the interviewees to describe in detail their
interactions with processes, hierarchical structures, and their daily routines with the system.
Finally, interviewees were asked to share their perspectives and explain important details, such
as routines before the adoption of HCDT, the role of individuals in the design or update of new
modules and digital technologies, and how the managemen t of new digital technologies is
conducted in the healthcare context. This interview structure allowed for the collection of open
narrative data, as well as factual and specific information.
As engaged researchers, it was essential to maintain constant att ention to potential
biases, which could arise both from the researchers and the interviewees, to prevent participants
from distorting or dramatizing their experiences and accounts (van Marrewijk & Dessing,
2019). Interviews were therefore scheduled at leas t one week in advance, ensuring greater
comfort for the participants. The interview times were set according to the availability of the
interviewees, ensuring they were well -rested and reducing the risk of responses being
influenced by time constraints. Ad ditionally, researchers avoided mentioning data or

141


information from previous interviews during subsequent conversations, eliminating potential
biases in the responses. Moreover, the interviewers paid close attention to the research script,
ensuring that it was focused on comprehensive questions (anticipating related topics that should
be addressed) and that it did not contain leading questions (such as: "Don't you agree that...?")
(Gioia et al., 2012). To further reinforce impartiality, at least two researchers that were directly
involved in the study conducted the interviews, reducing the possibility of individual biases
during the data collection and subsequent analysis.
In total, almost 20 hours of interview recordings were collected, resulting in over 69 0
pages of transcribed content. After conducting the 25 interviews, we observed that all
participants shared common points in their responses, indicating that theoretical saturation had
been reached, as highlighted by Lee (1999).
4.3.2.2 Phase 2: Participant Observation
To further corroborate the data obtained from the interviews participatory observation
techniques were applied (Atkinson & Hammersley, 1994; Spradley, 2016; Silva et al., 2025).
To understand, at a managerial level, how the process of prior itizing the adoption of digital
technologies occurs, one researcher participated three times (1:30 hours) in the hospital's digital
governance committee sessions. This allowed for evaluating, from a hierarchical perspective,
how decisions are made regardin g the assessment of digital projects, the definition of digital
strategies, the allocation of technological resources, as well as the development or acquisition
of new HMS modules and other digital technologies. The researcher also followed on six
occasions the routines and tasks performed by healthcare professionals in different hospital
departments, totaling nine hours. During this phase, it was possible to observe ongoing
processes, the usability of the HMS modules and other digital technologies, as well as the
professionals' interactions with these tools. Additionally, the researcher asked informal
questions, took detailed notes, and collected, reviewed, and validated hospital documents.
Additionally, three more visits were focused on administrative and care processes, totaling six
hours, while two more visits were dedicated to the data center and the HMS module
development room, lasting two hours. This approach allowed for objective verification of the
data collected during the interviews and a deeper analysis of the points discussed in the digital
governance committee sessions. In total, there were more than 18 hours of participant
observation in this study.

4.3.2.3 Phase 3: Document Collection
We had access to a rich set of additional data to complemen t the interviews and
participatory observations. This includes documents provided by hospital professionals,
summarized materials, and a search on the hospital's and HMS's official websites for primary
and secondary documents. Among these documents, the st rategic planning and the IT and
communication master plan stand out, since it was essential to understand the hospital's
organizational structure and how it was reconfigured over the years in line with the development
and evolution of the HMS.
4.3.3. Data analysis
Based on the records of the semi -structured interviews, participant observation notes,
and collected documents, we analyzed the data following Gioia's methodology (Gioia et al.,
2012). This methodology was chosen because it prioritizes the interviewees' interpretations,
positioning researchers as responsible for providing an accurate account of their experiences.
Data is categorized into first - and second -order categories to facilitate their subsequent
structured presentation in an organized manner. We u sed the qualitative analysis software
NVivo 15 to operate this methodological approach.
Data were first organized and categorized into first -order empirical concepts using the
model presented in Figure 10 as a reference. Thematic analysis techniques (Braun & Clarke,
2006) combined with correspondence logic (Yin, 2014; Webb et al., 1999) was applied.
Initially, there were many terms, concepts, and jargon provided by the informants that needed
to be organized. During the analysis, we made an effort to stay faithful to the terms used by the
informants and made little effort to distill the categories. As the analysis progressed, we began
to identify similarities and differences between the categories or coding identifiers previously
established (processes, structures, changes at work, expertise, experiential learning, and pre -
existing knowledge). This process allowed for a reduction of the initial number of categories to
a more manageable set, which was later labeled with short and precise descriptions (e.g., ' The
same doctor who works in the ICU also holds management positions in the digital health unit,
as well as on the digital governance committee').
We then identified second -order themes by consciously anal yzing the similarities and
differences between the first -order empirical concepts. Following the recommendations of
Corbin and Strauss (2014), axial coding was applied. For example, from the first -order
empirical concepts 'HMS modules aligned with professi onals' workflows' and 'Learning from

143


process errors,' the second -order theme 'Process mapping' emerged. Finally, the second -order
themes were grouped into overarching theoretical dimensions. For instance, the themes 'Digital
records' and 'Ad hoc problem re solution' were grouped under the theoretical dimension 'New
digital operating routines in healthcare.' When the first-order empirical concepts did not easily
fit into the predefined coding scheme, new second-order themes were created.
The coding model of second-order themes was iteratively refined until the researchers
achieved a final structure that provided a robust explanation of the case studied (Eisenhardt &
Graebner, 2007). Figure 13 illustrates the coding process and data structure, providing examples
of first-order empirical concepts, second-order themes, and theoretical dimensions. According
to Gioia et al. (2012), this data structure not only allows for organizing the data in a coherent
visual way but also provides a graphical representation of how we progressed from raw data to
terms and themes during the analysis, ensuring rigor in qualitative research.
To ensure coding consistency and establish inter -rater reliability, a second member of
the research team repeated the coding process for both the first-order empirical concepts and
the second-order themes (Gioia et al., 2012). This approach reinforced the reliability of the
analysis of the semi -structured interviews, as all participants answered the same structured
questions in the same order. The independent analysis by the second researcher resulted in a
high level of agreement regarding the key themes identified, reducing the risk of biases and
further enhancing the rigor of the qualitative analysis process (Armstrong et al., 1997).

4.4 RESULTS
Our results are presented based on the logic of the theoretical model put forward in
Figure 10. From a sociotechnical perspective, HCDT initially requires the structuring of
organizational aspects, including the definition of digital strategies and the identification of the
necessary resources to operationalize parts of these strategies and support the digitalization
process. Next, it is essential to determine which digital technologies will be implemented and
how they will be used. In this study, we focus primarily on the HMS, the core technology
developed internally by the hospital itself, which c omprises different modules for specific
departments but also allows integration with other digital technologies.

145


As argued previously, the organizational and technological aspect build the frame for
the social aspect, being it people that manifest in a st ructure and that execute processes. The
social aspect builds the link between structure and process, which main requirement is
alignment. The presentation of results should be read with this contextualization in mind,
building Section 4.4.1. and 4.4.2 the backdrop for Section 4.4.3, where we show how
organizational and technical aspects shape the interactions of the microfoundations of operating
routines, thus addressing the social aspect, and Section 4.4, where the role of these
microfoundations in promoting continuous improvements is discussed.
4.4.1. HCDT as a sociotechnical system – organizational aspects
Digital strategy
Regarding the digital strategy dimension, the hospital established a set of key objectives
and strategies to address HCDT. The main objectives include:
• Patient-centered care, aimed at maximizing the value delivered to patients by focusing
on quality, safety, and efficiency. This also involves delivering care that is coordinated
across the continuum of care pathways.
• Sustainability, wh ich refers to expanding environmental and social sustainability
initiatives, strengthening governance practices to achieve institutional goals, and
fostering relationships to attract funding and resources.
• Optimization of resources and spaces, which invol ves implementing the hospital's
master plan, including the mapping of productive capacities, adopting best practices for
continuous improvement of internal processes, and promoting data science, its
integration, and secure accessibility to support the hospital's operations.
Based on these objectives, the hospital established digital strategies to realize them.
First, internal and customized development of HCDT, which means that digital technologies are
developed in-house, leveraging available resources and encouraging the active participation of
professionals. Second, Leveraging the academic pillar for innovation , which means that the
hospital utilized its intrinsic characteristic as a teaching and research institution to develop its
own digital technologie s and/or other technological innovations, including its customized
HMS, designed for both clinical care and professional workflows. Third. Creation of an
external collaborative community , which means that the hospital established a collaborative
network wi th external partners to expand the development of new HMS modules and

146


applications. Simultaneously, it also seeks to expand the HMS services beyond the hospital by
making it replicable for other interested institutions, offering it as an HMS as a Service (SaaS).
This creates a collaborative ecosystem of actors for both digital technology development and
implementation. Fourth, Digital culture of continuous improvement , which includes ongoing
interaction with engaged professionals through regular feedback rounds, ensuring the evolution
of applications and optimization of user experience. Finally, establishing an organizational
structure for digital governance , which refers to the creation of an organizational structure
dedicated to digital governance that enables the ongoing management of initiatives focused on
digitizing and innovating hospital operations, as well as the evaluation of results, goals, and
indicators (e.g., patient-centered care, sustainability, and optimization of resources and space)
related to HCDT projects. These digital strategies were explicitly mentioned by the coordinator
of the Information and Communication Technology Management Coordination (R03) and
reinforced by the coordinator of the Digital Health Unit (R01). The secondary data hig hlight
these digital strategies (e.g., in the section “Definition of strategic pillars and indicators”
[Information and Communication Technology Strategic Plan 2021]). It is worth noting that the
hospital’s documents/reports related to digital transformati on are operationalized and updated
every four years.
According to interviewees R01, R02, and R03, which have leader roles, the main
objective of these strategic actions is to increase process efficiency, collect and integrate data
from different areas, str engthen communication between internal departments and external
partners, improve the quality of medical services, optimize the tasks performed by
professionals, and enhance patient interaction using digital technologies. Additionally, by
adopting a customized HCDT model for the development of digital technologies and the HMS,
the hospital aims to integrate all internal and external areas, centralizing patient clinical
procedures, professional routines, and administrative activities. This approach also enables the
incorporation of new digital technologies into the system, overcoming limitations often found
in off-the-shelf HMS solutions. Another relevant factor is the independence from vendors and
public procurement processes, which can require significant f inancial investment and time,
making HCDT more expensive.
According to interviewee R03: “The strategy of developing a customized HMS improves
our internal operations by meeting the needs of both our professionals and patients, while also
leveraging the pillars of education and research, as well as the resources available within the

147


hospital.” He further adds: “Offering the HMS as a service to other external institutions opens
several opportunities for the hospital. Becoming a software provider can serve as a source of
revenue—not necessarily financial, but by reducing the IT team’s workload in developing new
digital applications. Moreover, this strategy may attract more collaborators for the joint
development of new solutions, driving the digitalization of other institutions.”
Interviewee R02 emphasized the importance of the strategy to establish a digital
governance committee to manage HCDT within the hospital. According to him: “ This
organizational structure includes professionals from different levels—operational (e.g.,
representatives from various clinical departments and the IT team), managerial, and
strategic—who take part in decision-making regarding investments in technology projects, the
definition of strategic directions, and the planning of digital transformation initiatives over
time.” He also highlighted: “ The organizational structure for HCDT enables the monitoring
and growth of the HMS, the engagement of the HMS community, and the coordination of what
each partner contributes related t o the HMS. ” R02 further stressed the importance of a
digitalization process that goes beyond just the technological aspect, also considering the
hospital’s organizational structure, which is inherently geared toward education and research,
as well as the human factor, including both patients and healthcare professionals.
Digital resources
Several digital resources were integrated preceding the digitalization process to ensure
both the deployment and functioning of the HMS, as well as the incorporation of ot her digital
technologies. It is important to note that to manage the digital resources of HCDT, the hospital
adopted a hybrid governance model. According to interviewee R03, this model combines the
internal development of resources with the acquisition of external resources through its
collaborative partner network. The adoption of this model is facilitated by the hospital being a
public institution focused on education and research, which allows for leveraging existing
resources while also accessing external ones through R&D and innovation partnerships, or even
through bidding processes with suppliers.
Among the resources, the hospital initially established the basic infrastructure. It
developed a corporate Wi -Fi network and installed antennas to ensure dev ice connectivity.
More specifically, firewalls and routers, network points, Wi-Fi access points, telecom systems,
and auditing tools were implemented across the hospital. Additionally, a technological
environment was set up, including various hardware, suc h as workstations, computers and

148


microcomputers, printers, televisions, laptops, tablets, and QR code scanners and
multiparameter monitors. These resources are essential for the operation of HMS modules,
enabling real-time access and recording of patients' historical data and vital signs. They are
used, for instance, during bedside checks by the nursing team and by physicians who need to
record notes, patient progress, and observations within outpatient clinics and ICUs. The
importance of these resources wa s emphasized by interviewees R11 and R12 and further
supported by R09 and R10, who are involved in processes related to nursing, patient safety, and
the quality of care provided. To validate and confirm these statements, the secondary data
highlight the use of these digital resources (e.g., as presented in the "Hospital IT Ecosystem"
section [Hospital Institutional Web Page 2024]).
The hospital also built green data centers (with high availability and energy efficiency),
which mark a significant milestone b ecause they enable secure data backups and the
implementation of a robust information security infrastructure while contributing to its
sustainability goals. However, it was necessary to adopt additional security measures, such as
the development of "ethical hackers" to safeguard sensitive data. The hospital in this study also
has 400 servers, various databases (Oracle, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server / MySQL), 0.5
PB of storage capacity, and a certified secure vault room. These resources allow for histori cal
data queries, report generation, and indicator assessment, in addition to supporting the
development of digital applications like dashboards and big data analytics for clinical and
administrative decision-making.
Nurse R09 emphasizes the importance of ensuring the availability of digital resources
before introducing new digital technologies: “Digitalization is not just about software. A system
cannot function without supporting hardware. To implement HCDT in nursing processes, it
was also necessary to invest in infrastructure, such as Wi-Fi networks, to enable system use at
the bedside, which therefore required investments in hardware .” She adds: “ There’s no point
in having software without the necessary hardware, and this needs to be made clear when
presenting a project. These items must be acquired in a planned and gradual way, as it’s not
feasible to purchase them all at once.”
In terms of human resources, the hospital has a large IT team composed of 130
professionals with diverse backgrounds, includi ng artificial intelligence, computer science,
information systems, and digital transformation according to interviewee R35. More
specifically, the team is structured into coordination (9), technology (43), support and
relationship (35), business (13), and third-party contractors (30). These specialists are allocated
to different digital technology development and implementation projects, working on software

149


architecture, big data analysis, and programming, as well as the enhancement of HMS modules
(presented in the "Hospital IT Ecosystem" section [HMS Institutional Web Page 2024]).
Individual team constitutions consider the type of project, as well as the skills, competencies,
experience, familiarity, and availability of each professional. Within digital tec hnology
projects, these teams play a crucial role in capturing insights from frontline professionals to
ensure that system updates and operations meet the needs of both professionals and patients.
Additionally, they are responsible for managing implementat ion, collecting feedback, and
continuously maintaining the systems, ensuring that the HMS modules are consistently
improved to improve hospital processes.
Finally, internally generated knowledge and information by the hospital’s own IT
team—as well as that acquired through external partners such as consulting firms, universities,
and military entities, were identified as strategic assets for the development of HCDT. These
resources were considered by hospital management to be essential for advancing digital
healthcare transformation. The hospital established, for example, a strong culture of Business
Process Modeling (BPM), which became a key element in ensuring the success of HCDT
initiatives. Professionals are responsible for mapping processes and creating detailed process
descriptions, known as "descriptive memorials". The importance of BPM in the context of
HCDT will be discussed in more detail in later sections.

4.4.2. HCDT as a sociotechnical system – technical aspects
Digital technologies
According to interviewee R35, the HMS is the main technology adopted, functioning as
a monolithic system. The HMS integrates the functionalities of an Electronic Medical Record
(EMR), Electronic Health Record (EHR), Hospital Information System (HIS), and E nterprise
Resource Planning (ERP), consolidating everything into a single platform. This integration is
achieved through the various modules of the HMS, which include patient records,
hospitalization, outpatient services, emergency, surgery, therapeutic sessions, exams, supplies,
finance/accounting, hospital management, and clinical research. In this way, the hospital can
promote vertical integration across different internal areas and horizontal integration with
external partners. Additionally, because it is highly customized according to the hospital’s
needs, the HMS modules, as well as the implementation of digital technologies, consider the
perceptions and experiences of professionals to enhance workflows through digitalization. This
information was identified in the "HMS presentation brochures" available on the institutional

Regarding the results achieved using HMS modules and integrated digital technologies,
