2.3.3 Data Analysis – validity, reliability and interpretation
For the qualitative data analysis, we employed an interactive, multi-stage process (Gioia
et al., 2013; Merriam & Tisdell, 2015). The primary goal was to answer the research question
by identifying relevant categories or emerging themes (Merriam & Tisdell, 2015). Accordingly,
based on transcriptions of audio-recorded interviews, we analyzed the data following the steps
of the Gioia methodology (Gioia et al., 2013). This methodology offers a systematic approach
to theory development, ensuring qualitative rig or in the execution and presentation of case
studies (Gioia et al., 2013). Previous studies have used the Gioia methodology to strengthen the
robustness of qualitative research analyses (Schiavone et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023).
In the first step of the Gioia methodology, we organized and categorized raw data into
first-order empirical concepts. Initially, we explored a wide range of terms from informants
(e.g., "The IT Director of Hospital C and the Hospital Management System Coordinator of
Hospital C a re the same person" ). During this stage, we aimed to adhere faithfully to the
language used by the informants while making only minimal attempts to extract categories to
prevent an unmanageable proliferation of categories early in the analysis. As the proc ess
progressed, we identified similarities and differences among these categories, allowing us to

52


refine and consolidate them into a more manageable structure. These categories were then
labeled with concise descriptions (e.g., "Public and private actors play active and distinct roles
in digital transformation").
The second step involved identifying second -order themes. At this stage, we
systematically analyzed the relationships between first -order empirical concepts, using axial
coding (Corbin & Strauss, 2 014) to group and consolidate them into broader second -order
themes (Gioia et al., 2013). For example, from the first-order empirical concepts "The hospital's
business model impacts the definition of the digital transformation strategy" and "Each hospital
has distinct models that influence different paths for HCDT," we developed the second -order
theme "Business model."
Once we identified a solid set of themes and concepts, achieving theoretical saturation,
we proceeded to the third step , organizing second-order themes into aggregated or theoretical
dimensions. At this stage, we aligned the emerging themes with the dimensions of the
theoretical framework presented in Figure 3: (1) Technology, (2) Organization, and (3)
Environment—ensuring consistency with the research objectives. Figure 4 provides a graphical
representation of our data coding and structuring process, illustrating examples of first -order
empirical concepts, second-order themes, and theoretical dimensions.

53



Figure 4. Data structure of the qualitative analysis

For validation, we cross-referenced data across the three theoretical dimensions for each
type of management strategy, analyzing the most frequently occurring second-order themes and
identifying the most relevant ones. To ensure coding consistency and establish inter -rater
reliability, a second member of the research team independently repeated the coding process
for both the first -order empirical concepts and the second -order themes (Gioia et al., 2013).
This approach reinforced the reliability of our analysis of the semi-structured interviews, as all
participants responded to the same structured questions in the same order. Further more, the
independent analysis conducted by the second researcher resulted in a high level of agreement
on the key themes, minimizing biases and enhancing the rigor of the qualitative analysis
process. Following Gioia et al. (2013), we also made a conscious effort at this stage to avoid an
in-depth review of the literature. Engaging too early with existing research could introduce
confirmation bias and restrict our perspective. Finally, the use of multiple data collection
methods further strengthened the reliability and validity of our study.
For the presentation, interpretation, and discussion of the cases (Goffin et al., 2019), we
used the three dimensions of TOE as guidelines for our narratives in each case study. For each

54


dimension of TOE, we present a n arrative that interrelates its highlighted elements and those
considered relevant for data analysis. We focus on interpreting these dimensions using the
perspectives of RBV, RV, and the hybrid governance between them. We discuss how the
elements of these t heoretical lenses provide support and are present in managing digital
resources in TDHC. The narratives mentioned before were reviewed to establish data
documentation, considering all data sources, reflections, ideas, and insights. Finally, as
recommended by Ketokivi and Choi (2014), the authors considered the idiosyncrasy and
transparency of reasoning to conduct multiple case studies rigorously. Figures 5, 6, and 7
synthesize the data analysis conducted, including the narrative of the case studies, designe d
through a final framework.

2.3.4 External validation
Since the exploratory case study investigates three hospital types within a single region
to control socio -economic context, we conducted an external validation of our findings after
the initial analysis. To this end, we used secondary data from business reports focused on
healthcare and digital transformation. Specifically, we examined reports published by globally
recognized consulting firms and institutions. These reports included case studies of digita l
transformation initiatives in public, private, and research/teaching hospitals, which we
compared with our own findings. While this comparison is inherently subjective and has its
limitations, it provided insights into the extent to which our results mig ht be generalizable
beyond the original context. We discuss the generalizability of our findings in Section 4.5 and
address the study’s limitations in the Conclusion (Section 5.3).

2.4 RESULTS
2.4.1 Case study 1: Public hospital (hospital A)
Hospital A is the largest unit of a group of public hospitals in the southern region of
Brazil, providing high -complexity care in its outpatient clinic, emergency department, and
inpatient services through the Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde - SUS). This
hospital offers 784 beds, representing about 55% of the group's total capacity, and manages
approximately 25,000 patients per year. Recently, the hospital invested at least $3 million in
expanding its Intensive Care Unit (ICU) sector, aiming t o further enhance its facilities by

55


increasing the number of beds from 40 to 59, thus becoming one of the largest ICUs of the
Unified Health System in Brazil. Additionally, it features state-of-the-art digital equipment and
a monitoring center that enables remote patient monitoring. We summarize in Figure 5 the
findings regarding the different dimensions of TOE, which will be explained next.


Figure 5. Configuration of internal management of digital resources for HCDT within the public health system

2.4.1.1 Technological context
Regarding the technological context ( Figure 5), if Hospital A wishes to implement a
digital technology resource available in the market, it must issue public notice and conduct a
bidding process, seeking the most suitable market price. Since this makes the digitalization
process very slow compared to technological evolution and market dynamics, the management
of Hospital A decided to internalize the technological development, maintaining absolute
control over the development of digital technology resources through its IT team.
When a technological project is approved, and the hospital has the necessary resources
available, whether in terms of knowledge, information, human, technological, or financial
resources, the IT team takes responsibility for the operationalization of the project, using their
expertise and skills to develop and implement the required technologies. The IT team develops
corporate management systems for department integration (e.g. Enterprise Resources Planning
- ERP), electronic medical records, data mining systems (used, for instan ce, in cancer care),

56


KPI monitoring, mobile applications, telemedicine solutions and prediction and forecasting
systems based on artificial intelligence.
The strategy of developing technological resources internally was also motivated by
high costs, biddi ng process and time. As a public entity, most of the Hospital A's revenue is
funded by government institutions, resulting in limited capital expenditure. This restricts
Hospital A from making significant investments in digital transformation. Outsourcing t o
external suppliers can involve high costs, as it not only requires investments in the digital
resources themselves but also in associated support services. Consequently, the hospital's
budget could be affected, as unexpected expenses may arise from digit alization, such as
software updates or equipment maintenance, compromising other priority expenditures
necessary for operations. Furthermore, if support services are not provided, digital resources
may become outdated or lack necessary maintenance, negativ ely impacting the hospital's
efficiency. By acquiring a digital resource externally rather than developing it internally,
Hospital A will depend on the bidding process to form contracts with suppliers. In this context,
contract management can be challengin g and bureaucratic. Hospital A must prove and ensure
the transparency of the invested funds' destination to various governmental and public
instances. In some situations, suppliers may not fully meet the established requirements in the
contract, causing de lays in delivering the digital resource or service. As a result, Hospital A
may become dependent on the supplier, without the possibility of terminating the contract, since
the financial resources have already been transferred and processed through transpa rency
channels. Another limiting factor is the response time to meet internal demands of improving
their operation. This is because Hospital A needs to conduct a thorough technical analysis of
the environment that will receive the technology, considering r equirements, adaptations,
infrastructure, and presidential approval, among other factors that are to provide transparency
of the public funds. This, coupled with the procedures of bidding processes (in the case of
outsourcing), can take a long time, delayi ng improvements and even compromising patients'
lives.
In sum, this hospital prioritizes internal resource development, emphasizing self -
sufficiency due to the high transactional costs of dealing with technology providers. The
internal team has a detailed understanding of the integration among processes, people, and
technologies, facilitating the customization of digital transformation in the hospital. Manager
1A of Public Hospital A, for example, comments on the adoption of the strategy to customize
their own management system that integrates all information and data. According to him, “ the

57


volatility of software companies and the processes involved, especially for public environments,
as well as the exchange and/or the creation of new companies, can affec t the service provided
by them, leading to delays or contract breaches .” Additionally, he also explained: “ The
response time for customization demands is much faster than dealing, for example, with the
contracting of outsourced software, which is prevalent in private hospitals, managing their
healthcare services”.
2.4.1.2 Organizational context
In relation to the organizational context of managing internal digital resources for
HCDT (Figure 5), Hospital A adopts the business model of full internalization, which is
characterized by complete centralization of the development and implementation organizational
structure. In terms of governance structure, Hospital A consists of various departments,
including education and research, and information technology. Each of the se departments
reports to specific directorates, which, in turn, are under the oversight of the executive board.
During the interview with the IT coordinator, it was emphasized that Hospital A started by
establishing an internal culture focused on DT, with awareness programs for professionals and
top management, aiming to use internal digital resources to develop HCDT and address
operational issues. For this purpose, a specific committee was formed to manage HCDT,
aligned with the hospital's strategies. Add itionally, the executive leadership has established a
Technology Incorporation Core, which can decide whether a technology project should or
should not be integrated into the hospital. The HCDT process enables professionals,
departments, and management at Hospital A to establish informal linkage and communication
through suggestions, visits, and meetings with teams, such as doctors, nurses, administrative
staff, and supervisors, to identify issues and opportunities related to the development and
implementation of digital technologies. According to Interviewee 1A and reinforced by
Interviewee 2A, both these informal linkages and the strategies established in the hospital's
strategic planning are two of the main sources of origin for innovation in operations.
In terms of basic infrastructure resources for HCDT, initially, Hospital A decided to
make a more focused investment in primary processes, such as renovating rooms and
departments and implementing internal corporate Wi -Fi network access points that enable the
connectivity of mobile devices, IoT and medical sensors, equipment, and systems to integrate
processes and patients in real-time. According to the IT manager, this is one of the fundamental
first steps to initiate DT, as it serves as the foundation for data collection and monitoring, as
well as enabling interoperability within the hospital. All collected data (e.g. electronic medical

58


records, patient treatments, the number of consultations) is stored in a Data Center and will be
used in future technological applications. Digital resources are developed by the internal IT
team, consisting of 34 professionals, with 12 dedicated to development and 22 responsible for
Level I support, basic support, and microinformatics support, all with higher education. These
professionals possess specialized knowledge and are aligned with the hospital's organizational
culture, allowing them to drive the HCDT in operations through the valuable and rare digital
resources developed.
Finally, to maintain the quality in the development and use of technologies, hospital
employees undergo continuous training and capacity -building processes. Specific courses are
offered by teaching and research management, allowing employees to learn about the processes
and use of technologies. This practice is essential to ensure that the team is up -to-date and
possesses the necessary skills to handle evolving technologies. Additionally, the hospital
emphasizes the importance of intensity in research and develop ment (R&D) with universities
through applied projects.
2.4.1.3 Environmental context
In relation to the environmental context of managing internal digital resources for
HCDT (Figure 5), although Hospital A initially established a culture of complete internalization
of digital resources, the hospital also relies on external partners that provide support in activities
related to HCDT. According to interviewees A1 and A2, there are six main types of partners
that support Hospital A in managing digital resources internally for HCDT.
The government provides necessary financial resources for the hospital's operation,
maintenance, and technological investments. Additionally, they are related to compliance with
regulations and guidelines imposed by the Unified Health Syste m (SUS). Hospital A also
establishes partnerships with funding institutions through participation in calls for financial
resources to support the development of open -source software. Universities are essential
partners, establishing cooperation agreements with the hospital for the development of non -
profit research and development projects. These projects aim to advance the development of
technological resources, using data and information from the hospital as a foundation, as well
as gaining access to comp lementary information and knowledge. There are agreements
established with AI and Analytics Institutes, where cooperation agreements are signed between
the entities for project development. These agreements aim to leverage the expertise of these
institutes in the use of AI and data analysis to drive the hospital's technological advancement.

59


Finally, commercial technology suppliers are included as the hospital establishes collaborative
alliances through bidding processes with specialized technology companies or solution
providers, although this is specialized for only specific cases.

2.4.2 Case study 2: Private hospital (hospital B)
Hospital B is a private institution that offers comprehensive healthcare solutions in
various areas, including diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring, with a focus on providing
humanized, safe, and patient -centered care. It is part of a group of healthcare b usiness units,
serving as the main business of the group. It comprises four large units and three major colleges,
employing over 4,200 staff members. The hospital provides 312 active inpatient beds. It also
houses over 2,000 advanced technology equipment and has a team of professionals from various
fields, including more than 2,300 accredited physicians. This hospital stands out as an
organization with multiple accreditations and awards related to healthcare digital
transformation and was recognized as one of the top ten hospitals in Brazil in 2024 and holds
the Gold Seal of Accreditation from the American College of Radiology (ACR). Figure 6
summarizes the TOE structure of this case which will be described next.


Figure 6. Configuration of external management of digital resources for HCDT within the private health system

2.4.2.1. Technological context
In relation to the technological context for HCDT ( Figure 6), Hospital B has adopted
the strategy of acquiring digital resources exte rnally instead of developing them in house,
establishing strong outsourcing partnerships with commercial suppliers in the sector. This
strategy has allowed the hospital to implement cutting -edge digital technologies, adopt
innovative management practices, and deliver services, thus creating a healthcare innovation
ecosystem.
Interviewees 1B and 2B explained that the culture of the relationship with external
partners enables the hospital to access technological resources in a practical and fast manner.
According to the business coordinator (Interviewee 3B), Hospital B manages external digital
resources through direct contracts with suppliers involving three modalities: Software as a
Service (SaaS), full technology acquisition, and human services provision. Th is approach
combines different components to drive Hospital B's DT, enabling better integration of
technology and services to achieve its goals. Some of the technologies provided by the
ecosystem are IoT and biomedical sensors for connectivity, wearable de vices, cloud -based
applications and systems, collaborative robots, big data and analytics, artificial intelligence
algorithms, enterprise resource planning (ERP), patient management systems, telemedicine,
and augmented and virtual reality. Additionally, th e hospital utilizes technologies for process
simulation, 3D printing, and room service systems, among others. According to Interviewee
1B, "Together, they [these technologies] allow for vertical and horizontal integration of the
hospital, providing visibility into all operations and automation of repetitive human and manual
activities".
According to the IT Manager for digital transformation, the strategy of managing
external digital resources to drive HCDT was motivated by four main aspects: availability and
flexibility (changes and supplier replacement at any time) of technological options in the market
to reduce potential risks; from an economic standpoint, it is more viable for the hospital to
outsource rather than develop and manage internally, because Hospital B does not have costs
of suit as high as in the public case; availability of financial resources for outsourcing; and
streamlined bureaucratic processes for hiring, reducing the time required to implement new
technologies.

61


2.4.2.2. Organizational context
Regarding the organizational context ( Figure 6), over more than ten years, Hospital B
has become a data -driven organization, focused on collecting data from both managerial and
clinical aspects. Therefore, the strategies and investments for HCDT are defin ed considering
this scenario. Hospital B has a high level of maturity in terms of visibility and transparency of
its operations, as emphasized by the IT Manager: “ Being a data -driven organization, we are
aware of the main pain points and bottlenecks in processes and we know how DT can leverage
improvements, whether in administrative, financial, accounting, procurement, pharmacy,
surgical block, intensive care unit (ICU), hospitalization unit, among others ”. This allows top
management to communicate with ope rational teams, understand their needs, and integrate
information to support the decision-making process in technology-related investments.
In terms of organizational management, Hospital B is comprised of directorates that
collaborate to oversee and imple ment digital transformation strategies within the hospital.
According to the Business Coordinator (Interviewee 3B), the directorates have chosen to
decentralize the management of some of their operations to third parties, such as equipment,
systems, and te chnology maintenance, allowing the institution to focus on the creation of
solutions and innovation. This results in cost reduction and a decreased workload, as well as
production optimization.
When a digital resource project is implemented by an ecosyste m partner, the IT team
takes responsibility for monitoring and overseeing its functionality for six months. The IT team
receives instructions and utilizes their knowledge and skills to ensure that the digital resources
function efficiently and meet the hos pital's internal needs. The team is composed of 50
specialized professionals in DT and is aligned with the organizational culture of staying up to
date with market technological trends to drive digitalization in the hospital. This team strongly
focuses on orchestrating the ecosystem based on the hospital's power structure to purchase
advanced technology without major acquisition processes. In other words, they have financial
resources and freedom to ensure operations are based on the best technology availab le in the
market. The hospital has a service request to acquire technologies with well -defined rules. In
this system, professionals can file complaints, requests, or suggestions for solutions to the
problems they or their departments face. This process cre ates a record that the IT team will
analyze, potentially generating knowledge and leading to technological innovations within the
hospital. Thus, technologies are defined from a bottom -up approach based on the operational
needs of the professionals.

62


In ter ms of basic infrastructure resources for technological innovation, the three
interviewees highlighted that Hospital B prepares the environment for the implementation of
technological resources, encompassing everything from civil construction to the installation of
support equipment. According to Interviewer 1B, “You can't make any modifications without a
good infrastructure. This was a problem we had previously at the hospital, hindering the
implementation of technologies ”. Like the public hospital, Hospita l B also has an internal
corporate network that enables connectivity for mobile devices (e.g. smartwatches,
smartphones, tablets), IoT sensors, hardware, and medical equipment, integrating all
departments in real-time. Interviewee 2B also emphasized that t his is one of the fundamental
elements to starting DT in a hospital as it serves as a foundation for data collection and
transmission, enabling digitized processes and interoperability throughout the institution. He
also pointed out that, for the implement ation of digital technological resources, it is necessary
to have a gateway to input the information, allowing partners to quickly connect their solutions.
Another important factor highlighted to increase the hospital's digitalization is the
continuous investment in the adequacy, training, and capacitation of employees and monitoring
of new technologies. Specific courses are conducted for employees to learn about the use of
emerging technologies and services to develop new skills. Furthermore, participating in digital
health technology events and symposia allows professionals from Hospital B to conduct
benchmarking and exchange experiences with other hospitals regarding HCDT.
2.4.2.3. Environmental context
In relation to the environmental context of managing external digital resources for
HCDT (Figure 6), Hospital B has established a culture of relationship with external partners to
manage digital resources. In this way, it has created an ecosystem to adopt and develop HCDT.
This approach implies that the hosp ital had to create an orchestration capability to coordinate
the ecosystem of partners. The ecosystem is composed of eight different types of external
partners that develop innovative solutions for the healthcare sector.
Hospital B collaborates with publi c actors (e.g., government, regulatory or oversight
agencies, such as the Health National Agency - ONS) to comply with norms and guidelines
established for HCDT. The hospital identifies and selects suppliers that align with its
institutional guidelines and can contribute to the excellence of the provided services,
establishing collaborative relationships through contracts. This enables them to obtain relevant
certifications like the Joint Commission International . These suppliers are both national and

63


international, with some being located close to their facilities. Hospital B also develops and
implements technological projects in its operations in partnership with startups. This allows to
test proof of concepts within the hospital. Other hospitals and partn er clinics are also engaged
in such an ecosystem to provide knowledge on how to use new technologies. This is coordinated
through the engagement with the National Association of Private Hospitals in Brazil
(Associação Nacional de Hospitais Privados - ANAHP). Furthermore, insurers, health plans,
and covenants, are also partners of the ecosystem, and they provide data and information to
improve the joint digital services. The hospital also focuses on the innovativeness of the
healthcare system by developing c ollaboration with universities and research centers. From a
geographical perspective, Interviewee 1B emphasized that the proximity to the mentioned
partners favors communication and the relationship between the parties. In this sense, the
location of this hospital in a healthcare industry cluster is a keystone of this business model.

2.4.3 Case study 3: Research-oriented hospital (Hospital C)
Hospital C is a public research hospital focused on high complexity healthcare services
in a wide range of specialties through the Unified Health System (SUS). It is academically
affiliated to the largest public university of the region. The hospital offers approximately 836
inpatient beds and has 6.733 employees. In the last two years, the hospital has conducted over
60,279 hospitalizations and 883.507 consultations. The research conducted by this hospital, in
turn, generates new knowledge, techniques, and technological advancements. During the
Covid-19 pandemic, this hospital innovated by offering new technological servic es, such as
telemedicine and telehealth, as well as distance health education for remote communities.
Additionally, technologies were implemented for the protection of patients and staff,
management of patients with respiratory problems, and team training as contingency measures
to mitigate the effects of the pandemic. Figure 7 summarizes the TOE structure of this hospital,
which will be described next.

2.4.3.1. Technological context
In relation to the technological context for HCDT (Figure 7), Hospital C has established
a hybrid governance strategy to manage digital resources, combining the internal development
of digital resources with the establishment of collaborative alliances to acquire external digital
resources. Internally, Interviewee 1C explained that Hospital C uses its own available resources,
such as human, knowledge, and information, to develop digital technologies for HCDT. For
instance, the internal team develops IoT connectivity for equipment and patient monitoring,
cloud-based computing applications, corporate management systems for department integration
(e.g., ERP), electronic health records, e -prescriptions, telemedicine, and other solutions based
on big data analytics, and AI -based prediction solutions. A data science center is also under
development to store data and expand the hospital's DT capabilities.
However, according to Interviewer 2C, “ In some situations, there are limitations to
internally develop technological projects for HCDT, often requiring external digital resources
that are scarce for the hospital or that it lacks the conditions to develop ”. To overcome these
limitations, Interviewees 1C, 2C, and 3C explained that the institution maintains relationships
with external partners to support and accelerate HCDT at the hospital. This culture of
partnerships enables Hospital C to access complementary digital resources and capabilities (e.g.

65


financial resources, costs shared, human resources, new skills, hardwares and softwares),
whether for internal development or complete acquisition of the digital resources.
According to all interviewees from Hospital C, the strategy of managing digital
resources through hybrid governance for HCDT is primarily motivated by three reasons. First,
as a research hospital, its essence l ies in using teaching and research to develop technological
projects. Second, there is a large IT team available with expertise in the subject and flexibility
for updates. Third, the hospital aims to overcome the limitations and challenges of internal
digital resources by leveraging the support of external digital resources through collaborative
alliances. This is because, being a public entity, it shares the same configurations as a public
organization; for example, outsourcing alone may involve high costs and bureaucratic contract
management (see section 4.1.1). External partnerships are necessary to complement the internal
resources and capabilities of the hospital, but not to substitute them. In addition to these three
reasons, Interviewee 1C highlighted that Hospital C, being a teaching and research hospital,
was motivated by two additional objectives: the replication of the technological resources
developed and the organizational management model for HCDT in other hospitals (public or
private), and the acquisition of complementary resources to meet the requirements for HIMSS
certification (Healthcare Information and Management Systems Society). For this, the hospital
hired specialized consulting services to provide support in the development of the neces sary
actions.
2.4.3.2. Organizational context
Regarding the organizational context of hybrid governance of digital resources for
HCDT (Figure 7), Hospital C has adopted an open innovation model, involving multiple actors.
This model is particularly applied due to the institution's nature of education and research,
which receives resources from partners to drive R&D activities. Additionally, it plays a
transformative role, supporting the technological development of other healthcare entities.
Therefore, governance is focused on both internal and external resources. Strategies for HCDT
are defined considering this scenario, with the aim of fostering joint efforts for technological
development and innovation both within and outside the organization. This approach has
enabled Hospital C to stand out at the national level, being recognized as a benchmark for more
than 84 hospitals and healthcare institutions across the country.
The internal IT team is a large group with over 90 skilled professionals, including
statisticians and experts in BI and machine learning, responsible for the development,

66


operationalization, and maintenance of most technological applications used in both internal
and external operations. These professionals are aligned with the organizational cultur e of
research and development, enabling them to drive innovation both within and outside the
hospital. In terms of organizational management, Interviewee 2C explained that Hospital C has
a strategic HCDT committee (comprising representatives from all hospi tal directorates),
responsible for coordinating the entire institution's HCDT strategy. In this committee, projects
are defined and prioritized for technology adoption. The needs and demands of different
departments are brought to the HCDT committee throug h formal and informal channels. As a
result, problems and opportunities within the sector are meticulously assessed. This approach
allows top management to establish informal links and communicate with departments at the
operational level, understand their needs, and integrate the information to structure the decision-
making process regarding technological innovations.
Regarding the basic infrastructure for technological innovation, the five interviewees
emphasized that Hospital C invested in electronic equ ipment and an internal network that
enables connectivity for IoT sensors and mobile devices, as well as management systems that
allow real -time data and information transmission. Interviewees also highlighted that
modifications were made to rooms or depart ments for the adoption of digital resources.
Moreover, in terms of healthcare service quality and patient safety, Hospital C's employees also
undergo training and capacity -building to enhance patient satisfaction and operational
performance, making the mos t of available technologies. As explained by the ICT Manager,
“The hospital C invests in the training and continuous learning of professionals to achieve
better results in the development of specialized technologies”. Moreover, it is supported by an
innovation and technology transfer board composed of members from the IT department,
aiming to facilitate and enable innovation and technology transfer initiatives to society. This
allows for the creation of research projects to develop innovative technological processes and
resources. Additionally, the implementation of a data literacy culture within the institution is
underway, enabling employees to act as multipliers of the use of these technological resources.
2.4.3.3. Environmental context
From the environmental context point of view (Figure 7), Hospital C establishes external
partnerships to acquire specific and complementary digital resources. As observed in Hospitals
A and B, these external partnerships have also allowed Hospital C to access knowledge sharing.
However, as a research-oriented healthcare institution, its aim with such partnership is also to
share good practices and help to build together with the external partners an HCDT vision for

67


the ecosystem, which includes even the technology transfer of the digital solutions developed
internally.
The hospital’s environmental context comprises five main actors. First, government
actors operate as providers of the financial resources necessary for the investments in
technological development. On the other hand, the Hospital C, as an educationa l and research
institution, collaborates with the government in the development of public policies for the
expansion of HCDT in the Brazilian public healthcare system. The second partner are the
Universities and research centers, that act as collaborators in the development of R&D projects
for HCDT, sharing such kind of costs through cooperation agreements. Third, public and private
hospitals establish collaborative alliances with Hospital C to expand and adopt the technological
resources developed by Hospital C in their operations, promoting the sharing of knowledge and
information. Fourth, civil and military entities use their knowledge, information, and human
resources to update or develop new modules and complementary applications for the hospital
management system of Hospital C, especially when the hospital cannot do so on its own or
when these entities design technological solutions that can be utilized by Hospital C. This
collaboration is made possible through a cooperation agreement, in which Hospital C provides
its internal hospital management system for these entities to use in their operations. In return,
the military entities commit to supporting the management and continuous improvement of
Hospital C's hospital management system. Finally, Hospital C maintains collaborative
relationships with specialized technology companies or solution providers, which are
contracted through bidding processes for the supply of specialized technological solutions that
are beyond the skills of the internal IT team.
Another important element highlighted in the interviews was the capability of Hospital
C to orchestrate HCDT in a healthcare innovation ecosystem. Hospital C acts as an orchestrator
of the digital health ecosystem, harmoniously coordinating various resources, stakeholders, and
digital technologies to achieve digitization goals and enhance the overall performance of its
operations and partners. This role was emphasized by Interviewee 2C, who stated, “Hospital C
has the capacity to orchestrate HCDT, as it is a n educational and research entity. Managing
digital resources in collaboration with other stakeholders provides autonomy and leadership
for innovation projects”. He further adds, “Coordinating technological projects fosters a
culture of building alliances with partners, as well as developing high -quality and suitable
solutions to meet our needs or certification requirements ”. Compared to Hospital B (Section
4.2), an important difference in such orchestration is that Hospital C aims to create a knowledge

68


flow among the partners to create new knowledge and technological progress. On the other
hand, since Hospital B is a private profit -oriented institution, its goal is different, as it aims to
orchestrate the ecosystem to obtain integrated solutions for its operations.

2.4.5 Comparison with secondary data for external validation
To validate our findings beyond the original context, we examined secondary data from
KPMG’s (2024) business report on healthcare transformation, which presents international case
studies on how digital transformation is reshaping hospitals. One such example is Nova Scotia
Health in Canada (KPMG, 2024, pp. 26 –30), a public initiative aimed at transforming the
healthcare system. A notable convergence with our analysis is that their transformation was
guided by the principles of "people, process, and technolo gy," which aligns closely with our
use of the TOE framework. Moreover, like our public hospital case, Nova Scotia Health
implemented a centralized coordination center to internalize data-driven decision-making. This
indicates that, even in other countries, public healthcare institutions tend to internalize key
digital resources.
The KPMG report also highlights research hospitals, notably the case of the Digital
Health Village developed by Helsinki University Hospital in Finland. This initiative established
a hybrid ecosystem using a customizable digital platform —an approach that mirrors the
configuration we observed in our research/teaching hospital case. According to the report, “The
Digital Health Village was built in such a way that healthcare profession als could take
ownership of the design of the digital health pathways relevant to their specialty areas. That
meant that the Digital Health Village could be rapidly scaled up as healthcare professionals
worked in parallel on their own pathways” (KPMG, 2024, p. 29). These pathways are intended
not to replace, but to enhance, traditional care through digital tools such as guided self -care,
remote monitoring, and automated reminders. The project was designed with scalability in
mind, allowing internally proven solutions to be extended externally with appropriate support.
With respect to private hospitals, our findings are consistent with trends reported by
consultancy sources such as S&S Insider (2025), which emphasize the growing outsourcing of
IT and digi tal activities by private healthcare providers. This outsourcing is increasingly
adopted as a strategy to enhance operational efficiency and reduce costs, particularly in markets
like the United States, where private healthcare providers dominate (S&S Insider, 2022). In this
sense, private hospitals tend to build digital ecosystems as those investigated in our results.

2.5 DISCUSSION
Our results provide a new perspective on the study of digital transformation in
healthcare systems. The findings challenge the existing literature, as we demonstrate that there

70


is no single way to approach the management of HCDT. Prior studies simplify this aspect by
considering general elements involved in HCDT management without differentiating between
business model profiles (To rtorella et al., 2020; Tortorella et al., 2021; Raimo et al., 2023;
Mauro et al., 2024).
In this regard, our results show that the management system can follow different
orientations based on RBV, RV, or hybrid governance, depending on the type of hospital , its
objectives with digital transformation, and the financial sources supporting technological
changes. Prior literature typically considers HCDT either from the perspective of developing
competitive internal resources (Chaudhuri et al., 2023; Dicuonzo e t al., 2023) or building
external relationships (Schiavone et al., 2021; Aranyossy & Halmosi, 2024; Malik et al., 2024).
Our findings indicate that these two perspectives are linked to specific contexts: the first
(internal resources) is more relevant to p ublic hospital systems, whereas the latter (external
resources) is more prominent in private hospital systems. Of course, a private hospital may seek
to internalize digital resources for various reasons, just as public hospitals may opt for
outsourcing. Ho wever, we identified an interrelated mechanism that generates greater
advantage when combining public hospitals with internal resources and private hospitals with
external resources.
These interrelated mechanisms are summarized in the key drivers of adopti on, which
we present in Table 4. They are rooted in the reduction of switching costs resulting from public
healthcare bidding processes and in the pursuit of efficiency and specialization in private
healthcare organizations. In sum, while specific circumstances may justify the opposite choices
for public and private hospitals, the most expected approach can be clearly explained by our
findings.
Furthermore, hospitals must consider what Ayala et al. (2017) highlighted in another
research domain: although org anizations may choose to externalize or internalize digital
resources, it is always necessary to maintain the alternative as a complementary resource base.
When HCDT relies on external digital resources, it is important to establish an internal
foundation for long -term sustainability, particularly when digital transformation becomes a
central competitive element. In such cases, private hospitals that acquire highly specialized
digital technologies must at least internalize a basic level of digital capability (e.g., a small but
skilled IT team) to effectively orchestrate the external ecosystem, as seen in our case.
Conversely, when digital transformation is driven by internal resources, as in the public hospital

71


studied, the internal team must establish partn erships for technologies they cannot develop at
market speed (e.g., cybersecurity solutions). Thus, our findings highlight the priorities of each
model, rather than suggesting that resources are purely internal or external - we focus on the
predominant approach in each case.
We also contribute to the literature by identifying a third model of digital resource
management in HCDT: hybrid governance, which our findings associate with research hospitals
and their focus on R&D and innovation. We are not the first to explore this direction, as Franco
et al. (2024) recently demonstrated that hybrid governance is a key strategy for blending digital
resources in supply chain management. Their study highlights how hybrid governance helps
balance internal and external strengths and weaknesses to achieve a more robust digital resource
structure. However, our findings suggest that, in the case of research hospitals, hybrid
governance is driven by a different need. We show that these hospitals base much of their
development on R&D grants and combine internal development with external partnerships
through an open innovation approach, which helps justify funding sources. This governance
structure aligns well with the specific business model of research hospitals. While Franco et al.
(2024) emphasize hybrid governance as a means of balance, our study highlights its role as a
funding-driven strategy, revealing a distinct rationale behind its adoption.
The TOE perspective also helped us identify new elements not explicitly addressed in
prior literature. First, we show that the organizational and external environment dimensions
differ significantly among the three hospital types, particularly in their eco system approaches
and organizational structures. While the healthcare literature has discussed the value of
ecosystems and network activity in fostering innovation (Secundo et al., 2019; Schiavone et al.,
2021; Dal Mas et al., 2023; Aloni et al., 2023), we demonstrate that HCDT ecosystem
engagement differs between private and research hospitals. Private hospitals orchestrate
technology providers to ensure interoperability and seamless integration into healthcare
processes. Here, orchestration involves conso lidating and aligning external actors, with the
hospital as the central coordinator and focal point of the ecosystem (Schiavone et al., 2021). In
contrast, research hospitals, which are innovation -driven, engage in horizontal collaborations
with external institutions and stakeholders, treating them as partners rather than suppliers. These
two ecosystem models are fundamentally different: the former aims to extract maximum value
from external partners, while the latter focuses on co -developing value with ext ernal
stakeholders. Finally, public hospitals exhibit a more centralized approach, focusing on internal
coordination across functional departments. Given their scale and complexity, they resemble

72


internal ecosystems, managing a diverse array of employees a nd processes within the
organization.
Although the digital technologies adopted by these hospitals are fundamentally similar
– consistent with prior studies on HCDT technologies (Tortorella et al., 2020; Tortorella et al.,
2022; Raimo et al., 2023; Mauro et al., 2024) – we observed differences in their technological
approaches. The public hospital's HCDT is driven by internal organizational needs, with digital
transformation being primarily influenced by healthcare professionals’ demands. This explains
why an internal digital resource structure is often the most appropriate for this model. In
contrast, the private hospital adopts a more aggressive approach, with HCDT being propelled
by performance and competitiveness objectives. External digital resources are more suitable for
this model, as they enable rapid adaptation to the best solutions available in the market. Lastly,
the research hospital pursues an innovative technological approach, taking greater risks in
experimenting with new technologies. These di stinct profiles define different innovation
pathways within HCDT.

2.6 CONCLUSION
This study investigated how three distinct hospital models —public, private, and
research-oriented—manage digital resources in their HCDT efforts. Rather than treating HCDT
as a uniform process, we analyzed how each hospital’s business model, financial structure, and
institutional logic shape their approach, using the TOE framework and insights from RBV, RV,
and hybrid governance theory. Our findings reveal distinct configurations of digital resource
governance—internal, external, and hybrid —each aligned with specific organizational
contexts. We highlight the importance of ecosystem orchestration, the complementarity
between internal and external resources, and the unique role of h ybrid governance in research
hospitals. By offering a typology of HCDT strategies and explaining their underlying
mechanisms, this study refines the conceptual understanding of digital transformation in
healthcare and provides practical guidance for tailor ing digital strategies to different hospital
models.
2.6.1 Theoretical implications
Our study contributes to the healthcare management literature by focusing on an
unexplored perspective of digital transformation. We demonstrate that HCDT strategies are
highly sensitive to the hospital's business model, challenging the prevailing notion of a uniform

73


digital transformation path in healthcare. We also identified an interrelated mechanism that
generates greater advantage when combining the hospital’s operation model with the form of
managing the digital resources. Therefore, our study challenges the usual assumption of HCDT
literature by demonstrating that managerial decisions regarding the internalization or
outsourcing of digital resources are not as freely open to make-or-buy choices as healthcare
scholars might assume. Instead, these decisions are highly dependent on the hospital’s
organizational structure and the nature of its financial resources. This dependency also
influences the TOE dimensions, which vary significantly across different business model types:
private healthcare organizations, public healthcare organizations, and research -oriented
healthcare organizations.
From a theoretical perspective, we show that the resource-based view (RBV), relational
view (RV), and hybrid governance serve as valuable lenses for describing each organizational
structure we identified. However, none of them fully capture the dynamics of all hospital
business models. For instance, applying RBV to analyze a research hospital ma y lead to a
limited or even biased perspective, as our findings suggest that hybrid governance better
explains the underlying structure of HCDT in such organizations. Similarly, adopting a
relational view to examine public hospitals with bidding processes may fall short, as our results
indicate that focusing on internal resources provides a more accurate depiction of this profile.
Thus, our study contributes by characterizing hospital business models in relation to their
HCDT strategies and corresponding ma nagement structures. Furthermore, we highlight how
the institutional profile also shapes the hospital’s connection to the broader business
environment. Ecosystem dynamics vary depending on the HCDT approach, and orchestration
capabilities differ significantly, particularly between private and research hospitals.

2.6.2 Managerial implications
From a managerial perspective, hospitals can use these structural insights as a
foundation for digitizing specific smart healthcare dimensions, such as operations, workforce
management, consumption, supply chain, and services. As observed in our investigation, digital
resource management configurations also take into account the need to establish a healthcare
digital ecosystem. This approach helps reduce sociocultural barrier s and enables resource
sharing, facilitating both the internal and external development and adoption of HCDT (e.g., as
seen in the case of Hospital C). The digital transformation of healthcare organizations presents

74


an innovative scenario where the actual contributions of external actors to organizational
structures for HCDT management can be verified. Recognizing these contributions can help
convince key stakeholders —both internal and external —of the importance of implementing
HCDT. Furthermore, policymakers can leverage our findings to design policies that foster the
evolution of HCDT across different healthcare environments, whether public, private, or
research-oriented. This, in turn, can support the digital transformation of hospitals that are still
in the pre-digital stage, ultimately improving the performance of medical service delivery at a
national level.

2.6.3 Limitations and future research
This study presents several limitations that also suggest avenues for future research.
First, our analysis focused on a single hospital for each type of digital resource management
strategy. Although we conducted an external validation to demonstrate that our findings are not
necessarily limited to the original context, the limited availability of literature—both academic
and business—on the role of internal versus external digital resources in healthcare indicates
that this remains an underexplored area. Consequently, our results are still subject to the
inherent limitations of a qualitative study based on a small num ber of cases, which restricts
broader generalization. While the selected cases offer useful models for understanding how the
HCDT process unfolds, it is essential to examine additional cases that reflect incremental
developments in HCDT. Such efforts would provide further evidence on resource management
strategies and highlight potential challenges that hospitals may encounter throughout the
transformation journey. Moreover, future research should explore these dynamics in countries
with different healthcare systems, as national institutional structures and policies also influence
how individual hospitals pursue digital transformation.
Moreover, not all hospitals have a digital strategy as clearly defined as those analyzed
in this study. Future research could replicate our data collection and analysis in hospitals that
do not follow these digital resource management strategies for HCDT, enabling meaningful
comparisons on how digital resource management influences hospital operational performance.
Second, another limitation of our study is its macro perspective on the organizational
management structure of HCDT in hospitals. While this bro ad view is valuable, hospitals
consist of multiple departments with distinct functions and characteristics, such as emergency,
diagnostic, and outpatient services. Although our study provides an overarching perspective,

75


future research should explore the s pecific nuances within different hospital departments.
Finally, future studies could adopt quantitative approaches with larger samples to further
expand the insights generated here and identify potential patterns. For instance, quantitative
analyses could assess the relationship between organizational structure, digital strategy, and
digital resources in the context of HCDT, offering a more systematic understanding of these
dynamics.
