Regarding the results achieved using HMS modules and integrated digital technologies,
secondary data — specifically the HMS performance folders provided in 2023 and available on
the hospital’s institutional website — indicate significant progress. In the HMS supply module,
for example, with the adoption of RFID technology, the time required to complete inventory
was reduced from 720 minutes to just 10 minutes. Inventory accuracy increased from 84.5% to
98.45%. Restocking time dropped from 225 minutes to 21 minutes. Furthermore, the
discrepancy rate about the total number of items withdrawn, previously at -30%, was reduced
to 0%. The same secondary source also showed a substantial reduction in paper usage in

151


operations and storage: from 8,733 kg in 2018 to 2,675 kg in 2023 — demonstrating not only
significant economic savings for the hospital but also sustainable gains.
4.4.3. HCDT as a socio-technical system – social aspects
Individuals interacting within processes
The starting point for changes in interactions between healthcare professionals and
processes in the hospital was establishing a digital culture focused on the individual, in which
the healthcare professional was seen as a key agent capable of driving change. This is because
professionals possess knowledge of the processes, due to their daily interactions with patients
and colleagues, and the ability to identify digital resources and propose technological solutions
best suited to transform the processes the y engage with. From this perspective, the hospital
views healthcare professionals not merely as users of technology, but as active participants in
the development and implementation of digital technologies, working alongside the IT team
and hospital managers to shift from analog to digital processes. As a result, it becomes possible
to modify interactions between professionals and processes, making them digitally tailored to
the needs and expectations of each department, while also promoting patient well-being.
The interviewees strongly emphasized this aspect; for example, the IT coordinator (R03)
commented: “The relationship that the IT team has with professionals from the business areas
in the implementation of HCDT is a key differentiator for the hospita l. Often, we suggest
solutions, but when we arrive in a specific department, the physician or nurse in charge has
already developed the ideas and identified the necessary resources, using their knowledge and
understanding of the workflow to propose improve ments to the process and optimize daily
routines.” The nephrologist (R24) also reinforced this finding: “Nephrology is a highly complex
specialty with several branches. Therefore, when structuring a digital project for the area, it is
essential to understa nd how it previously functioned. In general, only the professionals who
work directly in the field can visualize the processes and their interactions, as well as anticipate
challenges, thus avoiding future issues related to poor implementation of digital t echnologies
or the lack of necessary support resources.”
In this way, the introduction of HCDT generated a self -reinforcing cycle, in which
professionals (e.g., IT professionals in the context of HMS’s module development, or doctors
and nurses in daily tas ks) learned from process -related mistakes and used this knowledge to
continuously propose improvements. This includes developing new HMS modules and/or

152


integrating additional digital technologies, as well as building the foundational infrastructure
for the processes carried out by professionals—generating knowledge through trial and error.
More specifically, the interviewees emphasized that changes in interactions between
healthcare professionals and processes with the adoption of HCDT begin with process mapping.
They highlighted that accurately mapping healthcare professionals’ processes and tasks is
essential to identify gaps in interactions with patients and other professionals. Furthermore, it
supports hospital managers in decision -making regarding investments and resource allocation
related to HCDT (e.g., IT teams, hardware acquisition, or outsourcing to an external partner) to
meet these needs. Process mapping also helps determine whether processes are rigid or flexible,
as they may follow different pat hs of change. According to interviewee R33, when properly
conducted, process mapping facilitates the effective adoption of digital technologies, benefiting
both the interactions between professionals and processes and the hospital's overall
performance, making it more resilient and sustainable. Interviewees R33 and R20 emphasized
that mapping processes alongside healthcare professionals strengthens their commitment to
developing new digital solutions, such as HMS modules, dashboard applications for data
visualization, electronic panels, exam scheduling, and telemedicine, and fosters the
development of resilient skills among professionals, such as monitoring, anticipating,
responding, and learning. For example, by participating in governance committees and working
groups or by taking on Project Owner (PO) roles in digital projects, healthcare professionals
actively contribute to process mapping and sharing of digital technology suggestions for
discussion with other members, drawing on their own and their colle agues’ prior experiences.
This generates a sense of professional appreciation and helps expand DT across processes.
Operationally, professionals help reduce workload in processes, improving the use of
time and space, and eliminate redundant procedures. Add itionally, they enhance clinical
decision-making and implement more structured information -recording processes, requiring
less cognitive effort. On the IT side, this enables the development of HMS module architectures
that better reflect actual workflows, with more intuitive interfaces, fewer clicks to perform
clinical procedures, and easier access to historical data. Nurse and manager R09 provided an
example of how healthcare professionals participate in changing process interactions: "My team
and I partic ipated in the development of a new application within the risk assessment and
prediction scales module in the HMS. We mapped all the processes and, in partnership with the
IT team, developed this application within the HMS. Nursing diagnoses related to pre ssure
injury and fall risks became more accurate with the updated HMS modules. In other words,

153


patients at risk received the appropriate nursing diagnosis. " She added: " This customized
digitalization supports healthcare professionals, especially nurses, in clinical reasoning. That’s
because when classifying the patient and applying the risk prediction scale, the system provides
a risk score at the end, along with the level of risk —low, moderate, or high —which supports
clinical decision-making."
At the same time did interviewees point out that the absence or incomplete mapping of
processes (especially based on experiences from previous technological projects), as well as
not considering the participation of professionals and their interactions with the processes, can
lead to failures in the development of new modules or updates to the HMS, or hinder the
adoption of new digital technologies. This impacts the hospital, including the IT team,
professionals, and patients. From the IT perspective, this includes rew ork for the team, errors,
and pop-ups during the usability of the HMS, lack of information in the modules, unforeseen
costs, waste of digital resources and labor, insecurity among IT professionals, processing time
of the HMS, and delays in other projects. From the healthcare professional's perspective, some
may bypass steps and clicks in the HMS modules, as they are not aligned with their workflow,
or even avoid using the technologies due to issues such as the system's inadequate architecture,
lack of proce ss standardization, and unintuitive design. This can result in a return to manual
paper-based processes, performing tasks outside the HMS, and difficulty in adapting, especially
for older professionals, whether due to low digital literacy or age.
Additionally, such challenges can generate frustration, and technostress, and reinforce
conservative barriers against the use of technologies, causing professionals to spend more time
learning to operate the system than focusing on clinical care, which negatively impacts both
their performance and that of the patient and the hospital. From the patient’s perspective, the
interviewees mentioned that the lack of proper process mapping and the absence of
professionals' participation in the implementation of digital tec hnologies can compromise the
quality and safety of care, especially in high -complexity sectors such as nephrology,
transplants, and chemotherapy units. For example, in interviews with nephrology professionals,
it was reported that when a patient needs to move between departments — especially in urgent
cases or to undergo dialysis — clinical procedures and decisions must be recorded in the HMS
modules for documentation and future reference, as well as to ensure complete patient mapping.
However, these proces ses are known only to the physicians and nurses in that area, who
understand what needs to be done, what must be recorded, and how to integrate these steps into
the system. Without the involvement of these professionals, as highlighted in the interview,

154


there is a risk of the patient moving between sectors without clarity on what has already been
done, which can compromise future medical decisions, increase waiting times, reduce patient
safety, and negatively impact the efficiency of care. In interview I07, interviewees R06, R07,
and R08 highlighted that the positive or negative impacts of changes in interactions between
professionals and processes, driven by elements of HCDT, are directly influenced by proper
process mapping and the incorporation of professionals' suggestions.
During the interviews, it was also observed that it is common for healthcare
professionals to provide feedback on their interactions with processes after the implementation
of digital technologies. This occurs through meetings with dir ectors, team events, or even
impromptu conversations in the hospital corridors, phone calls, and message exchanges. This
practice reinforces the establishment of new digital strategies and identifies the necessary digital
resources for their realization. W ith each update, professionals learn the new digital process
and tend to suggest new improvement ideas, allowing for the generation of new digital
operational routines thereby creating a cycle of continuous improvement for professionals,
processes, and esp ecially patients. These activities help build trust among healthcare
professionals and facilitate the sharing of ideas for the continuous improvement of HCDT in
the hospital.
Finally, depending on the type of process, rigid or flexible, the interactions be tween
professionals and processes are shaped by HCDT in different ways. The interviews revealed
that the complexity of the area where the process occurs is the main determining factor for its
rigidity or flexibility. Areas such as administration, pharmacy, outpatient services, medical
appointments and exams, for example, were classified as more rigid because they have clear
standards, which makes it easier for professionals to implement and handle technologies with
less effort, replacing analog and manual processes with digital solutions, and without requiring
extensive training. It is in this type of process that improvements are more visibly achieved. A
practical example occurred in the outpatient department, where the bedside check process,
previously performed with clipboards and papers that required more time and cognitive effort
from the professional to input into the database, was moved to tablets. This change allowed for
the immediate recording of information in a personalized HMS module, developed wi th the
contribution of professionals, enabling real -time access to patient data. These changes were
particularly evident in interviews with the unit's nurses and were later validated during a
technical visit to the hospital, where it was possible to observ e, in practice, the interaction

155


between doctors, nurses, and the technologies implemented in the processes, as observed in the
following observational data:
Observation data from an inpatient ward [08/06/24 – 11:10 AM]: While walking toward the ICU rooms, the researcher and
the Digital Health Unit coordinator discussed changes in the routines and tasks of nurses and physicians. At that moment,
the coordinator pointed to a section of an inpatient ward where four patients were receiving medication and highlig hted
the interactions of two nurses involved in the process. She explained: “At this stage, At this stage, the nurses have already
completed bedside electronic verification. They scanned the patient's ID wristband and the medication barcode using
tablets, enabling electronic verification. They also reviewed the multiparameter monitors displaying the patients’ vital
information. The nurses check which medications have already been administered and update the clinical status of each
patient in the system. Pre viously, they had to use paper clipboards, which were left hanging at the bedside for doctors to
later check what had been done for each patient. This change has accelerated the patient assessment process for healthcare
professionals and reduced the number of missing or incomplete records.”
Another example of changes in interactions between professionals and rigid processes
occurred in medical consultation services. Initially conducted exclusively in person,
consultations were later offered virtually after the development of an in-house teleconsultation
platform. This allowed doctors to remotely attend to patients for diagnoses and treatment
follow-ups. In 2020, the number of teleconsultations surpassed 52,000 appointments (as
presented in the "General Overv iew of the HMS" brochure [Hospital Institutional Web Page
2022]).
Processes considered complex within the hospital were classified as flexible, as they do
not follow complete standardization but rather involve task customization that can vary
according to the patient's stage, specific needs, and the professionals’ individual experiences.
This variability hinders both the adoption of digital technologies and the development of new
HMS modules, as mentioned by interviewee R04 in reference to a module for sur gery
scheduling and management. Changes require greater commitment and resilience from
professionals, especially during the development of HMS modules and training on the use of
technologies, such as in the case of using Da Vinci robots in surgical procedures. Additionally,
errors in this context can represent significant risks to patient safety. Examples of flexible and
complex processes include organ transplants, heart surgeries, chemotherapy treatments, and
nephrology procedures.
It was also observed tha t, in rigid processes, professionals tend to maintain the same
process, using technologies mainly to enhance it. When flexible, the interaction between
healthcare professionals and the introduction of HCDT indicates that professionals often
receive roles and responsibilities to decide what digital technologies to adopt, without collective
participation, together with technological support to make decisions in their routines. Flexible

156


processes centralized the decision-making on technology adoption in a few individuals, while
rigid processes encouraged collaborative adaptations to the HMS, allowing professionals to
contribute their experience to drive transformations.

Individuals interacting with structures
At the strategic and managerial level, an organizat ional structure was established
composed of members from all departments responsible for decision-making regarding HCDT
(as described in section 3.1). However, at the operational level, interviews revealed that
interactions between individuals and the type of hierarchical structure vary depending on the
hospital department, especially based on the number of professionals involved in each
department or process, as explained by the head of the hemodialysis unit, nurse R23, in
interview I18: " Depending on the department unit, when many people are involved, a PO is
designated to lead the digital transformation project and represent them, concentrating greater
decision-making authority on that individual. In such cases, involving everyone individually
would make the process unproductive and disorganized. On the other hand, when fewer people
are involved, actions are based on consensus, where everyone works together with the digital
governance bodies as well as the IT team for the development and implementation of digital
solutions."
When the hierarchical structure is o rganized by consensus, technicians, nurses,
nutritionists, physical therapists, pharmacists, and physicians, are encouraged to share ideas in
operational teams to develop new HMS modules and suggest digital technologies that enhance
their activities. In th is type of hierarchy, professionals work in an engaged and collaborative
manner, using a common language focused on improving daily tasks. This kind of interaction
allowed for considering collective participation and knowledge when digitalizing routines,
reducing potential tensions between professionals and technologies after implementation. More
specifically, professionals actively contribute to mapping current processes, identifying
problems and limitations, suggesting technological solutions, improving t he architecture of
HMS modules, and continuously providing feedback. A practical example was shared by
pharmacist R22, medication and logistics manager: " When a technological improvement
proposal is defined by the pharmacy leadership, we first listen to th e professionals’ concerns
and suggestions. Next, we conduct preliminary tests. However, before the technological
implementation, we inform the team. After adoption, if any issues arise, we encourage users to

157


report any unforeseen impacts, ensuring personalized adjustments and solutions developed by
them." This makes the construction of HMS modules truly multidisciplinary, as further
highlighted by the nursing manager R09. At the hospital, this hierarchical structure enabled the
development of a shared ident ity, reducing partial information among professionals and
establishing cooperation mechanisms that influence the pursuit of digital solutions.
According to the interviewees, professionals are constantly seeking to update
themselves on HCDT within the cons ensus-based hierarchy, diving into various sources of
knowledge to apply and share in collaborative DT projects. The main sources mentioned
include events, congresses, lectures on digital transformation, reading articles in the medical
field, LinkedIn, int eractions with healthcare professional groups, previous experiences with
digital technologies outside the hospital, benchmarking with other institutions, and short -term
courses. Professionals who contribute to technological projects are encouraged and recognized
through participation certificates, internal recognition within the hospital, and opportunities to
take part in new projects due to the knowledge they have shared or innovations they have
generated. However, there are no financial rewards, as this i s a public teaching and research
institution with a limited budget. This shows that professionals are motivated by a collaborative
digital culture, driven by the desire to improve work routines. An interesting point highlighted
was that when professionals actively participate in the development of DT, more improvement
ideas tend to emerge. However, one challenge noted is that not all suggestions are considered,
nor are the digital solutions always able to fully meet everyone’s needs.
Interactions within the authority-based hierarchical structure occur in two main ways.
First, it is used to centralize decision-making regarding the prioritization of digital technology
adoption projects, as well as to establish the strategic planning of DT and investment in digital
resources. Technicians, nurses, and doctors request technological improvements for their
processes directly through their respective departments, such as the Nursing or Medical
Directorate. These directorates assess the feasibility of the requests bas ed on factors such as
process maturity and proper process mapping. If approved, the requests are forwarded to the
Digital Health Core, which verifies whether they align with the broader DT scope. If validated,
they are then submitted to the Hospital's Digital Governance Committee, which makes the final
decision by considering investment, required resources, available infrastructure, and strategic
alignment. This committee also monitors implementation and seeks to understand the outcomes
of interactions between professionals and digital technologies within processes. Thus, although
professionals possess the necessary knowledge to propose improvements to their routines, the

158


execution of these proposals depends on the approval by these governing bodies, as expl ained
by interviewee R02: “In the HCDT, the Digital Governance Committee is the highest authority
responsible for deciding which digital technologies will be implemented in the hospital, with a
focus on project prioritization. Its main role is to align ini tiatives with the hospital’s capacity.
After approval, the committee also monitors the allocation of digital and human resources,
ensuring that each project is carried out within the planned timeframe, budget, and scope.”
Second, POs are appointed to manag e the interaction between unit staff and HCDT in
units with many professionals, as highlighted by interviewees from Interview I17. In this
hierarchical structure, although POs gather insights, knowledge, and suggestions from frontline
professionals, the direct influence of these professionals on HCDT decisions is more limited.
The PO centralizes the communication of process -related issues. They define guidelines and
dedicate time to meeting with teams to deeply understand professionals’ interactions within
processes, as well as to identify which HMS module updates and digital technology applications
should be considered by the board and later forwarded to the hospital’s digital health committee.
Once a technological project or new HMS module is approved, the PO takes the lead in
interacting with the IT team for development and implementation. They serve as the feedback
channel and absorb knowledge regarding digital workflow changes. Due to the authority
delegated to them, POs are also responsible for passing on updates to professionals through
training and capacity -building sessions. A practical example of this structure was shared by
nurse R09: “ Currently, we are developing the scheduling and verification module for
chemotherapy prescriptions in the HMS. We h ave a dedicated project team, including a PO
who serves as the liaison between the care areas and the IT team. In the case of chemotherapy,
professionals from the involved areas validate the PO’s decisions before the final approval by
the digital governance committee.”
Another role of the PO in the interactions between healthcare professionals and the
authority-based hierarchy was highlighted by R05, pharmacist and head of the pharmacy
department: "The pharmacy team is very large, with over 200 professionals. So, when there are
HCDT initiatives, we divide into four large groups to ensure collaboration and access for
everyone. However, there needs to be a PO to lead the implementation of the technologies,
gather information from the professionals, and coordinate the dissemination and training after
the implementation."

159


4.4.4. New digital operating routines in healthcare
Our findings suggest that, from a sociotechnical system perspective, the introduction of
HCDT shaped the microfoundations of operating routines, enabling the creation of digital
healthcare operating routines across various areas and units of the hospital u nder study, both
clinical and administrative. The interactions between professionals, structures, and processes in
HCDT went beyond the simple transition from manual/analog tasks to digital ones or the use
of technologies for clinical treatments. They inco rporated the social aspect of transformation,
through the formation of multifunctional teams focused on the customized development of
digital technologies, as well as their implementation journey adapted to the professional, rather
than the professional ad apting to the technology. New routines include, for example, the
replacement of paper or manually made records with real-time digital records, ad hoc problem-
solving, and the active participation of professionals in the development of customized digital
technologies. These new digital healthcare routines were identified through the analysis of
interview excerpts from participants across different areas of the hospital. Additionally, they
were confirmed during participant observation, which allowed researche rs to witness
professionals carrying out these routines in practice.
The interaction among professionals was particularly intense in highly rigid processes
and hierarchical structures based on consensus, where teams were assembled to solve well -
defined problems. Units such as the Internal Regulation Center, Emergency Depart ment,
Outpatient Clinics, Pharmacy, Laboratory, Pathology, and Cardiology reported consistent
adoption of the motto "learning from mistakes." This concept was particularly well incorporated
in services such as bedside checks, exam and historical consultati on requests, and patient
diagnosis, areas where information was previously recorded manually on paper. With the
development and implementation of new customized modules and associated digital
technologies (such as QR Code readers, paging guns, tablets, and electronic wristbands), both
in consensus-based and authority-based structures, a new operational routine emerged: digital
recording and tracking of patient and professional information. Data collection began to occur
in real time, with information being automatically or manually entered by professionals into the
HMS, centralizing data such as consultation history, hospitalizations, and medications
administered or restricted, even in cases where the patient cannot provide this information
directly. This new operating routine enabled the mapping of the patient, regardless of the unit
they were in, promoting communication, integration, and information exchange between
professionals from different areas (interoperability). Additionally, it enabled the generati on of

160


performance indicators, task automation, and quick access to the patient's clinical history. In a
way, professionals began to gain new power through their interaction with technological
change. In more flexible processes, they were able to quickly adapt to new tools to avoid delays
in activities and later reported suggestions for improvement based on their practical
experiences. The digital recording routine also contributed to strengthening a social structure
driven by a consensus-based hierarchy and reorganized processes.
The ad hoc problem-solving routine emerged from observing processes and collecting
feedback (Franke et al., 2024) from professionals about their experiences with digital
technologies, especially in contexts with authority-based hierarchical structures and more rigid
processes. In these cases, the responsible professionals — POs of the projects — periodically
meet with care teams to collect reports on process failures, difficulties interacting with
technologies, and functional deficie ncies in digital modules, and to promote the sharing of
knowledge and improvement suggestions, such as the creation of new HMS modules. This
information is then forwarded to the respective departments and the hospital's HCDT
management, to eliminate the identified problems. In practice, this routine manifested itself, for
example, when the digital prescription module exhibited unexpected failures during the clinical
activities of doctors or nurses. In these cases, the professional seeks a temporary solution to
avoid interrupting care while also alerting the IT team for immediate correction. Another
example mentioned refers to the excessive number of clicks required on HMS screen objects,
which caused professionals to become lost and stressed during processes , and, in some cases,
revert to using manual methods and paper records. Based on this, professionals made
suggestions for improvements. With the updates, it was possible to reduce the number of clicks
needed during patient care in the emergency department by over 45%, optimizing workflow
and increasing the efficiency of the care process. This routine contributes to the development
of resilient organizational skills, such as monitoring, anticipating, responding, and learning,
reinforcing the adaptive capacity of professionals in the face of technological uncertainties.
The accumulation of experience and deliberate learning by professionals led to the
emergence of active participation in the development of customized digital technologies . This
routine was espe cially driven by the nature of the hospital, an institution focused on care,
teaching, and research, with digital strategies and resources aimed at improving operations and
clinical care. This provides an environment conducive to experimentation and innovation. With
the introduction of HCDT in units with fewer professionals in the hospital, such as Hematology,
where activities as assessing hospitalized patients and requesting exams take place in a

161


predominantly consensus-based structure, healthcare professionals began to actively participate
in the development of the transplant and chemotherapy module in the HMS in addition to
dedicating themselves to care and administrative processes. Participation includes conducting
meetings, tests, and adjustments to ensure the system’s usability and alignment with the specific
needs of the unit. The active involvement of professionals in HCDT also helped mitigate
common tensions in technological adoption, particularly those related to sociotechnical factors
such as age, digital literacy, years of service, and the fast -paced evolution of HMS and other
digital technologies.

4.5 DISCUSSIONS
Our results offer a new perspective on the study of DT in healthcare systems. They
challenge existing literature by demonstrating that HCDT should be understood as a
sociotechnical system. Previous studies simplify the implementation of HCDT to a
technocentric view (e.g., Sharma et al., 2016; Wani & Malhotra, 2018; Guha & Kumar, 2018;
Mukherjee & Sinha, 2020; Bavafa et al., 2021; Tushe et al., 2025), while organizational and
social aspects, which involve the interactions of the microfoundations of operating routines,
have not been addressed in depth. Although these microfoundational interactions have been
analyzed in manufacturing contexts (Roscoe et al., 2019), our study is pioneering in the field of
healthcare operations management. Figure 14 presents an e mpirical model of the interaction
between individuals, structures, and processes shaped by HCDT as a socio-technical system.

162


Figure 14. Empirical model of how HCDT as a sociotechnical system shapes the interactions among the microfoundations of operating routines

163


Our findings indicate that contrary to what is assumed by the model presented in Figure
10 — which was built based on the literature — the management of HCDT in healthcare
systems does not necessarily occur in a strictly “top-down” manner. In other words, it does not
begin by addressing organizational and technical aspects first, followed by so cial ones. We
identified that organizational, technical, and social aspects interact differently in this context.
The empirical model presented in Figure 14 suggests that, when considering HCDT as a
sociotechnical system, the process for digitalization should begin from the social aspect (carries
greater weight in decision -making about HCDT), with frontline healthcare professionals who
demand solutions to support and shape their work. Management (e.g., the digital governance
committee), in turn, also reques ts tools that assist in monitoring professionals in their work
environments and support decision-making processes. A third stakeholder is the actual patient,
which may demand digital solutions to facilitate its treatment path.
The different stakeholders create what in the IoT and Smart Manufacturing literature is
called the application layer. It is the actual use of the digital solution, and the upper layer in the
three- layered structure of application, core service and resource management (e.g., Qu et al .,
2016). Core service and resource management are reflected in organizational and technological
aspect, respectively. Both need to be aligned. To realize this alignment, it is typically assumed
in the IoT and Smart Manufacturing literature that a central planner creates an integrated
solution. In larger systems, such that our case hospital, it emerges organically out of multiple
requests for applications. In this sense, the alignment between organizational and technological
aspects (as indicated by the line connecting the organizational and technical aspects) is shaped
by social interactions, according to professionals' practical needs and interactions within
hierarchical structures and processes. The feedback generated by individual interactions
provides the basis for structuring this alignment, as indicated by the bidirectional arrows in the
model in Figure 14 that integrate the social aspects with the organizational and technical ones.
This cycle is continuous: the interactions among healthcare profession als, structures, and
processes enable professionals to learn through practice, including patient feedback, generate
and share knowledge, and make new improvement requests. Managers then receive this
information and respond by structuring the organizational and technological aspects to once
again support and enhance the microfoundations.
These findings reinforce emerging themes in the field of Technology and Operations
Management, which emphasize that the implementation of digital technologies (such as the

164


HMS studied here) should be human -centered while also promoting sustainable practices in
organizational processes (Olsen et al., 2020; Heim et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2022; Angelopoulos
et al., 2023; Amaya & Holweg, 2024). According to the sociotechnical p erspective,
organizational, technical, and social aspects need to be aligned and treated in a balanced manner
to enable the adoption of technologies (Cherns, 1978; Manz & Stewart, 1997). However, this
is merely a technical premise. In practice, the results revealed that there is not necessarily a
balance between these aspects, but rather a continuous dynamic of interactions among different
actors. It is through these interactions that operating routines are enhanced and constructed,
which in turn generate d emands for specific strategies, resources, and technologies. Most
importantly, we enhance the existing literature by showing that in the context of digitalization,
there are three layers that determine the sociotechnical system. It is not a question of bal ance,
but the balance has to follow the architecture provided by the digital solution.
Our results further revealed that when the social aspect does not serve as the foundation
for aligning with the other components of HCDT —and instead, a top -down manageme nt
approach is adopted —tensions may emerge, such as technostress, rejection, or conservative
resistance to the use of technologies by professionals (Kellogg, 2022; Amaya & Holweg, 2024),
which directly impacts the success of HCDT initiatives. Although the model presented in Figure
14 is not immune to these effects, we believe it can serve as a useful approach to support
decision-making in contexts that involve interactions between digital technologies and human
collaboration. These results align with Kellogg’s (2022) study on experimentalist governance,
in which the reconfiguration of professionals’ roles within local units includes the autonomy to
adapt digital technologies to their specific contexts, allowing both routines and the technology
itself to evolve based on lessons learned. In other words, professionals no longer serve merely
as operational resources for the hospital but instead take on developmental roles within HCDT.
As shown in Figure 14, interactions within the social aspect, when HCDT is introduced,
enable the emergence of new digital operating routines, which is particularly significant in the
context of healthcare operations. The findings suggest that due to the high concentration of
knowledge among healthcare professionals — stemming from their academic background and
ongoing training — and their interactions within organizational structures and processes, it is
possible to develop routines that enhance operations and can effectively handle unexpected
situations, which are common in healthca re environments. As observed, three new routines
were developed: the routine of active participation in the development of customized digital

165


technologies, the routine of ad hoc problem -solving, and the routine of digital health record -
keeping and monitoring of patient and staff information. Focusing especially on the first two
routines, they are particularly important because, when a customized digital technology fails or
encounters errors, the professionals involved in its development may be able to identify the root
cause of the problem and notify those responsible for fixing it — or even implementing
temporary solutions. However, the most critical aspect in such situations is not just resolving
technological failure but ensuring the continuity of patient care despite the absence of
technology. Healthcare professionals cannot interrupt their activities, as they are dealing with
human lives. In other words, the care delivery process cannot stop. Therefore, by understanding
their interactions within the processes, they can implement quick solutions that allow operations
to continue even without technological support.
The key however, is to transition from ad -hoc solutions to new routines. The learning
from failure. For this, it Is not only a question of diff erent sources of knowledge but also of
different types. In fact, knowledge has to be seen as sociotechnical. There need to be knowledge
about organizational, technical and social aspects, and their interactions, to create a solution. It
needs to be known, what technical solutions can be realized given existing resources, how these
resources can be leveraged given the organizational structure, and how this will impact the
different stakeholders. This knowledge rarely resides in one person. Our study showed t hat
using simple tools such as Business Process Mapping to create a joint communication, and
knowledge exchange, structure over problems and their context is key to success.
The central point lies in the interactions that occur within the social aspect and how they
shape the entire surrounding environment. Zooming in on this aspect, it becomes evident that
HCDT fundamentally depends on the engagement of the business areas within healthcare
systems, as it is in these areas that the multidisciplinary concep tion and construction of
digitalization take place—driven by the professionals themselves. In this context, what makes
one area easier to digitalize than another is mainly related to the number of professionals
involved and the complexity of the processes. Areas with a larger number of individuals and
more flexible and complex processes tend to face greater challenges in digitalization. One of
the reasons for this is the lack of standardization. In such cases, professionals need to deepen
their understanding of the processes, applying their experience and skills to generate and share
knowledge. This knowledge becomes the foundation upon which management can shape the
alignment between organizational and technical aspects of digitalization. On the other hand,

166


areas with fewer professionals and/or more rigid processes tend to be easier to digitalize,
precisely because of the clarity and standardization provided by process mapping, as well as
the ease of working collectively and reaching consensus. This leads to more direct insights into
how strategies, resources, and digital technologies should be configured.
Finally, as identified in the results, when interactions among microfoundations are
considered the primary source of knowledge for the development of digit al technologies, it
becomes essential to recognize that solutions can be designed within these micro-level units to
bring patients closer to healthcare systems, rather than distancing them. Technologies such as
telemedicine, AI-based decision support systems, and digital monitoring tools require patients
to assume a more active role, ranging from self -monitoring and data sharing to performing
minor procedures with remote support , as noted by Bendoly et al. (2025). In this context, key
questions emerge from the microfoundations regarding whether digitalization may create new
barriers or, alternatively, foster solutions that strengthen interactions between professionals and
patients (Bendoly et al., 2025). As evidenced in this study, it is precisely at the lev el of
microfoundations that a customized HCDT can be developed —one that adapts digital
technologies to professionals’ tasks and patients’ needs, promoting integration rather than
distancing.

4.6 CONCLUSIONS
Hospitals are complex sociotechnical systems that r eceive much research attention. A
major focus of many hospitals is improving operational routines through digitalization. But how
can this HCDT be realized? In response to our research question – How does HCDT, as a
sociotechnical system, shape microfoundations and generate new digital operating routines in
healthcare? we found that the social aspect, which occurs in the interactions among individuals,
structures, and processes defines the alignment of organizational and technical aspects to adapt
to the reality of individuals (health professionals, managers, patients).
From a theoretical perspective, we present an empirically grounded model (see Figure
14) that provides a foundation for exploring the social dimension through the generation and
sharing of knowledge in the interactions among the microfoundations of operating routines, as
well as organizational and technical aspects. First, our analysis challenges the dominant
sociotechnical perspective in literature, which tends to view social, technical, and

167


organizational elements as integrated and balanced. In contrast, we found that the social aspect,
especially when centered on interactions between individuals, can play a more significant role,
particularly in HCDT, by influencing and shaping the other aspects.
This study contributes to both the sociotechnical view and the KBV by responding to
the call to open the "black box" of sociotechnical dynamics in DT (Heim et al., 2021). We
contribute by showing that the sociotechnical approach can be understood di fferently. The
relationship among these aspects is not fixed: while organizational and technical components
should be aligned, it is the social dimension, when integrated into the system, that provides the
knowledge and informational foundation to guide that alignment and to continuously feedback
into the process for ongoing improvement. This type of relationship between the aspects can,
in turn, give rise to new operating routines, transforming operations and generating benefits for
the organization. In the healthcare context, as observed in this study, this may be reflected, for
example, in an increased number of patient visits and a reduction in paper usage. We conclude
that studies on digital transformation in organizations should consider that social as pects may
play a predominant role in decision-making. This is because it is through individual interactions
that DT is operated, sustained, and adapted interactions that can even lead to the emergence of
new, collaborative organizational structures.
From the perspective of the KBV, this study contributes by demonstrating the ability to
generate new digital operational routines based on the tacit and experiential knowledge of
healthcare professionals. Given their high level of educational attainment, these p rofessionals
show strong potential to develop digital competencies through workplace interaction
identifying, developing, and implementing digital solutions that enhance existing routines and
enable the creation of new ones. Such contributions emerge parti cularly in complex contexts,
where new routines may arise independently of hierarchical structures or pre -established
processes. This perspective also advances the KBV by highlighting that the knowledge and
experience of these professionals constitute stra tegic organizational resources that can be
leveraged to drive operational improvements. Furthermore, another important contribution is
that the accumulation of experiences by healthcare professionals gained through their daily
work activities, serves as the source that enables the generation and sharing of deep knowledge
about processes —whether rigid or flexible —allowing for business process mapping. This
mapping is the initial step to identify processes' flaws, problems, and waste, uncover
improvement opportunities, and define technological solutions that transform manual or analog

168


tasks into digital ones using digital technologies. This issue is particularly relevant in
healthcare, where many processes are not standardized and require greater attention due to the
need to handle complex situations demanding quick and precise responses (e.g., diagnoses,
treatments, and patient follow -ups). Therefore, the knowledge required for mapping is often
limited to frontline professionals. Finally, we contribute by pres enting a new knowledge
framework in which solutions for changes in the activities and interactions of healthcare
professionals within hierarchical structures and clinical and administrative care processes
originate from the professionals themselves, enabling them to foster a continuous improvement
cycle.
From a managerial perspective, our study provides managers with a guide for
implementing HCDT as a sociotechnical system, emphasizing the social aspect as particularly
significant and as a key driver in shaping the relationship between organizational and technical
elements to build an effective structure for HCDT. That study can also support policymakers in
developing guidelines aimed at advancing the digitalization of healthcare systems in their
respective regions, leveraging available resources to promote HCDT in an internalized and
customized manner.
A major limitation of our study is the adoption of a single case. This was, however,
necessary to have access to the in -depth insights needed to answer our research question. But
this also implies that results are not directly generalizable. Future research is needed to
appropriately validate and contextualize our results. Our study was further limited to examining
the elements preceding HCDT and how these el ements shape the microfoundations, focusing
on healthcare professionals, as well as the emergence of new digital operational routines. Future
research is needed to determine how healthcare digital routines, customized from the
knowledge and experiences of professionals, influence the standardization of processes in
highly dynamic environments, such as healthcare. We believe this is a fertile area for future
research on the important topic of the intersection between HCDT, sociotechnical aspects and
microfoundations.

5. CONCLUSIONS
This study comprises three articles, each corresponding to a specific objective of this
PhD dissertation. Figure 15 illustrates the relationship between the three articles. While Article
1 addresses the management of digital resources for HCDT by considering the technological,
organizational, and environmental contexts across different hospital management strategy
models, Article 2 seeks to validate the alignment between strategy and digital resources,
supported by network embeddedness, for the implementation of Healthcare 4.0 technologies,
considering two main dimensions: smart operations and smart working. In turn, Ar ticle 3
demonstrates how the alignment among resources, strategies, and digital technologies shapes
the microfoundations of operating routines — comprising individuals, hierarchical structures,
and processes — which represent the level at which digital tra nsformation is effectively
operationalized in practice and enables the creation of new digital healthcare operating routines.


Figure 15. Articles relationship

The three articles that comprise this dissertation aim to build a theoretical framework to
understand how healthcare organizations can organizationally structure healthcare digital
transformation and promote the digitalization of their operations. Figure 16 presents a n
organizational structure that synthe sizes the main findings and guides the organizational
structuring of digital transformation in healthcare organizations.

177



Figure 16. Organizational Structure for the Healthcare Digital Transformation

178


Observing Figure 16, it can be noted that it is hierarchically structured from top to
bottom and organized into four main levels. At the first level, three types of strategies for digital
resource management are presented: strategies focused on developing internal digital resources,
strategies oriented toward combination –hybrid governance, and strategies focused on
developing external digital resources. Managers may choose and adopt one of these strategies
according to the capacity and specific characteristics of each type of hospital—public, private,
or teaching and research institutions —considering their specificities, constraints, and capital
availability., as discussed in Article 1 of Chapter 2.
Subsequently, the three organizational levels that should b e considered in the
organizational structuring of HCDT are presented: Macro, Meso, and Micro, reflected in the
integration of the Environmental, Organizational, Technological, and Social Aspects. At the
Macro level, the Environmental Aspect is identified, which corresponds to an organizational
level external to the healthcare system. At this level, the healthcare system should consider
Healthcare Network Embeddedness and/or the creation of a Digital Healthcare Ecosystem, with
the aim of supporting and acces sing external digital resources from partners that may
collaborate with HCDT. The boundaries of the macro level encompass the institutional
environment in which the healthcare organization is embedded, including public actors, private
organizations, regula tory bodies, policymakers, and other stakeholders that exert direct or
indirect influence on HCDT. This level corresponds to the sphere of governance and
institutional pressures that shape external norms, expectations, and directives. The macro level
is delineated at the point where decision-making shifts from being predominantly conditioned
by external forces to being internalized within the organization’s governance structure, where
it is translated into strategic directives by managers, decision-makers, directors, and executive
leaders.
The Meso level corresponds to the internal organizational sphere of governance and
management within the healthcare organization. It encompasses the presidency, executive
boards, directories, and departments responsible for strategic formulation and decision-making
regarding HCDT. At this level, directives stemming from the supplier and institutional
environment (Macro level) are interpreted and translated into organizational digital strategies,
policies, digital resource s and action plans. Simultaneously, the Meso level analyzes and
consolidates demands emerging from the micro level by assessing needs, priorities, and the
feasibility of implementation. Thus, the Meso level functions as a mediating and alignment

179


mechanism, connecting external institutional pressures with internal operational dynamics,
ensuring strategic coherence and organizational coordination in the HCDT process.
At the Meso level, positioned at an intermediate layer, the alignment between the
Organizational and Technological Aspects is established. This alignment is constructed and
continuously reinforced by feedback originating from the Micro level, indicating that HCDT
does not necessarily need to originate from top management, but can instead be managed based
on insights eme rging from the Micro level, while simultaneously being supported by the
Environmental Aspect at the Macro level. More specifically, the Organizational Aspect
comprises a set of Digital Healthcare strategies aimed at digitalization, as well as a set of
Internal and External Digital Resources that enable the operationalization of these strategies
and support the implementation of digital technologies. Additionally, this aspect should
consider the establishment of digital governance committees to support the m anagement of
HCDT within healthcare systems.
Still at the meso level, the Technological Aspect represents the practical manifestation
of HCDT, corresponding to the dimensions of digital technology applications to be
implemented. These dimensions may focus on Healthcare Smart Operations, which consists of
a set of digital technologies aimed at process automation, and Healthcare Smart Working, which
encompasses digital technologies designed to support healthcare professionals in their
activities. Both the te chnological dimensions and the types of digital resources and strategies
are presented in Article 2, in Chapter 3.
Finally, the micro level corresponds to the operational sphere of the healthcare
organization, where clinical and administrative activities are carried out. It encompasses
healthcare professionals, digital technologies used in daily practice, work processes,
hierarchical structures, and the operating routines that structure care delivery. At this level,
HCDT materializes through interactions among the microfoundations of operating routines —
namely, professionals, processes (rigid or flexible), and hierarchical arrangements (based on
consensus or authority). These interactions shape how digital technologies are operationalized
in practice and h ow professional knowledge is generated and shared. The experiences and
adaptations emerging from this level provide feedback to the Meso level, informing strategic
decisions, organizational adjustments, and the definition of resources and strategies necess ary
to support implementation. Such feedback may involve improving existing digital applications
or identifying opportunities for digitalizing previously manual or analog activities. As a result,

180


operating routines may be reconfigured, and new digitally en abled routines may emerge. The
interaction patterns among professionals, processes, and hierarchical structures, as well as the
routines that arise from them, are further examined in Article 3, presented in Chapter 4.

5.1 CONTRIBUTIONS
This study contributes to HCDT literature by offering a new organizational structure
model that highlights the interconnections among digital strategies, digital resources, digital
technologies, and the microfoundations of operating routines, as illustrate d in Figure 16 . The
results indicate that these interconnections require the integration of macro-, meso-, and micro-
level organizational dimensions, reflected in environmental, organizational, technological, and
social aspects, respectively, as suggested by Ahmadi et al. (2018), Mauro et al. (2024), Mao et
al. (2024) and Duus et al. (2026). When combined, these aspects support throughout the digital
transformation journey and must be considered jointly, since digital technologies
simultaneously affect all organizational levels. Addressing these aspects in isolation, or
neglecting any of them, may compromise the effectiv eness of the transformation process . In
this way, the study helps address a gap in literature by demonstrating that HCDT cannot be
understood from an exclusively technocentric perspective, as implied by the models presented
by Tortorella et al. (2020a), Tortorella et al. (2022a), and Bendoly et al. (2025). Instead, it
incorporates additional dimensions into an organizational structure, showing that HCDT can be
also conceptualized as a sociotechnical system (Marcon et al., 2022; 2025) in which technical,
social, organizational, and environmental aspects are treated with equal importance.
The proposed organizational structure (resulting from the organizational structur ing)
also contributes by addressing gaps identified in established models and structures in the
literature. Although it was developed for the HCDT context — which involves sector-specific
mechanisms, such as public hospitals that rely on procurement processes , for example — the
structure can be adapted to other contexts, such as manufacturing , or even serve as a basis for
developing new variants. Furthermore, the structure complements the consolidated RBV model
proposed by Barney (1991) by extending the discussion beyond resource ownership as a source
of competitive advantage. The proposed structure demonstrates that organizations may
simultaneously possess strategic resources and rely on a network of external actors to access
and integrate additional digital resources necessary for digital transformation. It also clarifies
how such resources can be orchestrated (Sirmon et al., 2007). The model further complements

181


the organizational structure proposed by Verhoef et al. (2021) by illustrating how
transformation-related resources and capabilities can be managed, as well as which governance
mechanisms — internal, external, or hybrid — may be adopted to implement digital
technologies. Furthermore, complement this by considering different organizational levels —
macro, meso, and micro—for digital transformation.
The organizational structure proposed in this study also incorporates elements found in
established HCDT-oriented models in the literature, such as the structure developed by Kraus
et al. (2021), which considers interconnected dimensions to be addressed in the HCDT
implementation process. However, the model developed in this study goes further by integrating
environmental aspects, such as the creation of digital health ecosystems and the importance of
being embedded in a network of actors to enable access to resources and support the
implementation of digital technologies. In addition, it highlights the social aspect by
demonstrating how the workforce and its interactions with other microfoundations of operating
routines can contribute to the implementation of a customized HCDT. Although
microfoundations have previously been examined in the manufacturing context (Roscoe et al.,
2019), it remained unclear how they could be shaped and mobilized within the HCDT context,
thus representing an additional contribution and novel insight into the HCDT literature.
The proposed structure also advances beyond organizational structure models focused
on the implementation of a single technology, such as the DTEM model for telehealth by Mishra
and Sharma (2022), the framework by Chaudhuri et al. (2023) for the co -creation process in
implementing 3D printing services in healthcare, and the model by Duus et al. (2026) for the
implementation of Artificial Intelligence in healthcare. Unlike these approaches, the structure
proposed in this thesis is not restricted to isolated technologies but addresses bundles of digital
technologies, which may serve as entry points to digitalization and feedback mechanisms, while
simultaneously guiding strategic definition and access to digital resources for multiple
technologies. Furthermore, it presents a continu ous HCDT flow originating from the
organization’s micro level.
Additionally, the results show that the organizational structur e of HCDT must account
for changes in the microfoundations of operating routines, which are considered here as a social
aspect, as they involve people. It is at this micro level of the organization that digital
technologies are effectively operationalized, making it essential to understand how these
microfoundations are shaped by HCDT and how new healthcare digital operating routines
emerge from this process. The findings reveal that, through the interaction of these three

182


elements, professionals mobilize their knowledge, practical experience, and learning derived
from trial-and-error processes to support the alignment between digital strategies, resources,
and technologies. This process enables HCDT to be tailored to the needs of professionals, who
are directly responsible for operationalizing digital technologies in patient care activities. In
turn, this provides hospital managers wi th insights into the strategies, resources and
technologies that need to be considered according to user requirements.
The study also contributes by demonstrating that the healthcare sector is highly
dependent on professionals and their interactions with processes, hierarchical structures, and
regulatory frameworks. Although regulatory, normative, and legal aspects were not directly
addressed in this study, they are inherently part of organizational structuring and therefore
represent a limitation in this study. Unlike manufacturing , for example, where processes can
often be fully automated, healthcare involves clinical care also characterized by high levels of
uncertainty for both patients and professionals. These uncertainties may pose risks to pati ent
safety, particularly in contexts involving professionals–machine interactions and potential
conflicts between technological systems and professional judgment.
Considering the proposed organizational structure, the central role of professionals and
their interactions with processes and hierarchical structures at the micro level of the
organization is emphasized. These interactions connect to the meso level, where project owners
and HCDT leaders bridge operational activities and strategic decision -making. At this level,
decision-makers define which digital strategies and resources are required. In turn, the meso
level interacts with the macro level —external to the organization —through contracts and
partnerships that enable access to and acquisition of digital resources and technologies, as well
as insights from the broader ecosystem to support internal digitalization efforts. Therefore, the
healthcare context plays a particularly significant role in digital transformation , making it
different from other ar eas since it involves lives . Proposing an organizational structure that
explicitly accounts for these multilevel interactions is essential for effectively supporting and
advancing HCDT.
Nevertheless, the results can support managers and policymakers in def ining digital
transformation strategies, particularly in the healthcare context, which is characterized as a
complex system due to the high level of process uncertainty. From a practical perspective, to
support the organizational structuring of HCDT, healt hcare systems—such as hospitals—may
begin by defining a digital resource management model that integrally considers environmental,
organizational, technical, and social aspects. In this regard, healthcare systems should develop

183


a digital transformation strategy that assesses which management model is most suitable for
governing the digital resources required for technology implementation, for instance, both for
process automation and for supporting healthcare professionals. This approach requires the
prior structuring of critical organizational elements to ensure successful implementation.
Subsequently, it is essential to encourage healthcare professionals to provide continuous
feedback on the implementation process and the use of digital technologies, as they interact
directly with patients and are therefore well -positioned to indicate how these interactions can
be improved, ultimately generating greater benefits for task performance and clinical care.
Another practical contribution, based on the three articles developed, a digital maturity
assessment model for healthcare systems was constructed. Although this model is not described
in detail throughout this thesis, it constitutes a direct outcome of the research and was applied
at HCPA. This application enabled the assessment of the institution’s level of HCDT maturity,
as well as the generation of insights to support decision-making and advance its organizational
structuring. Overall, the model is structured around three main dimensions. The first is the
technological dimension, which evaluates the degree of customization, scalability, expansion,
integration, and traceability of digital technologies. The second is the organizational dimension,
encompassing project management, infrastructure, and available digital resources. Finally, the
social dimension addresses changes in work routines and knowledge management practices.
This tool shows strong potential for use in future digital maturity assessments and analyses
across other healthcare systems.
The thesis may also significantly contribute to strengthening Brazil’s Unified Health
System (Sistema Único de Saúde - SUS), particularly within the context of the SUS Digital
Program, established by Ordinance GM/MS No. 3,232/2024, which aims to modernize the
Brazilian healthcare system through digital transformation. By proposing a structured approach
to HCDT, the thesis provides theoretical and practical support to assist the SUS in integrating
data through the National Health Data Network (Rede Nacional de Dados em Saúde - RNDS),
expanding citizens’ access to health information via the Meu SUS Digital application, and
improving care coordination across healthcare networks. Furthermore, the insights generated
are also applicable to private healthcare systems, which face similar challenges related to
interoperability, digital strategy development, technological resource allocation, and the
reconfiguration of operating routines. By addressing social, organizational, technological, and
environmental aspects, the thesis contributes to the development of a more integrated digital
health ecosystem (particularly in Brazil, an emerging economy undergoing a progressive

184


transition toward higher levels of digitalization ) capable of expanding access, strengthening
clinical care networks, enhancing interoperability, and maximizing resource efficiency in both
public and private healthcare contexts.

5.2 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH
The thesis also presents some limitations. The study focuses on the practical context of
Brazil, an emerging economy. In developing countries, digitalizing healthcare systems often
presents challenges, especially in public healthcare environments, where most financial
resources are allocated almost entirely to healthcare professionals' salaries and re ly on public
procurement processes to acquire external resources. As a result, HCDT in the public sector of
emerging economies may progress at a slower pace. In contrast, developed countries, with
greater capital to invest in digital transformation, are likely to be more technologically advanced
and have more initiatives to achieve HCDT. Therefore, the territorial context is considered a
limitation of this study. Future studies examining healthcare systems in other emerging or
developed economies, as well as different organizational structuring models, are needed to
enhance the generalizability of the findings.
Another limitation of this thesis is related to the si ze of the hospitals analyzed. This
study focused on large hospitals, as these institutions are more likely to be at more advanced
stages of HCDT compared to small hospitals. However, the organizational structuring required
for HCDT in smaller healthcare sy stems may differ substantially due to constraints in human,
financial, and infrastructural resources (e.g., Primary Health Care Units – UBS’s). In this
regard, future studies are needed to investigate the organizational structur e of HCDT in small
hospitals or UBS’s , considering, for example, the implementation of specific digital
technologies—such as telemedicine or artificial intelligence —as entry points for the gradual
adoption of other digital solutions. Moreover, literature remains limited in this conte xt,
highlighting relevant opportunities for further research in this area.
The organizational structure proposed in this thesis focuses on analyzing key
organizational elements — strategy, resources, digital technologies, and operating routines —
that are critical to the successful implementation of HCDT. However, each of these elements
encompasses a broader set of components that extend beyond the scope of this study. For
instance, within the digital strategy dimension, factors such as institutional pressures, regulatory
and legislative frameworks, normative guidelines, self-regulation mechanisms, interoperability

185


requirements, and policies addressing data duplication across health information systems —
particularly those established by the Brazilian Minist ry of Health — play a significant role.
Nevertheless, these aspects are not explored in depth. Addressing them would require highly
detailed analysis, including access to confidential data and the examination of multiple
stakeholders’ roles and interactions. Therefore, this study was delimited to a broader analytical
scope, aiming to understand the organizational structure of HCDT. However, this delimitation
opens avenues for future research about advances in organizational structure , given that
healthcare is a highly regulated environment that becomes even more complex with the
adoption of digital technologies. Understanding regulatory approvals, compliance mechanisms,
and institutional alignments represents a fertile field for further investigation.
Another limitation of this study concerns the lack of a deeper examination of healthcare
professionals’ digital literacy (also an element of the social aspect ) within the organizational
structure of HCDT. Although it is well recognized that this behavioral dimen sion is highly
relevant—since different levels of knowledge regarding digitalization and digital technologies,
as well as professionals’ age, may influence the speed and effectiveness of HCDT adoption —
this perspective was not analyzed in depth. Accordingly , future research is encouraged to
investigate these effects and related strategies, exploring differences across levels of digital
literacy, particularly within the context of interactions among the microfoundations of operating
routines. Furthermore, con sidering studies on professionals' resistance, work overload and
continuing education, as well as strategies to address this issue, represents an opportunity for
structural advancement.
Additionally, another limitation relates to the fact that the organizational structur e
proposed for HCDT does not focus on the implementation of a single specific technology —
such as artificial intelligence, which is currently a prominent topic —but rather on the
managerial organization required for the implementation of digital technology packages. In this
context, the study also does not examine in depth the security mechanisms associated with these
technologies, especially in the case of artificial intelligence and other emerging digital
solutions. The scope of the thesis is centered on the organizational and managerial structuring
necessary to enable the adoption of such technology packages, rather than on a detailed
technical analysis of how these technologies function or their security mechanisms.
Consequently, this delimitation opens avenues for future research to explore these technical
aspects, thereby further enhancing the organizational structuring of HCDT.

186


Finally, it is important to highlight that the organizational structure model developed in
this thesis ha s not been implemented in practice, which currently represents a limitation.
Therefore, it opens opportunities for implementation and, consequently, for analysis of its
application. Furthermore, considering the response time associated with organizational
structuring, strategies, resources , and technologies allocated to HCDT in healthcare systems,
future research may investigate the returns on investment and the associated costs of different
management models. Such an approach may help explain the nuances, as well as the advantages
and disadvantages, of different organizational structuring models for HCDT.
